phases.goal: An honest read on where the project actually stands, plus the vision, the driver and the game that every later decision gets filtered through.
phases.intro: Your brand is the movie and your music is the soundtrack. Before you touch a mood board or a content calendar, you need to know which level you are operating at, which of the eight failure patterns are currently costing you, and what you are actually building toward. Answer these honestly — the diagnostic answers stay private, the vision answers go in the book.

q.label: What is your artist name?
q.help: Exactly as you want it written everywhere — capitalisation, spacing, any stylisation. This is the name on the cover of your brand book.
q.eg: Mau P (formerly Maurice West)

q.label: Your legal name and the city you're based in.
q.help: Labels need the person behind the project and your market. Your city also determines your home-room strategy later in Phase 5.

q.label: Contact details — email, phone, and management if you have any.
q.help: One reliable email you actually check. If you have no manager, write 'Direct — no management' rather than leaving it blank; it tells a label exactly who to talk to.

q.label: Your links — Spotify, Apple, SoundCloud, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, website.
q.help: One per line, full URLs. A label will click every one of these within a minute of opening your document, so make sure each lands somewhere current.

q.label: Your project in one line, as you'd say it to a stranger.
q.help: Write this now, before you know the answer. You'll rewrite it properly as your elevator pitch in Phase 1 — this first version is the benchmark you measure that against. Keep it under 25 words.

items.h: You already make music. You have essentially no audience. Before you touch a content calendar, a mood board, or a release plan, you need three things: the model this playbook runs on, an honest read on where you are, and the order of operations.

1. The Core Operating Thesis: Your Project Is a Movie

Every framework on this channel drafts off one metaphor: your brand is the movie, your music is the soundtrack. Posts are scenes. Eras are chapters. Campaigns are story blocks. Visual identity is the cinematography. Your archetype is the main character, your plot is the script, your "brand foes" are the antagonists. A brand that's just music with no story is "a soundtrack with no movie."

Brand vs. marketing vs. music

What it is Answers When
Music The soundtrack "What does this sound like?" Continuously, inside a defined sonic sandbox
Brand The movie: story, POV, mission, rules, beliefs, archetype, plot, visual language "Who is this, what's it about, why care?" First
Marketing Distribution, awareness, campaigns, platforms, press, word of mouth "How do the right people find out?" After brand — and worth roughly half your total effort

Many artists have a great brand and great music and no marketing plan at all. "If you build it they will come" is called a lie outright: in 20 years and thousands of artists, Chris says he has never met an artist who likes marketing.

Why brand comes before content — four mechanisms

1. The classifier. You post, the platform shows it to a test group made mostly of non-followers chosen from your past posts. If your output is inconsistent in format, style, brand and story, the algorithm is confused, shows it to the wrong people, and the post dies after the test. "The algorithm isn't pushing your music, it's trying to match identities." Around 2024, platforms moved from discovery mode (rewarding volume, clips, randomness, trend chasing) to interest media, optimizing for identity, niche resonance, predictability, return viewership, and depth of connection. Variety now makes reach worse.

2. Decision cost. Definitional work up front kills thousands of downstream decisions. The filter shifts from "is this cool?" to "does this support the story we're telling right now?" On a collab shoot, one artist suggested fake acid tabs on their tongues; the other said within seconds, "No, sorry. It's not my brand." No drama, straight to the next shot.

3. Memory. Being unforgettable has almost nothing to do with talent. The brain encodes pattern breaks (Von Restorff effect), files what carries emotional intensity, and permanently stores what repeats over spaced time. You cannot repeat what you haven't defined.

4. Abundance. Roughly 100,000 songs are uploaded every day. If your identity is built on a style or genre, or is surface-level, AI is coming for you. Define your story, connect with like-minded humans, hold clarity on your POV, and you're bulletproof.

The claim: brand is now as important as the music

Channel estimates, flagged as experience-based: brand is 70–80% of a project's success; "point of view is 80% of it, the other 20% is sharing that point of view and finding like-minded people." When a brand feels broken, "the majority of the time it's not the music."

The evidence is a booking story. In the 2010s, submitting Hollywood offers, Chris put in an anniversary offer for Dada Life and, around the same time, one for another artist he'd been in the studio with — a talented producer with Beatport hits. Pound for pound in the studio they were equals. One offer was 20 times higher. Dada Life had time-coded visuals, champagne sprays, banana costumes, inside jokes, a world. The other had great DJ sets and no movie.

Mau P runs the same logic forward. Maurice West was a polished Dutch big-room hero-archetype artist playing big festivals with a small fanbase that "never felt organic." The rebrand was not a new logo — a new story and position in the culture — and he went from a few thousand a show to six figures plus. Chris Lake did it 2016–2017, keeping his name and grooming a new audience; it didn't catch immediately, but offers and revenue far surpassed the original brand.

Expanded Why this beats "just make better music": quality is necessary — the channel calls it table stakes, "a great soundtrack still needs the movie" — but at 100,000 daily uploads it is no longer the binding constraint. Attention and comprehension are. Improving something that isn't the bottleneck produces no throughput, which is why an artist can genuinely get better every year and grow zero.

2. The 5 Levels

Leveling up is not primarily about getting better at music or content. It's a video-game ladder, and the boss at every level is your own previous operating model.

LEVEL 1 — "Music for fun" → Part-time

Music is a love/addiction; you want to start earning from it.

  • Skills: the meta-skill of learning and retention. Diagnose your style — visual (tutorials), physical/kinesthetic, or mentor-led. Then "choose a thing and be semi-good at that thing."
  • Brand: minimum viable kit — a name, a vibe, a bio, a one-sheet/EPK, some visual.
  • Team: none, correctly. Restaurant logic: you'll own the restaurant one day, so it's good to have washed dishes and worked the bar.
  • Mindset: (1) Sacrifice — friend time, streaming, the summer blockbuster. Most people who never graduate fail here, on conviction. (2) Being okay with hearing no — send it out, expect silence, assess → analyze → learn → try again.

Do: the daily music journal — end of day, even two sentences, three fixed questions: What did you do with music today? What did you learn? What are you focused on right now? Then a volume play: send 500 messages to people who might care or hire you, or make 100 videos on one platform. Boss: your own lack of dedication and fear of no. Graduate when: other people pay — your first real coins, and decisions start mattering more.

LEVEL 2 — Part-time → Professional

A mini side business. Repeat invites, a few hundred to a few thousand people tied to your world.

  • Skills: a differentiating superpower — the music itself, marketing, ticket selling (reliably pulling hundreds, not a one-off), or networking. You're earning your 10,000 hours against it. Plus financial literacy: cash flow (not just how much but when), monthly burn, and separating look gigs from income gigs. "A lot of artists confuse busy with progress."
  • Brand: start forming what your movie is and telling that story — "at least the main elements of your initial brand in place."
  • Team: still you. Add help for anything pulling you out of your magic skill. This is usually where artists find their first manager — typically a friend who believes in the project.
  • Mindset: be open to help and scaling (pay collaborators or give equity against profits); hone the superpower by asking why is money actually coming in; eventually jump — never blindly with zero safety net.

Boss: the belief you must do everything yourself. Graduate when: you understand why money comes in, can predict it, and can sustain yourself without panicking monthly.

LEVEL 3 — Professional → Touring Artist

Out of the day job; multiple revenue streams; fans outside your home city. Early on you play small soft-ticket rooms or support a bigger act sharing their fans.

  • Skills: no more specialising — networking, music, content marketing, audience growth and buzz firing at once; you can no longer just be a great shooter. Demand signals and routing: "one strong city is worth more than five weak ones." Plus organization and time management, because touring makes complexity explode.
  • Brand: this is the moment, and where most artists get stuck. Two failure signatures: a viral breakout that produced nothing after (weak or confusing story), or a solid working pro who wants to tour with no audience to support it.
  • Team: the agent enters (10–20% of gross performance fee; a promoter offers $2,500, a good agent raises it). The business manager enters — vet extremely hard; it's "staggering" how many stories he's heard of business managers stealing. Plus specialists and consultants who audit and report.
  • Mindset: singular focus, kill shiny object syndrome. In his mid-20s Chris ran a concert promotion business, a clothing store, and freelance design while DJing funded his life; Valentino Khan told him "I only have Valentino Khan." If it doesn't serve the level-up, it falls down the totem pole. Also attention to state — social shows crowds and planes, not airport food and no sleep regimen.

None of these levels require a record label. They require leverage and an audience. Boss: your own confusing or absent story. Graduate when: people spend money to see you in cities you don't live in — not because it's free, not because you're the opener. "You're their artist."

LEVEL 4 — Touring Artist → Headliner

  • Skills: execution and speed (windows close fast). Expert time management — the calendar is a strategic asset; "what they don't do is often more important than what they do." Systems — the stall is "trying new outcomes on an old system." Leadership — motivate by communicating vision, not by grinding pros harder. Adapting to new mediums. Data analysis — content, money, performance.
  • Brand: master-level storyteller; every touchpoint from one world. Multi-month and multi-year calendars — think in arcs, eras, chapters, one movie inside a franchise. Brand moves to the top of the totem pole.
  • Team: major scaling, possibly dozens of people, plus roles dedicated to fans: "you're no longer borrowing audiences."
  • Mindset: doing everything yourself was your strength and is now a hindrance. "You're no longer just an artist. Now you're leading a company." Time becomes more valuable than money. Get a coach. Ask "Who do I need to become to operate at this level?"

Why artists stall: the transition runs against creative instincts. Jimmy Iovine forced himself to learn business so he could defend his creative ideas. Graduate when: your name alone anchors the show; "the system now bends around you." Next boss is legacy.

LEVEL 5 — Headliner → Icon

Top 1% → top 0.001%. Michael, LeBron, Kobe, Steph aren't great at one thing. To become an icon you must master multiple disciplines.**

  • Skills: master conductor (the whole orchestra), master listener, master visionary (vision documents and boards), master decision maker — and the Level 1 journal returns, same three questions.
  • Brand: bigger than you. Marvel framing — not writing Iron Man 1, looking at all the IP. Hard lines: "this is what we always do" / "this is what we never do."
  • Team: hundreds of people, multiple companies. "The way you used to make songs, now you make companies." Captain of a ship → admiral of a fleet. Inner circle: CEO, CCO, CFO, head of strategy, head of operations, head of day-to-day, head of legal and IP — and most of their decisions are about what not to do. Plus elite rotating contractors.
  • Mindset: never slip into other people's jobs. Bigger swings. Health as performance engineering — the headliners he knows are "insane biohackers": cold plunging, NAD, stem cells, meditation, clean food, little or no alcohol; body and mind tuned like an F1 car. Start this at any level. Shift from a results-driven mind to devotion around growth.

Graduate when: the work no longer depends on momentum — it endures, and your absence would leave a gap in the culture.

BONUS LEVEL — The Internal Climb

Icon-level artists frequently describe emptiness or sadness at the summit — nowhere left to go. The next mountain is internal, which is why many move into philanthropy: the feeling of chasing dreams and keeping promises to your younger self can be re-felt by helping others. It never ends — and you don't have to wait until icon level.

Two warnings on the ladder

Every level is a legitimate stopping point. Icon isn't inherently better; each level-up carries "life-altering sacrifice." And keep the day job as long as possible at part-time level — it buys creative freedom. Going all-in with no safety net produces desperate decisions that compromise the art, and compromised art fails, so you can move backwards. Mid-tier artists at $2K–$5K per show ask this most; quit only when music is your primary income and the driver of your quality of life.

3. The Four Quadrants as a Diagnostic

Skills / Brand / Team / Mindset apply identically at every level. Audit them separately, not as one vague feeling.

  • Skills — what you can actually do, not what you enjoy.
  • Brand — story, POV, look. A written document, or only a vibe in your head?
  • Team — who else is in the operation, and which roles are unfilled?
  • Mindset — the internal shift the next level requires.

Expanded Score them separately because they fail asymmetrically and the fixes differ in kind. Skills gaps close with reps and time. Brand gaps close with definitional work in a document — cheap and fast, which is why brand is the highest-leverage gap for someone at zero. Team gaps close by recruiting. Mindset gaps are slowest and masquerade as the other three: "I need better music" is very often a mindset gap wearing a skills costume. If three quadrants are strong and one is weak, the weak one is your ceiling, not your average.

4. The 8 Reasons Music Projects Fail to Grow

Fifteen years of the same eight fixable problems. Fixing even half leads to incredible results.

1. Inconsistent content offering. Why: talented artists just don't post. Cost: it isn't only fans watching — talent buyers deciding whether to book you check your socials: how often you post, what kind, what you're doing now. That influences buying decisions. Detect: look at your last 90 days — rhythm, or scatter? Have you ever thought "I haven't posted in a while, I should post something"? That thought should never occur. Fix: gym logic — one day a week gets one-day-a-week results. Calendar the making, not just the posting. "If it's on the calendar, it usually gets done."

2. No real identity or point of view. Why: fear of alienating people; trying to be everything to everyone — "you end up becoming nothing to no one." Detect: if your music is all good but sounds like several different producers, or your visuals are equally scattered, there's no through-line. Scattered output reads as confusing, not versatile. Fix: POV ≠ same genre. "You have a recipe, you have a way that you cook — it doesn't mean the food is the same." Audiences use art situationally; a defined flavor makes you findable.

3. Quality control. Why: two ends of one spectrum — perfectionists who never release, and (more common) knowing something isn't your best and putting it out anyway just to have something out. Detect: did your last release impact you? If not, it won't impact anyone. Fix: you must know what quality is before you can control it — study the greats and ask "Why does this move me?" Then the self-side: therapy, meditation, journaling, coaching. Note the tension with #1: consistency without quality accomplishes nothing, and quality without consistency also fails.

4. No real strategy or plan. Why: the arts default is "I'll create and throw it out there." Detect: do you have a written plan for the next 6–12 months? Fix: in music, your product is your songs — you need a growth and awareness strategy like any business. Named "step number one of actually growing it."

5. Unwillingness to try new things. Why: the way you cook and the business become habitual while the world changes. Detect: any platform or tool you dismiss on principle? Control was promoted with newspaper ads and a street team flyering windshields, then email blasts and SMS, then fully digital ad buys. Fix: adapting does not mean changing your POV — it means taking your art into the new world. AI is the live test: "it doesn't really matter where you land, but we're headed that way."

6. Discipline. Why: people enter music expecting a lax lifestyle. Detect: "How you do anything is how you do everything" — does anything in your operation feel loose? Fix: discipline becomes habit; habit produces results through volume. Lock one small habit for 6 months before stacking another — people get "discipline drunk" and end up with 30 morning-routine items before they can start.

7. No vision. Why: a rough dream instead of a clear picture, so you're productive with nothing to drive toward. Detect: can you state where this goes in 3 years, in a sentence? Fix: "Without a clear vision it's almost impossible to grow — because where would you grow to?" Named the number-one thing to define.

8. Wrong approach — you haven't named the game. Why: you copy an artist playing a different game. Detect: which are you playing — legacy, revenue, or awareness? Fix: name it, then align. A legacy-driven artist running an entrepreneurial playbook will struggle even with everything else in place.

5. The Self-Diagnostic

Score 1 if honestly true today, 0 if not. "Sort of" is a 0.

Foundations - [ ] I can state my vision in one sentence and it's written down. - [ ] I've named my game: legacy, revenue, or awareness. - [ ] I know my archetype (one dominant, two is normal at 80/20 or 70/30; three is the hard ceiling and the third is only a 5–10% spice). - [ ] I have 6–12 written beliefs starting "We believe" / "We do not believe." - [ ] I know my plot (one of Booker's seven) and can name the monster I'm facing. - [ ] I can deliver a 3-sentence, 30–60-second elevator pitch without stumbling.

Craft & output - [ ] I have a written signature-sound chart and I'm committed to it for a set period. - [ ] My last release genuinely impacted me. - [ ] I finish things — finishing is scheduled, not left over.

Look & assets - [ ] My visual language exists in a document a hired photographer could execute from. - [ ] I have a signature recognisable enough that someone could dress as me for Halloween. - [ ] Someone on my page for 60 seconds would understand what experience they're entering.

Marketing & audience - [ ] I have a content calendar with tentpoles and buckets, at least a month out. - [ ] I post on a describable rhythm, on one deliberately chosen primary platform. - [ ] I have at least one repeatable format — same setup, only the subject changes. - [ ] I can name why people follow me (attraction, aspiration, "we are the same," entertainment, status, novelty, guidance). - [ ] Someone else has spontaneously described my project to a third person, accurately.

Business & operations - [ ] Money has come in from music and I understand why and can roughly predict it. - [ ] I know my monthly burn and can separate look gigs from income gigs. - [ ] My week is time-blocked and I hit ~80% of it.

Score Read Start at
0–5 Level 1. Music exists; nothing else does. Move 1. Whole sequence in order. Do not skip to content.
6–10 Level 1→2. Craft is real, the movie doesn't exist. Move 1, fast through 1–3, depth on 4–8.
11–14 Level 2. Real skills and early money, incoherent packaging. Moves 3–4, then audit your look against 5–7.
15–17 Level 2/3 boundary. It all exists; consistency and marketing are the gap. Moves 8–10. Fix distribution before making anything new.
18–20 Level 3+. Past this section. Move 11 onward.

q.label: Run the 20-point self-diagnostic and write your score plus the specific items you scored 0 on.
q.help: Score 1 only if the statement is honestly true today; 'sort of' is a 0. The five blocks are Foundations (vision written, game named, archetype known, 6-12 written beliefs, plot and monster named, 30-60 second pitch), Craft & output, Look & assets, Marketing & audience, and Business & operations. List every zero — those are your work queue, not a judgement.
q.eg: Score 4/20. Zeros include: no written vision, no archetype, no belief system, no signature-sound chart, no content calendar.

q.label: Which of the 5 levels are you on right now, and what is the boss standing between you and the next one?
q.help: Level 1 is music-for-fun moving to part-time; Level 2 part-time to professional; Level 3 professional to touring artist; Level 4 touring artist to headliner; Level 5 headliner to icon. Each level has a named boss — at Level 1 it is your own lack of dedication and fear of hearing no, at Level 2 the belief you must do everything yourself, at Level 3 your own confusing or absent story. Name your level, your boss, and the graduation condition you are chasing.
q.eg: Level 1. Boss: fear of sending things out and getting silence. Graduate when someone pays me real money for music.

q.label: Score Skills, Brand, Team and Mindset separately out of 10, and name which one is your ceiling.
q.help: Audit them separately because they fail asymmetrically. Skills is what you can actually do, not what you enjoy. Brand is whether the story, POV and look exist in a written document or only as a vibe in your head. Team is who else is in the operation and which roles are unfilled. Mindset is the internal shift the next level demands. If three are strong and one is weak, the weak one is your ceiling, not your average — and 'I need better music' is very often a mindset gap wearing a skills costume.
q.eg: Skills 7, Brand 2, Team 1, Mindset 5. Brand is the ceiling — cheapest and fastest to fix, so it goes first.

q.label: Which of the 8 reasons music projects fail to grow are currently true of you, and what is the evidence?
q.help: The eight: inconsistent content offering, no real identity or POV, quality control, no real strategy or plan, unwillingness to try new things, discipline, no vision, and playing the wrong game. Use the detection questions — look at your last 90 days for rhythm or scatter; ask whether your last release genuinely impacted you; ask whether you have a written plan for the next 6-12 months. Fixing even half of these is stated to produce incredible results.
q.eg: Guilty of 1, 2, 4 and 7. Last 90 days: 6 posts, no pattern. No written plan. Cannot state where this goes in 3 years.

q.label: State your long-term vision for this project in one written sentence.
q.help: This is Move 1 and the playbook calls unclear vision the number-one thing to define: without a clear vision it is almost impossible to grow, because where would you grow to? It must be one sentence, written down, and specific enough that you could state where this goes in three years. Revisit it quarterly, but write it now.
q.eg: In three years this is a touring club project with a named community that sells out 500-cap rooms in five cities I do not live in.

q.label: Name the game you are playing: legacy, revenue, or awareness.
q.help: Failure reason 8 is copying an artist who is playing a different game. Pick one and say why. A legacy-driven artist running an entrepreneurial playbook will struggle even with everything else in place, so this choice decides which artists you should and should not be learning tactics from.
q.eg: Revenue. I want a sustainable business off a small committed audience, not a canonical body of work.

q.label: Which driver leads — creative endeavor, entrepreneurial, or community — and how will it settle real decisions?
q.help: It may be all three, but one must lead, and it becomes your decision system in both the build and growth phases. A creative-freedom-led artist protects legacy fiercely; a business-led artist takes the brand deal if the check is right because revenue funds bigger work. Write the driver plus one or two concrete decisions it would settle for you.
q.eg: Community leads. A brand deal that does not put something in the hands of the people who show up gets declined even if the check is good.

q.label: Finish the sentence: "I create to ___" — and write a private definition of success for this project regardless of what anyone thinks.
q.help: Two parts. The first line is short and goes in the book; the private success definition is for you only and should be specific enough that you would know if you hit it. The playbook pairs this with a two-self filter used on almost every decision: make sure 90-year-old you has no regrets and 12-year-old you would be proud.
q.eg: I create to make the room feel like the after-hours I never wanted to leave.

phases.goal: One story document containing the master concept, character, archetype, plot, foes, beliefs, point of view and elevator pitch that everything downstream drafts off.
phases.intro: None of this involves posting. You are writing the movie so that later you are not guessing at costumes. Budget two to four focused weeks and work in the given order — archetype after master concept, beliefs after archetype, plot checked against archetype. Get the order wrong and, in the playbook's words, it can poison the whole well.

items.h: You have music and essentially no audience. Everything here fixes that, and none of it involves posting. This is the foundation layer every later decision drafts off. Budget two to four focused weeks. The Cult Creatives spends months on this with paying clients — you can move faster as one person, but you can't skip it.

1. Why story comes first

Your brand is a movie, your music is the soundtrack. This metaphor runs through every video on the channel. Archetype = character. Plot = script. Foes = antagonists. Visual identity = cinematography. Each post = a scene. Each era = a chapter. You don't design costumes before you know what the movie is about. Without this you're "trying to make an incredible movie with no script."

The channel's actual reasoning:

  • The market is saturated and the bottleneck moved. Roughly 100,000 songs uploaded every day. Alba's verdict after 20 years: "your biggest problem now isn't your music, it's the attention and awareness around your brand." The music is usually fine; the story and the marketing of it is what's missing.
  • The algorithm is an identity-matching engine. Around 2024 platforms shifted from "discovery mode" (rewarding volume, clips, randomness, trend chasing) to the interest media era, optimizing for five things: identity, niche resonance, predictability, return viewership, depth of connection. Your post goes to a test group made mostly of non-followers, chosen from your past posts. Inconsistent format/style/brand/story confuses the classifier, it shows the post to the wrong people, and the post dies after the test. Variety now makes reach worse. "A confused audience doesn't grow."
  • Brand is most of the outcome. Alba's estimate — flagged as an estimate — is that brand is 70–80% of a project's success. Separately: "point of view is 80% of it. The other 20% is sharing that point of view and finding like-minded people."
  • The market prices it. As a talent buyer his venue's offers ranged $1,500 to $100K. He offered on Dada Life and, around the same time, on another producer who was pound-for-pound the same level in the studio with Beatport hits. One offer was 20 times higher. Dada Life had a movie — time-coded visuals, champagne, banana costumes, inside jokes, a world. The other had great DJ sets. Likewise Mau P went from a few thousand a show to six figures plus, not with a new logo but with "a new story and position in the culture."
  • AI makes it existential. Built on a style or genre, you're exposed. With a defined story, real connection and a clear POV, you're bulletproof. "AI doesn't live. AI doesn't suffer and AI doesn't evolve."

The order of operations

# Layer Why here
1 Master concept / controlling idea The one idea everything expresses
2 Archetype (character) Sets the motivation the audience reads
3 Beliefs + foes Beliefs draft off the archetype's motivation
4 Plot (script) Must line up with the archetype
5 Themes (3–5 pillars) The bridge from story to visuals
6 Elevator pitch + bio Compresses 1–5 into transmittable form
7 Sound / signature sound chart "Does the soundtrack match the movie?"
8 Visual identity, art direction "The brand should look how the story feels"
9 Content strategy, calendar, launch Scenes in an already-written movie

You build 1–6 now. Note item 7: the channel puts sound downstream of story. In the Mau P rebrand playbook, "define the sound" is step 6, after story and position, "so the soundtrack matches the movie." You already have music — you'll audit it against the story at the end.

2. The Master Concept

The master concept — also called the controlling idea, and in the systems videos the guiding idea — is the single idea holding everything together. Not a slogan, not a genre. One sentence of meaning every downstream choice gets tested against. Alba: "every part of the campaign is run through one controlling lens."

It nests: brand → era → chapter → campaign → post, each with its own guiding idea, each laddering up to the one above. A post with no guiding idea shouldn't exist. (A chapter is usually a 1–2 month song campaign.)

Worked examples. Mau P — freedom and attitude; rejecting formulas, trends, genre expectations; instinct-led, tied to your own history and taste; "chasing the freedom to freely create." Skrillex — freedom, creativity and cool; his rulebook is literally "the rules of cool." Fred Again — real life is where the art lies; intimacy can scale. The Joker in The Dark Knight — chaos versus order; he believes everyone thinks they're good until pressure proves otherwise, and that single idea drives every scene he's in. John Summit's "Comfort in Chaos" campaign — a guy in a 9-to-5 escaping into dance music; that one idea produced the album cover, tour flyer, DSP default images, banners, social posts, and the "Lights Go Out" video (bored in a warehouse office called Summit CPAs; accountants pulled into a trance, then an explosive dance party). Shapes named in the framing video: an avant-garde multi-medium creator; a relatable everyday hero climbing "the jagged mountain of the music industry"; a comedic artist; a rebel chasing freedom.

How to find yours

A — The Land. Step one of the Skrillex "House of Your Brand" build is deciding where to build. Test question: "If it were a movie, what genre is it?" — horror, thriller, arthouse, action, drama, rom-com, buddy comedy, sci-fi. On one large sketchpad page or a multi-column doc, list your favorite movies, shows, albums, songs, artists, books, and the stories you loved growing up. Read for patterns: darker and emotional? rebellion and freedom? comedy? Analyzing the list is analyzing your taste. It's directional — "You don't have to have it fully figured out."

B — Taste plus scars. List favorite things ever, then real-life moments of joy and real-life moments of pain, and pair them. "These life scars and happy memories define your taste" and create the themes that show up whether you plan them or not. The payoff heuristic: "The more specific around your taste you get, oddly, the more universal it becomes. The closer it is to you, the closer it gets to them."

C — The new recipe. Originality is a combination problem, not an invention problem: "all music is made or borrowed of stolen ingredients — new sounds come from new mixes." The canonical image is the Korean BBQ Mexican burrito truck off Wilshire — longest line on the block, run by a guy who's half Korean and half Hispanic, making something authentic to his own life: "this is good and this is good, but you haven't had it like this yet." Flosstradamus's Curt Cameruci runs the same filter as a verbal tic — "…but in a different way." Alba's gloss: different doesn't have to be good, different is interesting, and that's reason enough.

The niching formula: [brand archetype] + [genre fusion] + [world/space the brand lives in] + [feeling]. Its three examples: (1) not "DJ producer who makes dance music" → Everyman merging melodic house with yacht rock, living in a perpetual quest to vacation around the world — "brand is good times, soundtrack is good vibes"; (2) not "a band that makes metal" → Rebel/Hero blending modern metalcore with cinematic film score and apocalyptic world building, feels like surviving the end of the world; (3) not "typical female pop artist" → Lover/Rebel blending glossy pop with emotional honesty plus pop-punk, documenting life in real time, DIY, real and raw and rebellious.

Themes — the concept broken into pillars

Before art direction, the master concept becomes 3–5 brand themes — the shortest but most important section, because art direction, copy, voice and content all draft off them. Fred Again's five: Connection; Real & Raw (vs. synthetic/manufactured); Humanity; "Excitement lives in the moment"; Relatability.

The mechanism, via Guillermo del Toro's Frankenstein: theme is the life/death cycle → shape language becomes circles everywhere — circular lab, circular window, round chandelier, rounded cave doors, round electrical tubes, halo coils. Theme in, visual language out. Fred's deck also embeds three decision tests: "Does this feel human? Does this feel now? Does this feel real?"

Flavors, so you're not generic

A good archetype plus a good plot can still read as a stock character. Mau P's five flavors: (1) honoring the underground and his city, giving the rebel a purpose; (2) a sacred studio as home — his father, also in music, died when he was 18; he still produces in the studio his dad built and promised himself he'd hang a gold record next to his father's; (3) controlled chaos — choreographed, not a raw riot: revolutionary leader, not rioter; (4) quiet storm — calm in interviews and press shots, all energy saved for the stage; (5) reference the past, not the future — mine your original inspirations (deadmau5, Skrillex, early Tiësto, Disclosure) instead of chasing trend forecasts. Write five of your own.

q.label: Fill one page with your favorite movies, shows, albums, songs, artists, books and childhood stories — then answer: if your brand were a movie, what genre is it?
q.help: This is The Land, step one of the build, and it takes about 90 minutes. Write the favorites first, then read the page for patterns and circle them: darker and emotional, rebellion and freedom, comedy? Then name one genre — horror, thriller, arthouse, action, drama, rom-com, buddy comedy, sci-fi. Analyzing the list is analyzing your taste, and it is directional; you do not have to have it fully figured out.
q.eg: Patterns: heist films, 90s NY hip-hop, Michael Mann night cities. Genre call: neon-lit crime thriller.

q.label: Write your master concept — the one controlling idea everything expresses — in a single sentence.
q.help: Not a slogan and not a genre. One sentence of meaning that every downstream choice gets tested against, and that nests down through era, chapter, campaign and post. Pressure-test it by asking whether it could drive a music video, a flyer and a caption on its own. Mine it from your taste plus your scars: the more specific to you it gets, the more universal it becomes.
q.eg: Mau P: freedom and attitude, rejecting formulas and trends. Fred Again: real life is where the art lies, intimacy can scale.

items.h:
3. Jungian brand archetypes

Jung's hypothesis as Alba relays it: before we were globally connected we lived in small tribes, and although people are complex, other humans process us by sorting us into buckets based on perceived primary motivations. That guy is the funny one. That woman is our queen. That one's a warrior. That one's the shaman. Audiences do this to you in under two seconds whether you chose or not; choosing means the read is the one you intended. Audiences also self-identify with archetypes, so a clear one bonds deeper.

Definition: your archetype is the primary motivation of the main character in the movie the audience is watching — and you show that motivation 80–90% of the time. A creator is motivated to create, an outlaw is driven toward freedom, a controller toward status.

The full wheel

Traits, brand comps and music comps are from the source. Core motivation is my addition.

Archetype Traits (channel) Core motivation Expanded Brand comp Music comps given
Hero Courageous, determined, achievement-driven Prove worth through difficult, courageous action Nike James Hype; Martin Garrix; Taylor Swift; John Summit (current)
Rebel / Outlaw Disruptive, provocative, rule-breaking Freedom — Alba dislikes "outlaw," the drive is freedom not chaos Harley-Davidson Kanye; Travis Scott; Mau P; Skrillex (part); Rick Owens
Magician Mystical, transformative, visionary Transform reality; make the impossible happen Disney Prince
Creator Imaginative, expressive, innovative Make what didn't exist Adobe Fred again..; Tyler, The Creator (the name signals it); Pharrell; Childish Gambino; Anyma
Innocent Pure, optimistic, trustworthy Be good and happy; keep faith Dove Kacey Musgraves; Noodle (Gorillaz); Princess Leia
Sage Analyzes and spreads wisdom and guidance Understand the world and teach it Google Neighborhood Art Supply itself; Charlie Puth; Obi-Wan and Yoda
Explorer Adventurous, independent, restless Find out what's out there The North Face Diplo (started rebel); RÜFÜS DU SOL (part)
Ruler / Controller Authoritative, structured, status-driven Control, order, status, legacy Rolex Jay-Z; Beyoncé; Tiësto; Gesaffelstein; Rick Ross; Audemars Piguet
Lover Passion, emotion, sensuality Intimacy; be desired Chanel Usher
Caregiver Nurturing, supportive, selfless Protect and care for others American Red Cross Dr. Dre ("since he's a doctor"); RÜFÜS DU SOL (part)
Everyman / Everywoman Relatable, ordinary Belong; never be above the room Budweiser Post Malone; Fred again..; Dom Dolla; John Summit (original); Two Friends; Kylie Morgan; Carhartt
Jester Humor, play Live in the moment; make people laugh Old Spice Dillon Francis; Tenacious D; The Lonely Island

The rules

  • One dominant is ideal; always designate one.
  • Two is normal, three is the hard ceiling — "one dominant, two is normal, three is the hard ceiling — and the third only as a 5–10% spice." The masterclass and belief videos cap it at two; the Summit teardown says the agency "usually sticks to two, sometimes a third at only 5–10% spice."
  • Weight the split in percentages. Splits named: 70/30 (e.g. 70% hero / 30% rebel), 80/20, 90/10, and for three-ways 70/25/5 or 70/30/10. Three-way is "more advanced," not for beginners.
  • The archetype needs a corresponding story element to be legible. A hero needs something to be heroic against, so you must define villains and foes. A rebel needs something to rebel against. A lover needs someone to love.
  • Choose it after the master concept; place it first in the deck. It only means something once you know the story, but it drives every downstream art-direction decision.
  • You're directing a movie, not exhibiting every side of yourself. You don't show all of yourself to the barista, your grandparents, or the promoter.
  • Nothing syncs perfectly. On John Summit's brand Alba reads ~95% aligned; the outlier is the label name Experts Only, which reads ruler/elitist against an everyman brand (prior name Off The Grid leaned explorer; changed over a trademark issue).
  • Consistency warnings: an in-studio track breakdown "doesn't really do much to forward the story of an Explorer"; a rebel brand dancing in the studio to your latest song doesn't convey what you're rebelling against. Archetype governs content, not just aesthetics.

Every diagnosis the channel gave

Artist / brand Diagnosis Note
Fred again.. 70% Everyman / 30% Creator "Your friend Fred" plus obsessive maker → "artistry without distance." Masterclass gives the same read as 80/20, the creator 20% being the finger drumming
Skrillex Rebel + Creator "Uses creativity to find their own freedom"
Mau P 80% Rebel / 20% Ruler Rebels are freedom chasers; you needn't be dark or punk, and rebels can be the good guys. Ruler adds discipline, command, intentionality
Maurice West (his prior project) Hero Adjacent to Martin Garrix, Hardwell, W&W; polished Dutch big room
John Summit Everyman → Hero, live "Your fun friend John"; "one of us is making it." Shift evidence: fewer drunken rants, more workout and running content, giving his team flowers
Dom Dolla The cool everyman "If you bumped into him at a bar he'd be a great hang"
Calvin Harris Rebel → Hero (2010s) Precedent for Summit's move
Martin Garrix Everyman → Hero; elsewhere Hero Same maneuver
Melanie Martinez Creator / Rebel Signature split-hair look; intention from the start
Kylie Morgan Everywoman Country; family, kids, never above the audience
Justice Rebel + Creator Marshall stacks, leather jackets, the cross logo; started as graphic designers
RÜFÜS DU SOL Explorer + Caregiver Music is medicine; nature is a stage
Billie Eilish Creator + Rebel Vulnerability as strength; rejected the pop-star look
Diplo Explorer (started Rebel) Alba wasn't surprised he went country: "he hadn't been there yet"
Apple Creator now, Rebel originally David-and-Goliath vs. IBM and Hewlett-Packard
Anyma Creator Futurism, technology and art
Tiësto Ruler / Controller Lifestyle and status
Gesaffelstein Ruler / Controller Reads like a luxury house, not a DJ project
Steve Aoki Rebel / high-octane action Technology, rebellion, punk rock, stunts
ISOXO and KNOCK2 Rebel Celebrating outcasts
Two Friends Everyman Two lifelong best friends
Pharrell Creator Multi-medium, color, celebrating uniqueness
Dillon Francis Jester Sarcasm, ironic scenarios, recurring characters
Gorillaz cast 2D Everyman, Murdoc Rebel/Outlaw, Noodle Innocent Model for multi-character brands
Star Wars cast Luke Hero, Obi-Wan and Yoda Sage, Han Solo Rebel, Leia Innocent Han has funny lines but is not the comic relief
Chris Alba's own read Creator, with a Rebel streak; a hero story lights up his synapses Model for self-diagnosis

Non-music reads: Carhartt = Everyman, Aimé Leon Dore = Creator, Rick Owens = Rebel, Audemars Piguet = Ruler, Nike = Hero, Rolex = Ruler, Harley-Davidson = Rebel.

q.label: Write your character profile in five categories: archetype, strengths, flaws, beliefs, contradictions.
q.help: Hollywood starts with character, not plot or visuals — before anyone can care what is happening they need to care who it is happening to. Run the writers' idea dump first: who is this person, what do they want, what are they afraid of, what is broken inside them? If the brand is you, you are deciding which parts to show, not confessing everything. Keep it to one page.
q.eg: Strength: obsessive crate-digger. Flaw: goes silent for months. Contradiction: builds parties for strangers, hates small talk.

q.label: Name your archetype blend as a weighted percentage split, and name the story element it requires.
q.help: One dominant is ideal, two is normal, three is the hard ceiling with the third only 5-10% spice. Weight it: 70/30, 80/20, 90/10, or 70/25/5 for a three-way. Choose from Jung's twelve — Hero, Rebel, Magician, Creator, Innocent, Sage, Explorer, Ruler, Lover, Caregiver, Everyman, Jester — and then name the corresponding story element, because a hero needs something to be heroic against, a rebel needs something to rebel against, a lover needs someone to love. Add a short prose explainer clear enough that a hired contractor gets it instantly. You show this motivation 80-90% of the time.
q.eg: Fred Again is 70% Everyman / 30% Creator. Mau P is 80% Rebel / 20% Ruler. Skrillex is Rebel plus Creator.

q.label: Decide now: is this brand-led or person-led, and write the consequence of that choice.
q.help: You either play the brand or you play the man, woman or group. Person-led means your likeness on everything, close to a reality show — Taylor Swift, Steve Aoki, Dillon Francis, John Summit, Fisher, Dom Dolla. Brand-led means fans may not know what you look like — Gorillaz, Anyma, Eric Prydz, MF DOOM, Excision. This is a deck page in its own right (Fred's page 3: does the likeness lead, or do the visuals lead?) because it decides your entire photography plan.
q.eg: Person-led. My face leads, which means press photos and candid capture matter more than illustration or a mask.

items.h:
4. The Plot

Plot — not vibe, not aesthetics — is load-bearing. Most artists have a rough sense of their story; the difference at the top is knowing the exact structure and applying it daily.

Five reasons plot works: (1) Pattern craving — the mind is genetically wired to find patterns, tied to survival. (2) Tension and curiosity — once a loop opens you're primally wired to see it close; the cliffhanger that holds you through the ad break. (3) Emotional engagement. (4) Comfort and cognitive load — recognized structure is cheaper to process, and a confusing story loses people who would have loved the art but won't spend the effort decoding it. (5) Identification and reflection — when someone sees themselves, or who they aspire to be, the bond is categorically different from casual listening.

Christopher Booker's Seven Basic Plots

Booker spent about 30 years on mythology, biblical stories, Shakespeare, plays and Hollywood films and produced a roughly 800-page book (~700 in one telling) concluding there are only seven. Alba calls it the Bible of plot structure.

1. Overcoming the Monster — the monster can be literal, metaphorical or symbolic: fear, oppression, inner demons, an industry. Call to action / threat → initial defeat leading to preparation → confrontation → near defeat, lowest point → victory, transformed. A Quiet Place: aliens hunt by sound; the Abbott family survives in silence. Preparation is barefoot walking, sign language, sound devices, the mother's pregnancy as a ticking clock, a previously lost child setting stakes. Confrontation is labor. Near defeat is the father's sacrifice. Victory is the daughter's hearing aid weakening the creature.

2. Rags to Riches — greatness can be wealth, fame, power, love, or inner fulfillment. Rags → call to rise → initial success → crisis / fall from grace → redemption and growth → earned, lasting success. Cinderella (servant → fairy godmother → the ball → magic wears off at midnight → stays kind and true → marries the prince); Harry Potter (cupboard under the stairs → Hogwarts letter → becomes noticed → the dangers of being known → fights back and matures → defeats his enemies).

3. The Quest — call to the quest → journey begins, often with companions → trials and temptations → final ordeal → goal achieved → return home changed. The Fellowship of the Ring.

4. Voyage and Return — leave the familiar, enter the unfamiliar, face threats, return changed. Best structure for never-before-seen universes; pairs naturally with the Explorer. Call / entering the other world → initial fascination → challenge arises → nightmare or crisis → escape and return, wiser. Alice in Wonderland.

5. Comedy — Alba deliberately skips the structure. The brand is built on jokes, skits, characters and punchlines. Pairs with the Jester.

6. Tragedy — also skipped structurally. Themes become tragic: self-destruction, emotional detachment, judgment from society, mental health struggles; in visual art, anxiety, death, lost love, isolation, madness.

7. Rebirth — hero falls under a shadow — emotional (depression, arrogance, bitterness), physical (captivity, sickness) or supernatural (a curse) → threat worsens, more isolated or corrupted → the dark threat seems to win → miraculous redemption, sometimes sparked by another's love or sacrifice → renewal in a new vibrant state. Joker: Arthur Fleck trapped by poverty, mental illness, a dehumanizing society; symbolically dies when he kills for the first time; his rebirth is twisted — he embraces the persona, is finally free, and is reborn as a symbol of chaos rather than a hero.

Plot diagnoses given

Lady Gaga — Overcoming the Monster (rejection as "too weird, not marketable"; her plus the Little Monsters vs. the industry and social norms). Taylor Swift — Overcoming the Monster / Hero, with media, fame and bullies as villains. Mau P — Overcoming the Monster: "He doesn't join the system. He defines what's cool within it." Post Malone — Rags to Riches (Texas, little money, Guitar Hero, bedroom recordings on free software; recently named a new mountain: inner peace). Eminem — Rags to Riches. Gary Vee — Rags to Riches with a declared endgame: buying the New York Jets. J. Cole — Rags to Riches. John Summit — Rags to Riches, a Cinderella story where "the audience feels like they win the more John wins." Childish Gambino — The Quest, and a Creator brand; wants to do anything, like Prince or Bowie. Porter Robinson — The Quest, inward through depression and creative rediscovery. Skrillex — Quest + Overcoming the Monster; album literally called Quest for Fire, monster = industry, genre stigma, gatekeeping. Fred Again — Quest (dominant) + Voyage and Return (subplot). Gorillaz — Voyage and Return. Diplo — Voyage and Return, reality-based. Daft Punk's Discovery and Pink Floyd's The Wall — Voyage and Return. Dillon Francis, Tenacious D, The Lonely Island — Comedy. Linkin Park, The Weeknd, Nine Inch Nails, Kurt Cobain, Juice WRLD — Tragedy. Edvard Munch's "The Scream" — visual-art tragedy. Britney Spears post-conservatorship — Rebirth. Demi Lovato — Rebirth via addiction and sobriety, made an explicit recurring part of the narrative. Illenium — Rebirth + Tragedy; the logo is a phoenix, albums Ashes, Awake, Ascend. Dom Dolla — Rags to Riches meets Overcoming the Monster: local DJ to global headliner, defending against the noise and mediocrity of the typical EDM scene with higher-standard taste as the weapon. The Weeknd — Rags to Riches + Tragedy. Mixed-plot films: The Dark Knight = monster + tragedy; Everything Everywhere All at Once = voyage and return + comedy + rebirth; Barbie = voyage and return + comedy.

Rules for using plot

  • Mix if you want, but one must lead.
  • Do not script the climax or ending. That's years away, or never. Define the monster, the calling, and the current phase.
  • Check the plot against the archetype. Stay consistent — don't deviate from the main challenge.
  • Re-seed the setup constantly. New people land mid-plot, possibly in the confrontation phase with no idea what the fight is. Schedule recurring content re-establishing the monster.
  • Plot drives content strategy and can direct the music — "the soundtrack for your brand's movie."
  • Interviews are a plot-setup tool — "a great tool for storytelling and plot setup," citing Gaga narrating her rejection phase and Donald Glover setting an entire universe in three sentences.
  • When the hero wins, the story becomes boring. Summit's original plot resolved; the answer is a new story and an evolved character. New harder challenges + new villains = continued brand interest and growth.

Turning your biography into a plot

The Hollywood six-step build bridges real life to script: Character → Setting → Conflict → Logline → Visual identity → Transformation. Four are story work you do now.

Character. Hollywood starts with character, not plot or visuals: "before you can care about what's happening, you need to care about who it's happening to." Run the writers' idea dump: Who is this person? What do they want? What are they afraid of? What's broken inside of them? If the brand is you, you're deciding which parts to show. Deliverable: a character profile in five categories — archetype, strengths, flaws, beliefs, contradictions.

Setting. Where does the story live? What environments recur? A specific city or region? What tone? How does it play against the character? Heat and La La Land are the same city shaped for different narratives. Music: RÜFÜS DU SOL's deserts and sunsets; Bad Bunny's beaches, streets, Caribbean color and ties to Puerto Rico — "the setting makes the audience hear the music differently." Budget objection pre-answered: Lutezi Music shoots in New Orleans on buses, in vintage stores, on street corners, in burger shops, and has earned millions of impressions. Then narrow: region → city → neighborhood → venue type. "A future city → Tokyo → western Tokyo near Shinjuku or Shibuya." "A New York perspective → Brooklyn → bodegas, coffee shops, laundromats."

Conflict. The one-line spine: "A character wants something, but something is in the way." Artists historically run brands "more like documentarians than storytellers"; the smart ones find conflict in their own weaknesses. Eminem — lyrical precision and fearless honesty vs. anger, addiction, self-destruction: can he control the chaos without losing the edge that made him great? Kanye — visionary confidence vs. ego, impulsiveness, public self-sabotage: misunderstood genius or his own worst enemy? (He knows the audience splits; that's part of the appeal.) Billie Eilish — vulnerability and intimate world-building vs. anxiety and fear of being consumed by fame: how do you stay soft in a world that wants to eat you alive? Taylor Swift — narrative mastery and relatability vs. sensitivity to criticism and hyper-control: can she evolve without losing what defined her? Deliverable: ongoing tension in four buckets — internal, external, industry, personal.

Transformation. No one watches a story where nothing changes. Where are you now? Where are you going? What's the change? Think in short arcs and long arcs, like TV. Each era is a chapter and each chapter cues a progression forward. You hold the audience with "where does the story go next?" Gwen Stefani (punk rebel → matured, refined), Rihanna ("the people's princess" → confident ruler), Miley Cyrus, Olivia Rodrigo.

Universe rules. Define what is and isn't possible before any story happens — the Star Wars method. The Force, interstellar travel, light speed, a Galactic Empire ruling with an iron fist were set before characters, which is why endless spinoffs still feel like Star Wars. It applies to reality-format brands too. Dillon Francis's comedy universe has explicit rules: a piñata can talk without the audience hearing it but Dillon can hear it; DJ Hanzel and Dillon Francis can be two different real people in the same place at the same time — permitted "in the name of comedy."

Brand-led or person-led. "You either play the brand or you play the man, woman, or group." Person-led: your likeness on everything, close to a reality show — Taylor Swift, Steve Aoki, Dillon Francis, John Summit, Fisher, Dom Dolla. Brand-led: fans may not know what you look like — Gorillaz, Anyma, MF DOOM, Eric Prydz, Excision. Decide now.

q.label: Pick your lead plot from Booker's seven, plus a subplot only if one genuinely exists.
q.help: The seven: overcoming the monster, rags to riches, the quest, voyage and return, comedy, tragedy, rebirth. Mixing is allowed but one must lead, and it has to line up with your archetype — voyage and return pairs naturally with the Explorer, comedy with the Jester. Worked reads: Mau P is overcoming the monster, Fred Again is Quest dominant with Voyage and Return as subplot, Dom Dolla is rags to riches meeting overcoming the monster, Illenium is rebirth plus tragedy.
q.eg: Lead: overcoming the monster. Subplot: rags to riches. Same shape Skrillex runs on Quest for Fire.

q.label: Define your monster, your calling, and the phase of the story you are in right now — and do not write the ending.
q.help: The rule is explicit: do not script the climax or the ending, that is years away or never. Define the monster (it can be literal, metaphorical or symbolic — fear, oppression, inner demons, an industry), the calling that pulled you in, and which phase you are currently in: call to action, preparation, confrontation, near-defeat, or victory. Then plan to re-seed the setup constantly, because new people land mid-plot with no idea what the fight is.
q.eg: Monster: a scene that rewards trend-chasing over taste. Calling: the first warehouse night that made me quit my band. Phase: preparation.

q.label: Map your ongoing tension in four buckets — internal, external, industry, personal — then write the one-line spine.
q.help: The spine format is fixed: "A character wants ______, but ______ is in the way." The smart artists find conflict in their own weaknesses rather than running the brand like a documentary. Models: Eminem is lyrical precision versus anger and self-destruction; Billie Eilish is intimate world-building versus fear of being consumed by fame; Kanye is visionary confidence versus ego and self-sabotage.
q.eg: Internal: perfectionism. External: no audience. Industry: gatekept lineups. Personal: a day job that eats the evenings.

q.label: Where are you now, where is the story going, and what is the change? Write the next short arc and the long arc.
q.help: No one watches a story where nothing changes, and when the hero wins the story gets boring. Think in short arcs and long arcs like TV — each era is a chapter and each chapter cues a progression forward, and you hold the audience with 'where does the story go next?' Precedents: John Summit mid-transition Everyman to Hero, Calvin Harris Rebel to Hero, Gwen Stefani punk rebel to refined, Rihanna people's princess to confident ruler.
q.eg: Now: unknown local with a defined sound. Next chapter: the first out-of-town rooms. Long arc: outsider becomes the one setting the standard.

q.label: Narrow your setting from region to city to neighborhood to venue type, then write the rules of your universe.
q.help: Setting makes the audience hear the music differently — RUFUS DU SOL's deserts and sunsets, Bad Bunny's Puerto Rican beaches and streets. Narrow it the way the playbook does: 'a future city, then Tokyo, then western Tokyo near Shinjuku or Shibuya'; 'a New York perspective, then Brooklyn, then bodegas, coffee shops, laundromats.' Then define what is and is not possible before any story happens — the Star Wars method, where the Force, light speed and the Empire were set before characters. Budget is not an excuse: Lutezi Music shoots New Orleans buses, vintage stores, street corners and burger shops for millions of impressions.
q.eg: Region: US Midwest. City: Detroit. Neighborhood: Eastern Market at 4am. Venues: 200-cap basements, never a festival main stage.

items.h:
5. The Belief System

Beliefs convert a casual liker into someone who adopts your brand as identity — "I like this" → "I am this." Alba argues the belief system matters more than the product; without it even a hit decays and "the eyes and ears you earn will slowly float away." The unlocking question: "If your brand was a cult, what would be the beliefs that united everyone who followed it?" The belief system is the flag — an army won't just follow it, they'll carry it.

The psychology

Need to Belong Theory — Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary, 1990s: the drive to form strong lasting relationships is as fundamental a need as hunger or thirst. It explains all group formation. In survival-era conditions exclusion meant death, so rejection registers with genuine intensity and acceptance reads as a safety signal — we will survive. Measured harms of non-belonging: higher depression and anxiety, shorter lifespan; widows and widowers dying within months of a spouse; health collapse shortly after retirement from lost purpose.

Point of conversion / initiation. Entry requires a transformative ritual that signals commitment and sets a hard in/out boundary: gang initiations, fraternity and sorority pledge week, Army boot camp, country club applications that also require sponsorship by an existing member. For brands: buying your first product, first ticket, or first piece of merch. "Boot camp turns civilians into soldiers." Earned status accumulates as stripes — Alba likens Taylor Swift show counts to army stripes.

In-group / out-group. Insider logic: they don't believe what we believe. Which is why step one is the enemy.

The seven-step process

1 — Define the enemy (method below).

2 — Define the archetype. Beliefs draft off the archetype's motivation and wording. Max two recommended, 80/20; three at 70/30/10 is "more advanced."

3 — Mine deep personal beliefs: the Five Billboards. Five billboards in five world locations, contractually up for 500 years, one phrase each — encouragement for future generations that reveals your point of view. Seven sample outputs: Make things and share things. Freedom is all there is, chase it with every breath. Life is hard, might as well laugh through it. Do the right thing no matter the cost. There's so much unexplored, go further. Believe in the unseen power of the universe. If everyone wears white, put on black. Contradictions are fine and expected. (A single-billboard variant in the framing video works as an archetype finder: whether your phrase reads as a hero's inspiration, a rebel's freedom, a relatable underdog, or a dark tragedy tells you the archetype.)

4 — Ideate on beliefs. Unlimited statements, each starting "We believe…" or "We do not believe…" Think community-level, not personal-level. Ideate with friends, family, colleagues, other artists, or AI. Raw material offered: different is better; being ourselves; variety is beautiful; power in diversity; time to take down the old guard; art can save the world; not following trends; not needing to fit in; bigger isn't better; not bending to others' will; not quantity over quality; no genres or boxes in art.

5 — Edit down. Target 6–12 beliefs, each formatted as one-or-two-word concept header → belief sentence → short rationale. Edit questions: complete and well-rounded? emotional? redundancies? unique to you? can you publicly own these as community leader?

6 — Archetype check. Does each belief sound like your archetype's voice? Rebel beliefs center on freedom and creating your own path; creator beliefs on imagination, making and sharing.

7 — The six-part stress test.

Test Question Pass condition
Hater Does this create a clear enemy? "To have super fans you're also going to have super haters"
Unique Could this be pasted onto another brand? If yes, too generic. Named failure: "we believe in being authentic"
Time Will you stand by it in 5 years if trends change? Justice's "electronic music should hit as hard as a live band" passes — held ~20 years
Flip Reverse it. Could someone still choose you? If yes, too weak
T-shirt Throwaway slogan, or something you live by? Directional, not disqualifying — Aimé Leon Dore's heritage belief is a bad t-shirt but still ownable
Pledge Could a fan recite the set like a pledge and adopt it? Must hit emotional chords and be about humanity, not product or music

Worked belief systems

Fred Again — eight (Alba's inferred set): real life is where the art lies — the most powerful emotions come from real moments: conversations, voice notes, laughter, silence, mistakes; we do not believe perfection makes things better — chasing it removes the feeling, the cracks, the off-timing, the breath in the voice; music is made to connect people; we do not believe the artist should stand above the audience on a pedestal; the moment you're in right now is what it's all about; intimacy can scale — the more specific the feeling, the more people see themselves in it; we do not believe fans and artists are separate; we do not believe you need to be loud to be heard — "scale what's real."

Mau P (educated guess): the underground is a way of thinking, not a place; rules exist to be tested, twisted, broken; freedom doesn't come from playing safe; we do not believe in genres or boxes; the coolest thing you can be is yourself; express what you think is cool even if taboo; if everyone's wearing black, wear white; hard work plus authenticity builds your own kingdom; freedom above everything; energy in its most raw form.

John Summit (Everyman) — six: the party is the point; honesty is relatability; "we do not believe in fans, we believe in friends"; find the energy (moments over technical perfection); real humor disarms ego; music is a lifestyle, not a job.

Billie Eilish (Creator + Rebel) — six: vulnerability is strength; expression comes from internal not external; family and creative integrity first; youth has a voice; shadows can be alluring; bottle the bedroom and take it to the stage.

Justice (Rebel + Creator) — five: dance music can have teeth; rebellion is freedom; iconography creates connection; raw meets polish; mystique over exposure.

RÜFÜS DU SOL (Explorer + Caregiver) — five: music is medicine; togetherness is sacred; nature is a stage; light in darkness; authenticity over trend.

Outside music: Carhartt (Everyman, 7 — work ethic as identity, durability over trend, quality over efficiency, community, utility is beauty, respect for heritage, evolution without losing roots); Aimé Leon Dore (Creator, 5); Rick Owens (Rebel, 6); Audemars Piguet (Ruler, 6 — including "to break the rules you must first master them").

The rulebook variant

The Skrillex build calls this the Foundation — a rulebook used to settle every creative argument. His center is freedom, creativity and cool, so his rulebook is the rules of cool: (1) success is something you attract, not chase — build your own house and pull people in; (2) if everyone is headed one way, look the other direction — when everyone built huge LED walls and CGI he went basement-set, raw, human, intimate; (3) don't try to make hits, make music that joins the conversation and moves culture forward; (4) mix above-ground, underground and the in-between — the filter is "do I like it and does it feel cool"; (5) attach yourself to cool things and people, because collaborations set the room your brand sits in; (6) earning wisdom and developing technique is cool, be a student of the game; (7) be real — much of the music world is "facades built on sticks"; (8) be yourself, and make work meticulously for people who share your taste. Other centers named: Kendrick Lamar → the rules of truth; Metallica → the rules of power; Usher → the rules of love.

The Brand Foe Hierarchy

Humans bond fastest through shared belief or shared conflict, and what you stand against is more powerful than what you stand for. Independence Day: the second aliens attack, all inter-country fighting stops. Rank your enemies as a totem pole from big boss down — the Star Wars structure of the Empire, then the Emperor, then Darth Vader, then a general, then a stormtrooper.

HERO hierarchy, 6 (lowest) to 1 (big boss): 6. Haters and trolls — "fully stormtrooper vibes"; a well-built tribe handles these for you. 5. Not being seen / being overlooked — an idea, not a person; most people feel the world doesn't see who they really are. 4. Staying on the path — the distractions of the world; being pulled off the main mission. 3. The physical demands of the pursuit — burning the candle at both ends. 2. Time — American football has roughly 10 clocks (game clock, play clock, timeout clock, two-minute warning) all making time the antagonist; excellent hero-brand content. 1. The shadow self / the ego / your inner thoughts — the daily battle with the voices in your head.

REBEL hierarchy, 6 to 1: 6. Rule followers. 5. Fake people who edit themselves based on societal rules. 4. Dopamine culture — people addicted to endless content and autopilot existence, stuck in an invisible prison built for them. 3. The regulators — people who tell you who you're supposed to be, out of their own fear. 2. Self-censorship — "you versus you" through a rebel lens. 1. Established systems — corporate entities, gatekeepers, people in power controlling everyday people's freedom for their own gain.

Rules: enemies don't have to be people — superficiality, fake social-media lifestyles, bullies, corporate culture, the status quo, real musicianship vs. AI music, time itself, your own mind. Six is the worked example; never exceed 10. Never invent an enemy because it's good for the brand. All battles must come from one singular place. Then never deviate — express the same foes in varied forms.

Artist foe sets given: Rage Against the Machine (corporate greed, political corruption, government oppression, economic inequality, media manipulation, blind obedience, social injustice); John Summit (the over-serious world of dance culture, fake cool-guy energy, wasted potential, the corporate nine-to-five trap); Chappell Roan (shame around self-expression, conservative expectations, industry pressure to play it safe, people who judge you for being weird); Blackpink (limitations on women, being underestimated, industry control over identity); Jimmy Buffett (escaping corporate culture, the man, your boss, material obsession, the idea you're alive only to work); Anyma (digital disconnection, emotional numbness, artificial identities, living online, fear of technology replacing human soul).

Alba models it on himself: he makes videos on a Saturday because he stands against the big corporations, big tech companies and gatekeepers making it hard for artists to reach their audience — then asks whether you now feel a different bond than to "another guy on YouTube giving music marketing advice."

Core warning: don't be everything to everyone — "you end up becoming nothing to no one." Fear of alienating people is exactly why most artist brands are soft.

items.g: The enemy and the belief system

q.label: Write your Five Billboards: five phrases, one per billboard, in five locations around the world, contractually up for 500 years.
q.help: Each is one phrase of encouragement for future generations that reveals your point of view. Do not self-censor, and contradictions between them are fine and expected — this is mining, not editing. The sample outputs given: make things and share things; freedom is all there is, chase it with every breath; life is hard, might as well laugh through it; do the right thing no matter the cost; there is so much unexplored, go further; believe in the unseen power of the universe; if everyone wears white, put on black. These become the raw material for your beliefs.
q.eg: If everyone wears white, put on black.

q.label: Rank your brand foes as a hierarchy, from the stormtrooper at 6 up to the big boss at 1.
q.help: Six is the worked example and you must never exceed 10. Enemies do not have to be people — superficiality, fake social-media lifestyles, corporate culture, the status quo, dopamine culture, time itself, your own shadow self all qualify. Two rules: never invent an enemy because it would be good for the brand, and all the battles must come from one singular place. Worked sets: the Hero hierarchy runs haters and trolls, being overlooked, staying on the path, physical demands, time, and the shadow self at the top; John Summit's are the over-serious world of dance culture, fake cool-guy energy, wasted potential, and the corporate nine-to-five trap.
q.eg: 6. Trend-chasers. 5. Playlist-first thinking. 4. Distraction. 3. The nine-to-five. 2. Time. 1. My own self-censorship.

q.label: Write 6-12 beliefs, each starting "We believe" or "We do not believe," formatted as concept header, belief sentence, short rationale.
q.help: Ideate without limit first at community level, not personal level, then cut to 6-12. Each belief must sound like it came from your archetype's voice — rebel beliefs centre on freedom and building your own path, creator beliefs on imagination and making. Then run all six stress tests and rewrite or cut anything failing two: Hater (does it create a clear enemy?), Unique (could you paste it onto another brand? 'we believe in being authentic' is the named failure), Time (will you hold it in five years? Justice's 'electronic music should hit as hard as a live band' has held about 20), Flip (reverse it — if someone could still choose you, it is too weak), T-shirt, and Pledge (could a fan recite the set as their own?).
q.eg: John Summit's set includes "we do not believe in fans, we believe in friends." Fred Again's includes "intimacy can scale."

items.h:
6. Point of view and brand beliefs

Point of view is 80% of the game. The other 20% is sharing it and finding like-minded people.

A POV is not a genre. "You have a recipe, you have a way that you cook — it doesn't mean the food is the same." Make any genre; if you use the same ingredients there'll be a through-line. The greats jump genres and tempos but keep a consistent way of cooking, a similar perspective on process, and similar filters for when something is done. With a great artist, any piece of their work is instantly identifiable as theirs.

POV shows up in the decisions you repeat: what you align with, what you ignore, what you say yes to, what you turn down, your collaborators, your stage clothing, the clips you repost, your brand partners, the venues you play, and the trends you decline. "Taste is the brand."

How to write yours. Run the POV exercise — favorite things ever paired with real-life joy and real-life pain; those scars and memories define your taste and create the recurring themes that surface in your work, sometimes subconsciously. Make things for other versions of you — you now, teenage you, college you, childhood you (Alba wrote the AI video for his younger self). If you feel alone, make art about feeling alone for other people in that place.

Where POV comes from: experimentation, repetition and reflection. Make things, make more, share them, notice what makes you feel alive. When something you create hits you emotionally and feels true, you've tapped it — follow those threads until it becomes your fingerprint, shaping what you make, how you make it, and why you share it.

The fan-interview journal session. Interview yourself as though you were a fan. Ask: "What are the things we always do?" At icon level this hardens into two phrases used with real conviction: "this is what we always do" and "this is what we never do."

The five-year test: which of these, if I focused most of my attention on it for the next five years, could I compete and be one of the best in the world at?

Two warnings. Don't look at peers in your space for direction — mimicking is "a great way to get to the middle, absolutely the wrong method to get to the top"; when top artists see a bunch of people doing the same thing, that tells them where not to go. And run every idea through: "Is this me? Does this represent the things I care about?"

7. The Elevator Pitch

The compressed movie. Alba's framing: "what would be on the back of the DVD." Spec: three sentences or less, 30 to 60 seconds — the time you actually spend with someone in an elevator.

Template: "A __ kind of artist who _ is trying to but struggles with ___."

  • Dom Dolla — an Australian house artist bringing humor, groove and personality into club culture; trying to make dance music feel fun, human and culturally relevant again; struggles with balancing underground credibility against a global mainstream audience.
  • Leon Bridges — a soul artist channeling the sound and spirit of the past into modern music; trying to preserve authenticity and emotional depth in a fast, disposable music culture; struggles with maturing and evolving without losing the timeless identity that defined him.

The pitch library (all written through the archetype-plus-plot filter — use as tonal models). Taylor Swift — a relatable hero brand where the hero teaches the audience how to navigate love, heartbreak, challenge and bullies while ascending to the top of the music industry mountain. Eminem — a rags-to-riches story about a relatable rebel from Detroit who is free to say what he wants when he wants, bringing the audience into his experiences of celebrity. Fred again.. — an everyman brand built on authenticity, creativity and being real; he feels like your best friend from school who happens to be crushing it. ISOXO and KNOCK2 — two high-energy rebel brands focused on freedom of expression; the brand celebrates outcasts and incites positive rebellion at every turn; visual identity has an edge with undertones of nostalgia and rock/metal. Two Friends — an everyman brand about two lifelong best friends focused on relatability and fun; they bring you into their normal, authentic world where extraordinary moments happen. Anyma — a creator brand merging futurism, technology and art into remarkable experiences. Pharrell Williams — a multi-medium creator full of color and inspiration; celebrating uniqueness and embracing change across all touchpoints. Steve Aoki — a high-octane action-based experience where energy is king; technology, rebellion, punk rock and memorable stunts make it irresistible to thrill seekers. Gesaffelstein — a ruler/controller brand matching avant-garde electronic music with high-end elevated visuals; resembles an expensive luxury fashion brand more than a DJ-producer project. Martin Garrix — a hero brand where a pure heart, determination and an undying love of music drive the hero toward greatness. Dillon Francis — a relatable comedy brand using sarcasm, ironic scenarios and recurring characters. Mau P — born in the Netherlands, raised in the underground; while others polished to be scene-ready and on trend, he wrote his own rulebook; his presence is singular and confident without asking permission; he designs his own lane and makes the world adjust.

How to construct yours. (1) Write the template sentence ten times; keep the one that makes you slightly uncomfortable. (2) Convert it to a mini artist bio written as a story — one paragraph, filtered through archetype and plot. Hero + rags-to-riches means writing the humble past and the surge; rebel + overcoming-the-monster means positioning the character as rebelling against norms, seeking independence and creative freedom. (3) Apply the "extra sauce" / new recipe rule: balance a unique story with familiar references; don't straight-copy one successful artist, pull from multiple artists, modern and historical, and combine. "In the world of music, predictable equals boring." (4) Sanity-check against Blake Snyder's Save the Cat rule — tell me a story about a person who… I can identify with, I can learn from, I have a compelling reason to follow, I believe deserves to win, and whose stakes are primal and ring true. (5) Alba has a standing offer: post your pitch in the comments of the Hollywood video and he'll reply with honest feedback.

items.g: Point of view and the pitch

q.label: Write your point of view: your way of cooking, evidenced by the decisions you repeat and the trends you decline.
q.help: Point of view is 80% of the game; the other 20% is sharing it and finding like-minded people.
