A POV is not a genre — you have a recipe, you have a way that you cook, it does not mean the food is the same. Derive it by pairing your favorite things ever with real-life moments of joy and real-life moments of pain; those scars and memories create the themes that show up whether you plan them or not. Then evidence it with what you align with, what you ignore, what you say yes and no to, your collaborators, your venues, and specifically the trends you decline. Taste is the brand.
q.eg: Everything gets one imperfect human element left in — a room mic, a false start, a voice note. I decline any trend that requires a hook in the first five seconds.

q.label: Write your elevator pitch using the template: "A ___ kind of artist who ___ is trying to ___ but struggles with ___."
q.help: Spec is hard: three sentences or less, 30 to 60 seconds spoken. Write the template sentence ten times and keep the one that makes you slightly uncomfortable. Sanity-check with Save the Cat — tell me a story about a person I can identify with, learn from, have a compelling reason to follow, believe deserves to win, and whose stakes are primal.
q.eg: Dom Dolla: an Australian house artist bringing humor and groove into club culture, struggling to balance underground credibility against a mainstream audience.

q.label: Expand the pitch into a mini bio written as a story — one paragraph, the back of the DVD.
q.help: Filter it through your archetype and plot: hero plus rags-to-riches means writing the humble past and the surge; rebel plus overcoming-the-monster means positioning the character against the norms. Apply the extra sauce rule — balance a unique story with familiar references, and pull from multiple artists modern and historical rather than straight-copying one. In the world of music, predictable equals boring.
q.eg: Mau P: born in the Netherlands, raised in the underground; while others polished to be scene-ready, he wrote his own rulebook and makes the world adjust.

items.h:
8. Framing

Framing is "the borders around an idea" — the setup an idea sits inside, the frame around the painting. It determines how work is perceived, valued and felt, often more than the work's intrinsic quality.

The 2-second subconscious question sequence. Someone encountering your brand runs this in under two seconds, then decides yes or no: 1. What is it? 2. What's the story about? 3. What does it look like? 4. What does it mean for me? 5. How do I feel about it? 6. Do I care? 7. Does this meet any of my needs? 8. Am I interested in following the story? (The Fred playbook gives a compressed version: "What is this? Who is this? Do I care?") Every encounter is an at-bat — strike out enough times and they're off your brand permanently. Related benchmark: every fan, booker, label and playlist editor scans your digital world and decides in 60 seconds or less; Cult will sometimes spend half a year building a brand purely to be perfect for that scan.

Pre-framing is arriving already primed: existing IP, a known director, "based on a true story." It's why studios greenlight sequels. Nolan's Interstellar and Coogler's Sinners are original but pre-framed by director reputation. A new artist with an original project has the least pre-framing of anyone — that's you. The thought experiment: the same samurai-protects-a-gifted-child script set in modern Japan vs. the Star Wars universe. Identical story, radically different audience.

The strategic answer when you have none: stand on existing stages. Completely original first offerings struggle because there's no prior reference in the viewer's mind, so the brain files it under "this doesn't matter to us." Shorten the runway with an official remix, a bootleg, a sampled song, a cover, a release through a trusted label or channel with an existing audience, or attaching to reputable brands and individuals. Alba says this is the 0→100 path for about 90% of the big electronic artists he watched come up; introduce fully original works as your profile grows.

Other framing types: scarcity (limited drops; price reflects story and meaning, not production cost); value (retail environment, packaging, ritual — Gentle Monster, Apple, Tiffany); emotional (composition matched to emotional state — close is intimate, wide is distant, as in La La Land and The Notebook).

The evidence. Wine experiments: told one glass was $100 and one $10, subjects rated the "expensive" one better ~90% of the time; when both were secretly the same $10 wine they still preferred whichever was labeled expensive, and brain scans showed taste and experience regions lighting up more under the expensive framing — run on over 5,000 people, consistent results. Virgil Abloh's candle: the same dented candle is art in a white gallery and trash in a garage — "I could design the candle… or I could just design the room." Design the room, not the candle. Basquiat and Banksy: graffiti was vandalism, up to a year in prison in early-'80s New York; the same act framed as fine art put Basquiat in prestigious galleries, and the illegality itself became framing for coolness. Apple hides weights inside product boxes because the mind associates heavier with more valuable. Alice Cooper at Piccadilly Circus: two weeks out from a 10,000-capacity Wembley Arena show they had sold 50 tickets; manager Shep Gordon put a billboard of Alice Cooper nude with a snake on the side of a truck, sent it to the heart of Piccadilly Circus and paid the driver to break down and refuse to move even if arrested. Hours of gridlock, an arrest, wall-to-wall coverage — "Alice Cooper shuts down Piccadilly." Parents furious, kids thrilled, kids who missed the news heard it from friends. The show sold out.

Setting the room — the five elements. 1. Story and position — define the brand story first, before any visuals. Story sets the emotional tone and controlling idea. 2. Visual identity — the "mood board the audience lives inside": photography, video style, graphic design, language, colors, fonts, layouts. Must match the story. An avant-garde room feels avant-garde; an everyman brand should not be too polished; a rebel brand should look imperfect, like "stolen moments from the chaotic world." 3. Show presentation. Cheap, memorable ideas offered: request your setup on the floor in the center of the audience instead of on stage; bring a strobe and smoke machine both on foot pedals; monochromatic outfits matched to color-coded gear, White Stripes style. Also Johnny Cash at Folsom Prison — perfect rebel framing, with the prisoners' reactions deliberately left in the mix. 4. Daily content — where most people first find you, so it's the primary room. Must match the archetype. 5. Marketing and press — venue choice, showcase context, stunts, and scripted press talking points. Write key bullet points before every interview, podcast and radio spot; you won't hit them all, but you don't go in blind, and it should still feel candid.

Show frequency is framing too. Playing your city once a year makes it a special annual moment. Once a month or every couple of weeks kills urgency — "I'll catch them on the next one" — and lowers perceived value.

Self-check: What am I telling people with the room I've set? How is the story executed? Is the brand framed for value or relatability? What kind of room does the brand sit inside? How am I staging this for the audience?

9. Storytelling craft

Music audiences get the story sporadically, in snippets and scenes, so you need a system that stays coherent across fragments.

Structure Source Use for
Hook → Conflict → Climax Shareability video ("a three-act movie") Any social post
Setup → Curiosity → Tension → Payoff Algorithm video Short-form video
Hook → Lean-in → Story → Punchline Content video, "the universal short-form structure" Everything short

The lean-in opens the curiosity loop; the punchline closes it and delivers the shareable moment. Self-test: Would I stop and watch this? Would I be curious? Would I lean in and stay till the end? Would I engage with or share this?

Named techniques: - Curiosity loops — open one early, re-hook every 5 to 10 seconds in short form, delay the payoff to the very end. - No dead space, no filler. Cut anything that doesn't drive the story forward. - Write mini scripts for shareable concepts — each is a mini scene in your greater movie. - Interviews as plot setup; re-establish the monster on a schedule for people arriving mid-plot. - Rewatchability, four methods: hidden elements and Easter eggs that only surface on rewatch; a twist ending that makes people rewatch through a new lens; moving fast enough that watch two or three reveals more (but not so fast it's incomprehensible); engineering a seamless loop with no clear stop point. - Remix the concepts — take one good concept and layer three elements: shot in a unique or atypical way (not necessarily expensive), built to spark conversation via a polarizing opinion, and built with a shareability trigger. - "Remarkable" means "to remark about," not "incredible." Will people remark on this, will they tell someone? - The Purple Cow. Driving past a field of ordinary cows you don't stop; a purple one makes you pull over and tell everyone. Build purple-cow moments so people become your marketing vehicle. - The shareable content formula, in order: shareable concept + what makes this authentic to my brand + how can I present this creatively versus how I saw it done before. The concept goes first — research what's getting shares, filter through your brand, then push further than the version you saw. - Uniqueness has a neurological basis — the Von Restorff effect: items that break surrounding patterns are remembered better. Early on, being better isn't enough; you need to be different. "You don't need to reinvent the wheel, just remix it. The brain will remember both the shape and the surprise." - Every touch point is a scene — social posts, your bio, music videos, interviews, song themes and titles, EP skits, interludes.

10. The worked exercise set

In order. Roughly 15–20 hours total, spread over two to four weeks so ideas settle.

1. The Land — 90 min. Output: one favorites page + a one-line genre call. Favorites (movies, shows, albums, songs, artists, books, childhood stories) on one page; read for patterns; answer if my brand were a movie, what genre is it? - [ ] Favorites page — [ ] Patterns circled — [ ] Genre named

2. Taste, joy and pain — 90 min. Output: three-column POV inventory (favorite things ever / real-life joy / real-life pain), then the themes across all three. - [ ] Three columns — [ ] 3–5 recurring themes

3. Idea dump / character profile — 60 min. Output: one-page profile. Who is this person? What do they want? What are they afraid of? What's broken inside of them? - [ ] Archetype — [ ] Strengths — [ ] Flaws — [ ] Beliefs — [ ] Contradictions

4. Archetype selection — 60 min. Output: weighted split + prose explainer clear enough that a contractor gets it instantly. - [ ] Dominant — [ ] Percentages — [ ] Explainer — [ ] Corresponding story element (hero → villain, rebel → what you rebel against, lover → what you love)

5. Five Billboards — 45 min. Output: five phrases, 500-year horizon, no self-censoring. - [ ] Five phrases written

6. Brand foe hierarchy — 60 min. Output: 6 ranked foes (max 10), stormtrooper to big boss. - [ ] Six ranked — [ ] Nothing invented for convenience — [ ] Singular origin confirmed

7. Belief ideation and edit — 2 hrs, two sittings. Sitting one: unlimited "We believe / We do not believe" at community level. Sitting two: cut and format as header + sentence + rationale. - [ ] Ideation — [ ] Cut to 6–12 — [ ] Formatted — [ ] Archetype check — [ ] All six stress tests passed

8. Plot selection — 60 min. Pick your lead plot; subplot only if genuinely there. Answer What or who is the monster? What is the calling? What phase am I in? How could I show defeat, or confrontation? Do not write an ending. - [ ] Lead plot (+ subplot) — [ ] Monster / calling / phase — [ ] Coherent with archetype

9. Conflict map — 45 min. Four buckets (internal, external, industry, personal) then "A character wants __, but ____ is in the way." - [ ] Four buckets — [ ] One-line spine

10. Setting and universe rules — 60 min. Narrow region → city → neighborhood → venue types; define what can and can't happen; decide brand-led vs. person-led. - [ ] Setting narrowed — [ ] Universe rules — [ ] Brand-led vs. person-led decided

11. Master concept and themes — 60 min. - [ ] Master concept in one sentence — [ ] 3–5 themes — [ ] Three decision-test questions

12. Five flavors — 45 min. Mau P's model: a purpose for the rebellion, a sacred place, a texture, a demeanor, a reference direction. - [ ] Five flavors written

13. Elevator pitch and bio — 90 min. Ten passes on the template; keep one; expand to a DVD-back paragraph; cap at three sentences / 30–60 seconds. - [ ] Ten passes — [ ] Pitch under three sentences — [ ] Bio paragraph — [ ] Save the Cat five-reason check — [ ] Posted for feedback (optional)

14. Framing audit — 45 min. Run the eight 2-second questions against your own profiles as a stranger, then plan the five framing elements. - [ ] Eight questions answered as a stranger — [ ] Five elements sketched — [ ] Pre-framing plan chosen (which existing stage you stand on first)

15. Cohesion pass — the last 5% — 2 hrs. Great producers obsess over the last 5% of a song while intermediate producers call it good at 90%. Lay every artifact side by side: does the plot line up with the archetype? Do the beliefs sound like the archetype's voice? Do the foes come from one place? Does the soundtrack match the movie — does your existing music belong to this story, and what needs adding or shelving? - [ ] Everything cross-checked — [ ] Music audited — [ ] Document dated and locked

11. What "done" looks like

One document — your story document or brand bible. If you can hand it to a photographer, videographer, designer, manager, promoter or label and they can act without asking a question, it's done.

Two commitment rules before Phase 2. Lock into this concept for at least 12 to 24 months — Alba's floor for a new brand is 24 months before you judge it, because artists routinely abandon a concept after weeks and never learn what was possible. And run the pre-mortem: write out every scenario that might make you quit, pause, or abandon this identity. Naming the problem solves half of it — your brain starts pre-solving. Planning for the storm before it comes.

The last word from the source, and the reason the weeks are worth it: "The brand should look how the story feels." You can't start the next phase until this one exists.

phases.goal: A defensible place to stand: a position a stranger can reconstruct, one superpower category you commit to, five flavors that stop you being a generic version of your archetype, and a locked sonic sandbox.
phases.intro: The order here is explicit — story, then position, then uniqueness, then superpower, then sound. Sound comes last on purpose so the soundtrack matches the movie instead of the movie being retrofitted to whatever you happened to make. You already have music; you will audit it against this chart rather than letting it dictate the chart.

items.h:
Phase 1 gave you the character. Phase 2 turns that into a place to stand in a real market: a point of view, one thing you can win on, the specific flavors that stop you being a generic version of your own archetype, and the sonic sandbox the music lives in.

Alba's order is explicit — story → position → uniqueness → superpower → sound. Story first, because a position is a point of view held by a specific character. Uniqueness before superpower, because the superpower is how you broadcast the unique thing. Sound last, so the soundtrack matches the movie instead of the movie being retrofitted to whatever you happened to make.

His framing for why all of it matters: "point of view is 80% of it. The other 20% is sharing that point of view and finding like-minded people."

1. Positioning

What a position is

Not your logo, genre or bio. It's your point of view — what your brand stands for and believes — plus where you sit in the culture relative to everyone else. A logo is only a symbol; it has to stand for a set of beliefs, not just music.

Expanded Three answers a stranger should be able to reconstruct fast: What does this person believe? Who is it for? What room are they standing in?

Position vs. story

Story Position
Answers What's happening, to whom, what's in the way What we believe, what we stand against, where we sit
Made of Archetype + plot + conflict + arc Beliefs + elevator pitch + world alignment
Behaviour Moves constantly — "where does the story go next?" Holds still for years; the fixed lens
Failure Boring, confusing, nothing changes Soft, generic, could be pasted onto anyone

Expanded Story is why they watch episode to episode. Position is why they'd wear the shirt.

The method (Mau P playbook, Step 3) — four deliverables

a) The belief system. Single sentences that all start "We believe…" or "We do not believe…" Target 6–12. Each gets a one-or-two-word concept header, the sentence, then a short rationale. The seven-step build:

  1. Define the enemy first — who's outside, who "doesn't believe what we believe."
  2. Confirm the archetype — beliefs draft off its motivation and vocabulary (rebel beliefs centre on freedom and building your own path; creator beliefs on imagination and making).
  3. Mine deep personal beliefs with the Five Billboards exercise: five billboards in five world locations, contractually up for 500 years, one phrase each, encouragement for future generations. His samples: make things and share things; freedom is all there is, chase it with every breath; life is hard, might as well laugh through it; do the right thing no matter the cost; there's so much unexplored, go further; believe in the unseen power of the universe; if everyone wears white, put on black. Contradictions are fine.
  4. Ideate without limit — community-level, not personal-level.
  5. Edit to 6–12. Is it complete and well-rounded? Emotional? Redundant? Unique to you? Can you own it publicly as a community leader?
  6. Archetype check — does each belief sound like it came from your archetype's voice?
  7. The six-part stress test: Hater (does it create a clear opposition? "To have super fans you're also going to have super haters"); Unique (could you paste it onto another brand? "We believe in being authentic" is the named failure); Time (will you hold it in 5 years? Justice's "electronic music should hit as hard as a live band" passes at ~20 years); Flip (reverse it — if someone could still choose you for the reverse, it's too weak); T-shirt (livable and ownable, or throwaway slogan? Directional only — Aimé Leon Dore's heritage belief is a bad t-shirt but still ownable); Pledge (could a fan recite the set like a pledge and adopt it? Is it about the human experience rather than product?).

Mau P's set, as Alba's educated guess: the underground is a way of thinking, not a place; rules exist to be tested, twisted, broken; freedom doesn't come from playing safe; we do not believe in genres or boxes; the coolest thing you can be is yourself; express what you think is cool even if taboo — fashion, music, art, speech, how you show up; if everyone's wearing black, wear white; hard work plus authenticity builds your own kingdom; freedom over everything; energy in its most raw form.

b) The elevator pitch — "the summary on the back of the DVD." Spec: three sentences or less, 30–60 seconds. Template: "A ___ kind of artist who ___ is trying to ___ but struggles with ___."

Worked examples: - Dom Dolla — an Australian house artist bringing humor, groove and personality into club culture; trying to make dance music feel fun, human and culturally relevant again; struggles with balancing underground credibility against a global mainstream audience. - Leon Bridges — a soul artist channeling the sound and spirit of the past into modern music; trying to preserve authenticity and emotional depth in a fast, disposable culture; struggles with evolving without losing the timeless identity that defined him. - Mau P — born in the Netherlands, raised in the underground; while others polished to be "scene-ready and on trend," he wrote his own rulebook; he designs his own lane and makes the world adjust. - ISOxo and Knock2 — high-energy rebel brands focused on freedom of expression, celebrating outcasts; visual identity with an edge and undertones of nostalgia and rock/metal. - Gesaffelstein — a ruler/controller brand matching avant-garde electronic music with high-end visuals; resembles a luxury fashion house more than a DJ project. - Two Friends — an everyman brand about two lifelong best friends focused on relatability and fun. - Fred again.. — an everyman brand built on authenticity, creativity and being real; your best friend from school who happens to be crushing it.

Then convert it into a short bio written as a story, filtered through plot and archetype: hero + rags-to-riches means writing the humble past and the surge; rebel + overcoming the monster means positioning the character against norms. (Alba's standing offer: post your pitch in his comments and he gives feedback.)

c) World and cultural alignment. Your position is partly determined by who you stand next to. Mau P's rebrand moved him out of big room (Hardwell, W&W, Garrix adjacency) into "the world of cool" — Defected Records, Repopulate Mars, Fisher, Chris Lake circles. His skill didn't change; how the industry read him did. Skrillex's Rule of Cool #5 says it from the artist side: attach yourself to cool things and people, avoid uncool ones — collaborations set the room you sit in. His recent alignments (Fred again.., ISOxo, Nitepunk) are "the next wave of cool"; his early ones were Zedd, Porter Robinson, A$AP Rocky, Valentino Khan.

Alba's umbrella term is framing — "the borders around an idea," or Virgil Abloh's design the room, not the candle (the same dented candle is art in a white gallery, trash in a garage). Evidence: wine studies on over 5,000 people where subjects preferred the glass labeled $100 over $10 ~90% of the time — including when both were secretly the same $10 wine, with brain scans showing taste regions lighting up more; Tesla putting stores in malls near Louis Vuitton and Gucci where someone who could afford a $100,000 Model S already hangs out; Basquiat and Banksy making work that was vandalism (up to a year in prison in early-'80s New York) until framed as fine art.

Expanded With no audience, world alignment is your cheapest lever. You can't buy a fanbase, but you choose which labels you submit to, which artists you ask for features, which night you play, whose visual language you borrow. Those choices are your position for two years.

d) Who the position is for. The persona exercise Cult nicknames "who's coming over for dinner" — who you're having over determines what you cook. First: who do you want in the community and why? Then per persona: what kind of person are they, what interests, who are their cultural icons, what cultures are they part of, what jobs, where are they from, what do they struggle with, what do they care about? The payoff: you can guess where they are, then go there.

The test the position has to pass

On contact, in under two seconds, they run: What is it? What's the story about? What does it look like? What does it mean for me? How do I feel about it? Do I care? Does this meet any of my needs? Am I interested in following the story? Every encounter is "an at-bat" — strike out enough and they're gone permanently.

q.label: Write your positioning statement: what you believe, who it is for, and what room you are standing in.
q.help: A position is not your logo, genre or bio — it is your point of view plus where you sit in the culture relative to everyone else. Where story moves constantly, position holds still for years and is the fixed lens. A stranger should be able to reconstruct three things fast: what does this person believe, who is it for, what room are they standing in. Test the failure mode: if it is soft, generic, or could be pasted onto anyone, rewrite it.
q.eg: Gesaffelstein reads as a luxury fashion house, not a DJ project. That is a position, not a genre.

q.label: Build your world alignment map: 10 labels, 10 artists, 5 venues or nights and 5 brands you want to sit next to — and 10 you deliberately do not.
q.help: Your position is partly determined by who you stand next to. Mau P's rebrand moved him out of big room adjacency (Hardwell, W&W, Garrix) and into the world of cool — Defected, Repopulate Mars, Fisher, Chris Lake; his skill did not change, how the industry read him did. Skrillex's Rule of Cool #5 says the same from the artist side: attach yourself to cool things and people, because collaborations set the room your brand sits in. With no audience this is your cheapest lever — you cannot buy a fanbase, but you choose which labels you submit to and whose night you play.
q.eg: Adjacent to: Defected, Repopulate Mars, a specific 300-cap Tuesday night. Not adjacent to: big-room festival packages, EDM meme pages.

q.label: Write 2-3 audience personas using the "who's coming over for dinner" questions, each ending with a line on where they actually are.
q.help: Who you are having over determines what you cook. Start with who you want in the community and why, then per persona answer: what kind of person are they, what interests, who are their cultural icons, what cultures are they part of, what jobs, where are they from, what do they struggle with, what do they care about. The payoff is the last line — you can guess where they are and then go there. Go to the people, do not make the people come to you.
q.eg: 28, line cook, into skate media and Japanese city pop, resents being sold to. Where they are: a specific record shop, two Discords, one weekly night.

items.h:
2. The Superpower

The top 1% aren't good at everything. They identified one superpower, picked the matching lane for growth and community building, and committed for years without switching. "Lane" means growth strategy, not sound.

The formula: find your superpower + define the mission + map the path / understand the game you're playing + stay committed all the way through the climb. Remove one piece and they probably don't make it.

The Mountain Climb, 5 steps: (1) pack for the trip — audit strengths; (2) define the path — pick one bucket; (3) set your compass — mission, strategy, and filling gaps with other killers; (4) the climb — don't switch paths; (5) commit to the summit.

Finding yours — the four strength exercises

From "brand therapy," Cult's discovery process. They exist to route around the humility trap: "what do I have that others don't?" is nearly impossible for a humble artist to answer head-on.

  1. "What do you do when no one's watching?" Journal. What do you spend free, no-pressure time on? What do you enjoy researching, learning about, getting lost in? Where do you find joy even alone?
  2. Ask ~10 of your closest adult friends why they're still friends with you. They answer with history and loyalty first. Acknowledge it, then push — "minus obligation and history, why are we still friends?" The real answer emerges and is usually consistent across all ten. Alba and his wife Lindsay both ran this while reading Simon Sinek's Find Your Why. His result: he inspires people and gets them fired up to build — "guide type energy." Hers: warmth, "like being in a cozy blanket next to a fire."
  3. Review your wins, without being hard on yourself. Where have you succeeded? What got traction? Wins can be tiny — friends made, adapting after a move, surviving what got thrown at you, how a song performed, a few viral posts.
  4. "When do you feel powerful?" Not confident, not arrogant — the flow moments where time disappears.

Then a third party reads all four and looks for patterns where you're strong by your own account and others'. Their job is to "define what's already there."

The five competitive categories — pick ONE

1. Content Machine. Content, advertising, presence. Masters of awareness who understand advertising strategy and operate in volume. May not be for everyone, but easily find the people they are for. Examples: Steve Aoki and James Hype, who document their lives "almost like a reality show" at staggering monthly volume — Alba has worked with both and confirms it's a deliberate edge. Aoki understood press, moments and narrative from the early days: "a relentless mind for marketing." Hype's fans call him "La Machina," the machine; he'll tell you he built it over years of tiny efforts, filming on a few hours of sleep across three days of shows. Expanded Cheapest in money, most expensive in weekly hours.

2. Music. The music is undeniable; even haters acknowledge it. "10,000 hours will happily become 50,000 hours." The obsession with getting better is the superpower. Examples: Skrillex, Calvin Harris; from the Mau P list, Zedd, Illenium, Max Styler. Analogy: Michael Jordan "did all of his talking on the court" — Nike, McDonald's and the trophies followed from being undeniably great at the core thing.

3. Performance and creativity. Visuals, scale, spectacle; out-create the field and present music memorably. Hard to look away even if the music isn't for you. Examples: Anyma — hyper-detailed characters and scenes at the Sphere, "even my mom knows what he's doing"; Lady Gaga — visuals and performance notable from the start; Eric Prydz.

4. Relatability and likability. Millions of strangers feel they know you and that you'd be a good hang. Not manufactured — the tactic is putting your authentic self out consistently. Examples: Dom Dolla ("would be such a good hang"), Fred Again ("your best friend from school who's crushing"), John Summit.

5. The Cool Factor. Taste and curation. You see details others can't; obsessed with quality and with the motivations of the people making things; protective of the cool. Fans "wear being a fan like a piece of clothing that makes them feel cool." Examples: Black Coffee, Justice, and from the Mau P list Cloonee, Skrillex, Boys Noize, ISOxo, Knock2. Mau P is category 5.

Picking the one you can win

  • The 5-year test: "Which of these, if I focused most of my attention for the next 5 years, could I compete and be one of the best in the world at?"
  • Dominance analogy: like being right- or left-hand dominant. You use both. Hone in on what's strongest and most frequently present.
  • Choosing a lane doesn't mean the others are bad — it tells you where the focus goes.
  • Fill the gaps with other killers. Alba says this change "changed everything" for him personally.

Expanded Cross-check against archetype and actual resources. A Cool Factor lane with no taste library collapses; a Performance lane with no budget and no visual collaborator is a two-year detour.

Testing whether you truly have it

  • Both-sided evidence. Does it appear in your own accounts (1, 3, 4) and in your friends' (2)? One-sided evidence is a preference, not a superpower.
  • Convergence across the ten friends after you push past the history answer.
  • The unwatched check — do you already do it unpaid and unprompted? If no, you picked an aspiration.
  • Best in the world, not "good."
  • The daily question, run a month: "Did I do one small thing today that served my strengths or superpowers?" One post, one beat, one follow-up email. "Low effort but high alignment." If you can't find one most days, the lane is wrong.

Committing

  • Anchoring habits tied to moments, not schedules — your calendar and time zones move. Performance superpower: a three-line journal entry after every show. Music superpower: learn one new music thing on every flight or long drive. "It's not about when or where, it's about the context triggers and the habit."
  • Seasonal focus: month 1 content (shooting, editing, planning), month 2 music (collaborations, mixing, releases), month 3 performance (set design, rehearsals, new transitions). Small things continue; the season forces planning instead of reacting.
  • External accountability. Team-based guilt beats self-motivation; with no team, use a friend or family member. "There needs to be some sort of stakes or consequences."
  • The stakes game (Tony Robbins). To lose 30 lbs by a date: take a nude photo, give it to a friend who would actually do it, instruct them to post it if you fail. Brains move toward pleasure and away from pain — set up a game that forces you to win.

Warnings

The biggest mistake is starting over every time it gets hard — new plan, new name, new brand, new sound. "The climb gets hardest right before the elevation kicks in." Path-switchers circle just above base camp and end where they started. "Commitment is the attribute that wins every time" — bad music, a scattered brand and non-connecting content can all be taught; a lack of commitment can't. "Hard work beats talent when talent stops working." Just getting focus clarity puts you ahead of 90% of artists.

q.label: Journal the three solo strength exercises: what you do when no one is watching, your wins however small, and when you feel powerful.
q.help: These exist to route around the humility trap, because 'what do I have that others don't' is nearly impossible to answer head-on. What do you spend free, no-pressure time on and enjoy getting lost in? Where have you succeeded — wins can be tiny, like friends made or adapting after a move. And 'powerful' means the flow states where time disappears, not confident or arrogant. Keep these as three separate journal entries; they get read together later.
q.eg: Unwatched: I rip and catalogue records nobody asked for. Powerful: the last 40 minutes of a set when I stop planning.

q.label: Ask about 10 of your closest adult friends why they are still friends with you, push past the first answer, and write what came back.
q.help: They will answer with history and loyalty first. Acknowledge that, then push: "minus obligation and history, why are we still friends?" The real answer usually emerges and is consistent across all ten — that convergence is the evidence. Alba's own result was that he inspires people and gets them fired up to build, 'guide type energy'; his wife's was warmth, 'like being in a cozy blanket next to a fire.' Allow several days for replies.
q.eg: Eight of ten used a version of the same word: you make people feel like they are allowed to try something.
q.time: 1 hr plus a week of replies

q.label: Pick ONE of the five competitive categories and justify it with both-sided evidence and your 5-year answer.
q.help: The five: Content Machine (Steve Aoki, James Hype), Music (Skrillex, Calvin Harris, Zedd), Performance and Creativity (Anyma, Lady Gaga, Eric Prydz), Relatability and Likability (Dom Dolla, Fred Again, John Summit), Cool Factor (Black Coffee, Justice, Cloonee, ISOxo, Knock2, Mau P). The test is: which of these, if I focused most of my attention on it for the next five years, could I compete and be one of the best in the world at? It must appear in your own journals AND in the friend survey — one-sided evidence is a preference, not a superpower. Focus clarity alone puts you ahead of 90% of artists.
q.eg: Category 5, the Cool Factor — same lane as Mau P. Evidence: curation shows in both my own entries and eight of ten friend answers.

q.label: Set your commitment mechanics: one anchoring habit tied to a recurring moment, a seasonal focus rotation, the daily alignment question, and one accountability person with real stakes.
q.help: Anchor habits to moments, not schedules, because your calendar and time zones move — a three-line journal entry after every show, or learning one new music thing on every flight or long drive. Seasonal focus rotates: month 1 content, month 2 music, month 3 performance. Run the daily question for a month: did I do one small thing today that served my strengths or superpowers? If you cannot find one most days, the lane is wrong. And there must be actual stakes — money, time or embarrassment — held by someone who would really follow through.
q.eg: Habit: three lines after every gig. Stakes: $200 to my accountability partner for every missed monthly release.

items.h:
3. Uniqueness — the "flavors" model

A great story and position mean little if the brand isn't unique and memorable. A generic rebel is still generic. Flavors are what you add to the story soup.

Mau P's five flavors

  1. Honoring the underground and his city — gives the rebel a purpose instead of free-floating defiance.
  2. A sacred studio as home — his father, also in music, died when he was 18; he still produces in the studio his dad built and promised himself he'd hang a gold record next to his father's.
  3. Controlled chaos — choreographed, not raw riot. Revolutionary leader, not rioter.
  4. Quiet storm — calm and cool in interviews, press shots and videos; all energy saved for the stage. "The cool is in the restraint."
  5. Reference the past, not the future — mine original inspirations (deadmau5, Skrillex, early Tiësto, Disclosure) instead of chasing trend forecasts.

Expanded The shape is a usable template: one flavor from place, one from biography, one from behavior, one from demeanor, one from reference set.

The "extra sauce" rule

Balance a unique brand story with familiar references. Don't straight-copy one successful artist in your niche — pull from multiple artists, modern and historical, and combine into a new recipe. "In the world of music, predictable equals boring."

Underneath it is memory science. The Von Restorff effect: distinctive items that break surrounding patterns are remembered better, because we evolved to notice the tiger in the grass — "being better than someone isn't enough, you need to be different." But the break must sit inside enough familiarity to be processed: predictive coding theory says the brain loves patterns and rewards surprise. "You don't need to reinvent the wheel, just remix it. The brain will remember both the shape and the surprise." And the claim that makes it workable: "all music is made or borrowed of stolen ingredients." Originality is a combination problem, not an invention problem.

The three warnings

Don't be derivative. Mimicking peers is "a great way to get to the middle… absolutely the wrong method to get to the top." Mid-tier artists are "great mimics" who get "caught chasing the dragon." Top artists don't look to peers for direction — when they see everyone doing the same thing, that tells them where not to go. Don't take visual references from other artists. Be careful with Pinterest: not bad, but so widely used that everyone ends up homogenized. And don't jump on the bandwagon or copy another artist's sound or look — the brain only flags pattern breaks.

Don't be everything all at once. This is its own rebrand trigger: a project built purely on experimentation reads as incoherent, "throwing stuff at the wall." "Everything to everyone… nothing to no one." If the music is all good but sounds like a bunch of different producers made it, there's no identity. Note the distinction: point of view ≠ same genre. "You have a recipe, you have a way that you cook — it doesn't mean the food is the same."

Don't copy a peer's approach without checking the game. A legacy-driven artist running an entrepreneurial artist's playbook struggles even with everything else in place. Name your game: body of work / legacy, revenue, or awareness.

q.label: Write your five flavors — one from place, one from biography, one from behavior, one from demeanor, one from your reference set — with a sentence of evidence each.
q.help: A great archetype and plot can still read as a stock character; a generic rebel is still generic. Mau P's five are the template: honoring the underground and his city (place), the sacred studio his late father built (biography), controlled chaos — revolutionary leader not rioter (behavior), the quiet storm, calm in press with all energy saved for the stage (demeanor), and reference the past not the future, mining deadmau5, Skrillex, early Tiesto and Disclosure rather than trend forecasts. Each of yours needs real evidence, not an aspiration.
q.eg: Demeanor: never explain a record. Reference set: 1998-2004 only, nothing from the current cycle.

q.label: List 10 artists in your lane and the 5 things they all do — then name your 3 deliberate pattern breaks.
q.help: The questions to run: what does everyone expect from the genre world I am in, and how, while still being myself, can I break that expectation and create a mental flag? What is missing from this scene? The gap-seeking strategy appears four times in the source — Alba picking the uncontested french horn instead of competing for trumpet and guitar, A-Trak asking what the polar opposite of the cheesy prevailing DJ typography would be, Skrillex going basement-set and human when everyone built LED walls and CGI. Different does not have to be good; different is interesting, and that is reason enough.
q.eg: All ten do: track ID teasers, studio breakdowns, festival recaps, black-and-white press shots, hype captions. My break: no recap content, ever.

items.h:
4. Signature Sound

The sonic sandbox

What it is: a fixed set of sonic ingredients laid out "on a metaphorical counter." You may make anything — but only with what's on the counter. Different genres, tempos and styles still sound like you because the same ingredients recur. Alba calls these positive constraints. "You can only use what you've laid out on the counter."

Why you have to manufacture it: fifty years ago constraints were automatic — a band had a handful of instruments, one drum kit, a synth or two, one vocalist's range, each player's ceiling. That produced a sound by default. Modern production lets you make literally anything, so deciding what to make is now the hard part.

How wide: wide enough that a pop song, a club song and a downtempo song all fit — Skrillex makes pop, dubstep, hip-hop and UKG records that all sound like Skrillex — and narrow enough that a listener can name the through-line. The tighter one-season version from the systems video: one narrow guiding idea for six months (his example: "mixing deep house with hip hop and lo-fi"), with 6 completed originals or remixes as the target and everything outside it left unfinished.

Boundaries are set by the chart in Step 4 below. And it must match the movie — sound is defined after story and position specifically so the soundtrack fits. The wrong soundtrack kills a good movie; if you can't name a good movie with a bad soundtrack, that's because misaligned movies are simply forgettable.

The diagnostic: five things your favorite artists share

A cohesive body of work; art that resonates enough that you come back curious what's next; uniqueness against everything else out there; a brand that lines up with the music; and music that's genuinely great.

The seven-step process

1. List your favorite things from your past. A real journaling session: favorite all-time songs; favorite albums; what your parents listened to; what played in the house growing up; favorite life memories with music behind them; favorite experiences at shows or with music videos.

2. List what currently inspires you. Current favorite songs and albums; what you return to; who inspires you; who's pushing boundaries; who you'd see live right now.

3. Mix and match. Both lists are ingredients. Which apply to what you're doing now? Lay those on the counter and write as many candidate recipes as you can — you're not making anything yet. Alba's own: 80s new wave from his parents' house plus 80s synth soundtracks (The NeverEnding Story, Scarface, Giorgio Moroder-type material), plus his current love of Rezz's mid-tempo sound design — recipe: "Rezz mid-tempo bass meets 80s synthwave soundtrack meets 80s new wave."

4. Build the chart. This is the sandbox; each category locks for the duration.

Category Decide
Drums Hip-hop, organic/live, electronic; swung or on the grid. Build one drum kit and use it the whole process.
Synths 80s new-wave? Organic? Real analog only? Soft synths with organic instruments? Pick a few and stay in them.
Vocals Featured or not, and what kind. Alba's own period was male falsetto only, so he hunted ranges like Michael Jackson, The Weeknd, Prince, Phil Collins. Strong, aggressive, pretty, ethereal, street, anthemic, soulful/R&B?
Key Major or minor; which keys; target feeling — sad, uplifting, powerful, triumphant, cool.
Subject matter What songs are about. Look for through-lines in your Step 1 list; if most of what you love is about love, that's a legitimate well.
Samples Not one-shots — clips from other songs. Will you sample, and in what style?
Instrumentation Synthetic vs. organic. E.g. Serum-style sound design plus orchestral instruments.
Sound design Your sonic signature: bass-music-inspired? Early-2000s hip-hop synths? Soft synths through analog guitar pedals? Vocal samples as synths or lead lines?
Arrangement Structure, which can cut across genre — techno with pop arrangements, a rap record arranged like alt rock. Target ~90% consistency across the season.
Catch-all Anything unifying not covered above.

5. Commit to a body of work around a specific point of view. In time (this sound for 12–24 months) or volume (40–50 demos; you may release only 10–20%, but you commit to making 50).

6. Make the art. If a strong off-brief pull hits, make it, then triage: fits this season, or shelved. The tactical version: spend 15–20 minutes getting the bare bones down, save it, return to the plan. Self-talk technique: "yes, but not right now" — talk to your creative brain like a child ("we can write that after the six-month run, if we still love it"). "Saying yes, but not right now is better than saying no."

7. Rinse and repeat after the commitment ends. Expect five or six full cycles before a breakthrough.

The chart as a decision filter

It answers questions for you — this cover, this remix, this collab? Check the chart. You've "saved your brain from thousands of hours of computing."

Run it backwards on artists you love:

  • Calvin Harris (2011–2013): "We Found Love" (Rihanna, 2011), "I Need Your Love" (Ellie Goulding), 18 Months with "How Deep Is Your Love" (Disciples), "Feel So Close," "Sweet Nothing" (Florence Welch). Club drums; dance synths; soulful powerful vocals; all minor keys; always love and passion; no recognizable song samples; organic plus synthetic instrumentation; sound design lifted from the dance underground and simplified for a broad audience; arrangements that were pop, not dance.
  • Purple Disco Machine: club plus disco drums; 70s-analog-inspired synths; indie-meets-pop vocals with disco inspiration; majority minor keys; love, dancing, nostalgia, self-expression; light sample use; modern disco with strings, guitar, funk bass, 70s drum-machine sounds; dance arrangements.
  • Kanye West: hip-hop drums; analog-inspired synths; soul singing plus his rap style; minor keys; subject matter always what he's currently living; very sample-heavy; sample chops over hip-hop and synthetic drums; pop arrangements. Across College Dropout, 808s, Pablo, Donda the visuals change and individual albums have sonic focuses (Yeezus electronic, Jesus Is King gospel) — but how he cooks stays constant, and that's the rapport.
  • LSDREAM: bass-music drums swung like hip-hop; bass-music synths and sound design; vocals often reggae or hip-hop-inspired samples; synthetic and analog-inspired instrumentation. The unique element is bass genres with swung hip-hop drums — rooted in his real history as a dancer and b-boy who then made bass music as Brillz and combined the two.

Why some artists never find it

  • They make everything and then double down on whatever gets plays — "letting the audience tell you what to make."
  • They switch after a few songs. The main failure mode Alba sees. Changing chapters is fine; the sin is changing too early.
  • They're talented and all over the place, so nobody can tell who they are. Top-tier artists commit to cohesion.
  • They never inventory their own life. "The answers are already inside you."
  • Party Favor is the counterexample. He cracked "Bap U" by accident — made late 2012/early 2013, released October 2013 on Mad Decent, a minor mode stepping into a major key that someone told him years later was "not supposed to work," built by playing with a sampler using his own distorted voice, with zero theory knowledge (he argues the ignorance helped — it made composition purely feel-based). It's still sometimes his top Spotify track and he has never topped it. Because he never locked a chart, he got years of "what's the next Bap U," fans locked to the twerk era (~100 BPM, which he calls a universally ideal dance tempo) demanding more while he wanted to move, and records written because they looked like hits that then sat on the hard drive. His rules from that: "you're only as good as your last release," and don't release records that don't feel like you.

Why it pays

If the sound is clear enough, copycats follow and you permanently occupy the "original creator" slot — you want listeners saying "this sounds like [you]" or "somebody trying to be [you]." A defined sound makes it easy for festivals, collaborators and brands to place you. And the bigger artists Alba works with compete with previous versions of themselves. Your career will hold multiple projects and aliases; this chart defines one project, one season.

q.label: List your past influences and your present inspirations, then write 10 or more candidate recipes by mixing them — without making anything yet.
q.help: Step 1 is a real journaling session on the past: favorite all-time songs, favorite albums, what your parents played, what was in the house growing up, life memories with music behind them, best experiences at shows. Step 2 is present: what you return to, who is pushing boundaries, who you would see live tonight. Step 3 lays both on the counter as ingredients and writes every plausible recipe. Alba's own: 80s new wave from his parents' house plus 80s synth soundtracks plus Rezz's mid-tempo sound design, giving 'Rezz mid-tempo bass meets 80s synthwave soundtrack meets 80s new wave.'
q.eg: LSDREAM's recipe is bass-music synths with hip-hop-swung drums — from a real history as a b-boy who then made bass music.

q.label: Fill the signature sound chart across all ten categories: drums, synths, vocals, key, subject matter, samples, instrumentation, sound design, arrangement, catch-all.
q.help: This is the sonic sandbox — you can make anything, but only with what is on the counter. Specifics the playbook fixes: build one drum kit and use it the whole period; define the vocal box tightly enough that you know who to cast (Alba's own period was male falsetto only, so he hunted Michael Jackson, The Weeknd, Prince and Phil Collins ranges); target roughly 90% arrangement consistency across the season. Wide enough that a pop song, a club song and a downtempo song all fit, narrow enough that a listener can name the through-line. Then audit your existing tracks against it — which belong to this movie, and what does the soundtrack still need? Print the finished page and tape it where you produce.
q.eg: Calvin Harris 2011-13: club drums, dance synths, soulful powerful vocals, all minor keys, love and passion, no song samples, pop arrangements.

q.label: Write your dated sound commitment: 12-24 months, or 40-50 demos at a 10-20% release rate.
q.help: Commit in time or in volume and put a date on it. Expect five or six full cycles before a breakthrough. Hand the dated commitment to one accountability person. The main failure mode Alba sees is switching sounds after a few songs — changing chapters is fine, the sin is changing too early; if you switch entirely at three months you may never learn what was possible. When an off-brief idea hits, spend 15-20 minutes getting the bare bones down, save it, and return to the plan: 'yes, but not right now' is better than saying no.
q.eg: Locked from 1 March for 18 months, 45 demos minimum, releasing no more than 9. Handed to my accountability partner, dated and signed.

items.h:
5. Standing out in a crowded space

Baseline condition: ~100,000 songs uploaded every day. A-Trak's version — "eight bajillion artists," "100 billion releases every Friday."

Build a taste library

Taste-as-download: everything you consume settles into conscious then subconscious memory and resurfaces when you make. So take deliberate inspiration trips — museums, art openings — with no immediate application. You're "downloading it for taste for later."

This extends into the everyone-is-born-creative argument: creativity is making choices. You choose dinner anyway; the difference is whether the choice is backed by a reason drawn from your taste. An artist is a curator — acting choices, sample choices, set choices are the same act.

A-Trak's discipline: know your influences, verbalize the specific references, articulate why, intellectualize it fully — then roll your sleeves up and make it fun and spontaneous again. Alba's summary, which A-Trak endorses with "100%": define the sandbox, then you can shoot from the hip because you'll know when you land inside it. His own library came from record covers first (he became a DJ because of record covers), Beastie Boys handstyles, The Pharcyde's Bizarre Ride II, the 90s Def Jam run, New York as the Mecca that "shaped my whole taste palette," then Swiss typography and fine art still read through a hip-hop lens.

Habit 7 — sharpen the creative saw. Go to a lo-fi jazz show, a metal show, watch international movies, study old album covers, hang out with fashion designers, talk to photographers and filmmakers about process. "The more inputs you have, the more interesting your outputs become." Alba studies art like most guys study sports — runways, museums, design books, books on story. Over 10, 20, 30 years that builds "a vast ocean of references." "That's all art really is — using tools, referencing, and remixing, making new recipes out of the ingredients you've collected." The three drivers: discovery, creation, sharing.

Sourcing rule: references from outside your genre bubble, often outside music entirely, and from the past rather than the current moment. "Looking where other people aren't looking."

The gap-seeking strategy

It shows up independently four times:

  • The french horn story (Alba's own). Everyone competes for trumpet, guitar, drums — the "lead singer instruments." Pick the uncontested instrument, own it, use it as the vehicle out.
  • A-Trak's polar-opposite method. Survey what exists in the DJ world, identify the strong (typically cheesy) prevailing trends, and ask "what can we do that's going to be the polar opposite?" That question literally produced his typography direction.
  • Skrillex's Rule of Cool #2. If everyone heads one way, look the other. If the status quo wears skinny jeans, baggy becomes unique — worn confidently. Applied: when everyone built huge LED walls and CGI, he went real, basement-set, no big graphics — "the opposite of big: raw, human, intimate." Everyone else asks "how much promotion can we do?"; his team asks "how little can we do, and how much impact can that have?" Explicit warning: don't copy the tactic (the Stories-only Soma announcement runs on ~17 years of brand equity). Take the principle.
  • Curt Cameruci (Flosstradamus) finding literal market gaps. He spotted in early 2021 that nobody was doing physical-to-digital minting and built a vape you can actually smoke that also mints NFTs. Earlier: the Wi-Fi lunch boxes at SXSW (2011) — captive-portal boxes broadcasting SSIDs mimicking Linksys/Apple networks; devices auto-connected, and any attempt to reach Facebook redirected to the Flosstradamus site, where you got their music, a phone icon pack, a wallpaper and their SXSW schedule.

Questions to run on your scene: "What does everyone expect from the genre world I'm in? How, while still being myself, can I break that expectation and create a mental flag?" and "What's missing from this scene?" — then merge that gap with the things you love. Expanded Do it in writing: list ten artists in your lane and the five things they all do. That list is your menu of pattern breaks.

The mashup operating system (Flosstradamus)

Curt tags nearly every description with "…but in a different way," and Alba names it his permanent filter. Alba's gloss: different ≠ good, different = interesting — and interesting is reason enough.

Method: take element A that works plus element B that works from a different world, and force them together. Records: Led Zeppelin loop + drums from another song. DJing: trance + 808s; Percolator-style 128 BPM house + Laffy Taffy-style rap; hip-hop + indie dance + house in one set. Tech: code base + code base from GitHub and Hugging Face, which he calls "the SoundCloud / Hype Machine of tech." Now: AI audio + Ableton + his own stem-separation apps — prompt Suno for a genre ("an 80s funk song about ___"), treat the output as a custom crate-digging sample made for himself, generate ~10 times before one lands, then Ableton and stem separation, new drums, remix — "within 15 minutes I'm lost, in a flow state."

Validation loop: "They worked well on the dance floor for years. Let's just try it in a studio session and print it." Years of DJing produce the evidence; the studio documents it. The Original Don remix followed it — he asked Diplo for stems, stripped the hardstyle drums, dropped trap drums over it, added a slightly longer build and a couple of switches. Roughly 30 minutes. Intent was a quick trap edit and a show moment, not a movement. "The simplicity is key in everything."

Origin: Kalamazoo, Michigan — geographic midpoint between Detroit and Chicago, a car-parts shipping waypoint, so Detroit techno and ghetto tech and Chicago house and juke all landed at the same record store. A geographic mashup that produced a mashup artist.

The ethic: "give a penny to the culture so I can take a penny from the culture." Enter a scene — skateboarding, DJing, mopeds, NFTs, AI — learn, contribute a perspective nobody else thought of, never be a taker, and don't let the culture become your identity: "I really want to show up as Curt." Discovery precedes contribution.

Alba's canonical metaphor: the Korean BBQ burrito taco truck off Wilshire, run by a guy who's half Korean, half Hispanic. Line down the street while neighboring trucks had 5–10 people. "This is good and this is good, but you haven't had it like this yet." Two already-good things, authentic to the maker's life, executed as an attempt to be best in the world at it — and the customers did the marketing.

Keep shooting, and protect the "why" (Party Favor)

The why shift. Why #1 (pre-career): "I want to make something cool for me and see if I can." Why #2 (post-career): "I need a hit or this stops." Symptoms of #2: desperation; peer comparison ("we started at the same time and they're crushing"); writing records you think are hits that aren't you, then leaving them on the hard drive.

Artist vs. business is structurally opposed. Business logic: "if they want Coke, just make more Coke." Artist reality: what made the Coke exciting was that it was fresh, so the only way to reproduce the effect is to make something new.

Keep shooting. One unsafe shot young landed, and he learned to shoot again; repetition retrains the brain to tolerate discomfort. Great artists live "right up to the edge of being comfortable."

Fast feedback beats slow feedback early. Film: a friend wrote a script in college, got it funded with big actors, festival run — 4–5 years to learn whether the hunch was right. DJing: write it in the afternoon, test it in the club that night, "like being a standup comic." Caveat: crowds differ, so one bad test is not a verdict.

Fans bond to the era they discovered you in and resist evolution. Expect it — attachment is strongest for high-school-era memories because of how memory forms, which is why every generation thinks their music was better. Also: not having formal training can be an asset early — you don't know what you're "supposed" to do.

His exemplars of defined sound: Flume (identifiable from day one, obvious parameters, things he wouldn't remix, a signature way of processing vocals and chopping), Tame Impala (moves the needle while unmistakably himself), Porter Robinson (the depth of fan bond he's jealous of), Rick Rubin ("simplify, keep it simple").

Returning to initial innocence

Over time "a plaque builds up on everything" — creation, relationships, business. The fix is to find the initial seed and go back. Alba's therapy analogy: "date your spouse" — act as if you must win it again. Applied to art: how would I date this work? The other move: be creative in an adjacent medium, then return — "let me go cheat and then come back." Curt's tech/AI detour is what "made me so stoked on making music again."

The loop it prevents: success → fear of losing it → lean into what worked → repeat → drift away from play and experimentation → it falls apart. "You're doing all of these things to support something that isn't the thing that got you here."

His closing artifact is the cuckoo clock necklace from Slauson Flea Market — he wears it because people called him crazy for the mashups, for trap, for every turn. Final advice: trust yourself, develop your taste, believe in yourself, and accept that you might be cuckoo sometimes. "My batting average isn't 100" — but the times he did it for the cuckoo side meant the most, and the times he did it for other people didn't work.

Differentiation heuristics

  • Different ≠ good. Different = interesting. That's sufficient reason.
  • Not more expensive, more creative. Paranormal Activity — the trailer showed night-vision footage of audiences reacting instead of scary scenes; budget under $20,000 → $193 million worldwide. OK Go — the 2006 "Here It Goes Again" treadmill video and the 2010 "This Too Shall Pass" Rube Goldberg machine; millions of views, neither expensive, both effort and choreography. The "Smile" campaign — people with creepy smiles placed at events across the US, and major outlets did the awareness for free.
  • Make it remarkable — "to remark about," not "incredible." Will people tell someone else?
  • Stand on existing stages. Completely original first offerings struggle because there's no prior reference, so the brain files it as "doesn't matter to us." Shorten the runway with an official remix, bootleg, sample, cover, a trusted label or channel, or attachment to a reputable brand or person. Adidas did this in 2014 with Rihanna, Pharrell, Rick Owens, Y-3 and Raf Simons. Alba says it's the 0→100 path for roughly 90% of the big electronic artists he watched.
  • Cool people know cool people — trust transfers through relationships.
  • Stack the odds. His anchor case: attempt 1 copied the local model — booked a venue, printed flyers, went out every night for weeks handing out thousands, and got only 10 people outside their friend group; ~40 total in a 150-cap room. Attempt 2 was an art show with music in his downtown LA warehouse loft, stacked with a dozen local artists, 24 DJs across multiple rooms including two known headliners, bartenders with their own friend groups, a local clothing company doing live screen printing with limited shirts, and a paid flyer feature in LA Weekly. Break-even was 150 people at $8. Result: almost 800. That became the template behind an Avalon residency doing 1,000+ almost every week.
  • Go to the people; don't make the people come to you.
  • Digital is good, experiential is better — even a small pop-up or listening party. Real-life events self-select for real fans.

6. Rebranding

A rebrand is "not a new logo, a new story and position in the culture." It doesn't mean changing everything — change a few high-impact things. If "rebrand" feels heavy, call it an upgrade.

The five diagnostic scenarios (Step 1)

  1. Stuck with no growth — months or years of banging your head, nothing connecting, regardless of follower count or engagement.
  2. Everything all at once — built on experimentation, incoherent, "throwing stuff at the wall" — but you now have clarity on the next few years, and it isn't based on trends or mimicking heroes.
  3. A reputable reputation — the market knows you for something else. Alba's own case: known as an LA promoter and talent booker, so his DJ project deliberately distanced from the promoter identity and focused only on art, music and story. It grew ~10x faster and larger.
  4. Bad packaging — the music is fine, the story and visual identity are unclear. Retool story and look; don't burn everything down.
  5. A new mission — the why changed: fun-as-outlet became build-a-business, or business became taste-driven creativity after burning out on the system's rules.

Expanded If none fit, don't rebrand — commit harder. Scenario 1 is the most misdiagnosed: four flat months isn't a trigger. Alba's threshold for judging any brand is 24 months.

The 10-step playbook

# Step What it means
1 Decide if a rebrand is right for you The five scenarios. Before anything else.
2 Define the story Cult story framework: master concept / controlling idea → archetype → plot. The controlling idea is the one idea holding it all together.
3 Define the new position Point of view, beliefs, elevator pitch, world alignment (Section 1).
4 Define what makes it unique The flavors added to the soup (Section 3).
5 Define the superpower Which of the five categories you win in (Section 2).
6 Define the sound The sonic sandbox — must match the movie (Section 4).
7 Mood board the visual identity The art direction deck, page by page, so any contractor absorbs it instantly.
8 Execution for assets to launch Hire photographers, videographers, graphic designers, motion artists; compile a brand guide / brand bible so promoters, contractors and labels absorb story, position and visual rules fast.
9 Content strategy and marketing plan Content buckets plus nested calendars: 12-month high-level with tentpoles, 6-month detailed, 30-day day-by-day across platforms. Half your total effort belongs here — many artists have a great brand and great music and no marketing plan.
10 Launch and commit The pre-mortem, then at least 24 months before judging it. Launch is the second-to-last act; committing is the final and hardest.

The pre-mortem (do it before launch): write out every scenario that might make you quit, pause, or abandon the new identity. Naming the problem solves half of it — your brain starts pre-solving. "Planning for a storm before it comes."

The named #1 mistake in 20 years: hiring the wrong people to execute the vision — no budget for the right people, or moving too fast without vetting. Perfect script plus the wrong CGI team and the whole thing crumbles.

The Mau P case in full

Before — Maurice West. Dutch big room. Polished. Hero archetype, positioned adjacent to Martin Garrix, Hardwell, W&W. Played big festivals with a small fanbase; Alba's read is it "never felt organic." A few thousand dollars per show.

After — Mau P. - Master concept: freedom and attitude — rejecting formulas, trends and genre expectations; instinct-led, tied to his own history and taste; "chasing the freedom to freely create." - Archetype: 80% rebel / 20% ruler. Rebels are freedom chasers who go against controlling systems — you don't have to be dark or punk to be one, and rebels can be the good guys. Ruler adds discipline, command, intentionality. - Plot: overcoming the monster. He faces a dominant system limiting creative freedom and confronts it not for power but to prove individuality and reclaim authenticity. "He doesn't join the system. He defines what's cool within it." - Tension: can he keep rising and beat the system on his own terms? Can the spirit of illegal Dutch underground raves be embodied in artist-brand form and beat cookie-cutter brands? - Position: the beliefs and elevator pitch quoted in Section 1; world alignment out of big room and into Defected / Repopulate Mars / Fisher / Chris Lake adjacency. - Uniqueness: the five flavors (Section 3). Superpower: category 5, the cool factor. - Visual pillars: his own likeness; 2000s nostalgia; unpolished, raw, candid images and video that feel "stolen"; luxury street fashion and cool lifestyle. On-camera flash candid, subject centered, wide-angle to pull in the environment, "almost voyeuristic," never over-posed. Selfie art direction as its own page. A posing reference pool — their guides run 40–50 poses. Noise/grain texture. Minimal sans-serif plus a handwritten element. Long-form references: the Aziz Ansari standup special trailer shot by Spike Jonze, and 2000s rave mini-DV camcorder grain. - The defining track: "Drugs from Amsterdam." The title alone signals rebel and freedom; nostalgic but fresh underground sound that works in an after-hours club and on a festival stage. Early on he played it smoking a cigarette with sunglasses on — something Garrix, Hardwell or Maurice West would never be caught doing. - Content pillars: (1) photo shoots, curated studio mixed with candid on-camera-flash street; (2) selfies — bathroom, car, plane; "dueling middle fingers up" is on-brand; (3) show footage, only significant moments, not recaps; (4) music videos, elaborate show announces, unique Spotify Canvas videos — "if it feels expensive, even if it isn't expensive"; (5) lead with one defining track instead of a barrage of bootlegs and edits; (6) content that lets the internet do the work — edits, memes, track IDs, hype threads. - The "Mau P is dancing" Coachella moment. The internet trolled him for not dancing and being too cool with no energy; he put himself on the dance cam as a rebel troll-back. 100% planned, not improvised. His Coachella 2025 set video executes the whole board — Spike-Jonze-style handheld, 2000s camcorder moments, on-brand styling.

Result: from a few thousand dollars per show to six figures plus per show. A Google image search of the two brands shows "almost polar opposites."

Companion case — Chris Lake (Cult client). Mid-2000s big-room/progressive house with "Changes," "Carry Me Away," "Only One," "Sundown," aligned with Dirty South, Fedde Le Grand, John Dahlbäck, Funkagenda. Around 2014 he started talking about shifting toward a more underground, higher-taste sound; the rebrand began ~2016, fully from 2017 — released with Skrillex and OWSLA, featured on the Howse compilation Skrillex curated, distanced from big room. It did not catch fire immediately, but show and festival offers and total revenue far surpassed the original brand, and he built the community over the following eight years. Rare case of changing sounds without changing names, grooming an existing audience into the new sound.

Patience case — Max Styler, a client since 2014 when he was 18: ~15 years grinding on the brand, only now seeing the full fruits.

q.label: Do you need a rebrand? Name which of the five scenarios fits, what changes and what stays — or write down that none fit and you are committing harder.
q.help: The five scenarios: stuck with no growth over months or years; everything all at once, built on experimentation and incoherent, but you now have real clarity on the next few years; a reputable reputation where the market knows you for something else (Alba's own DJ project distanced from his promoter identity and grew about 10x faster); bad packaging, where the music is fine but the story and look are unclear; or a new mission because the why changed. If none fit, do not rebrand — commit harder. Scenario 1 is the most misdiagnosed: four flat months is not a trigger, and the threshold for judging any brand is 24 months. A rebrand is not a new logo, it is a new story and position in the culture.
q.eg: Scenario 4, bad packaging. The music stays exactly as it is; the story, the visual identity and the world alignment all change.

items.h:
7. Age and timing, as positioning inputs

Being an artist in your 30s or 40s

Seven structural advantages — realized only if you commit to communication (content), the single gating factor.

  1. You have a real story. People want the story, not just the music, and real stories come from real experience. Nobody has lived your life.
  2. You know yourself better. "The clay is starting to harden." You know who you are and aren't, accept that some won't like you, and chase your own approval. Art is expression through choices; choices get easier with honed filtering systems, and filters come from experience. You're better at self-editing.
  3. Your why is different. A teenager's mission isn't a 40-year-old's. You know it's a marathon — less hunting a breakout moment, more long-term world-building.
  4. Your taste is honed. A bigger arsenal of references you can't buy and can't get from a chatbot. You also see cycles.
  5. You manage time differently. "Consistency beats hunger every time"; "hard work beats talent when talent stops working." You measure results, not busyness.
  6. Your fan base may be older — good. You don't need to be a household name to be a millionaire artist; you need a community that supports with dollars and time. Older fans have disposable income and honed taste, so once bonded they stick; younger audiences can be fickle. Proof point: a friends' band with only ~20–30k followers all-in but average annual spend per fan of $300 — described as an eight-figure business.
  7. You have actual stakes. When it costs your time, family time, money or comfort, you stop making disposable work.

Precedents: Christian Dior started Dior at 41. Ridley Scott made Alien, his breakout, at 40. Mark Rothko was in his late 40s for the color-field paintings. George R.R. Martin started Game of Thrones at 44. Solomun broke out in his late 30s and kept ascending through his 40s. Virgil Abloh was late 30s / early 40s when it connected. And Nolan as the general case: "it's not sports, it's art."

The trap is content resistance — most artists in this range don't love content, and appetite for discomfort fades with age. Alba's reframe: it's "more of a shift in mindset than the skill itself." Call it communication, and treat each platform as a language. He'd never done YouTube and knew nothing about YouTubers, and committed to learning the language anyway. His verdict: committing to communication is "100% the difference between a local artist and one that can sell out a stadium."

Seven tactics he gives for cashing the advantages in: hone the story (decide what movie you're showing this time); section out moments alone — "spend time with the roommate that lives inside your mind"; make a vision board around your mission and look at it daily, aimed at adding value rather than gaining attention; take idea vacations — block travel time, even just driving somewhere new, and "download those experiences"; build a time-blocking system and check the week against the mission; have conversations with friends about what they're into and what they miss from the past — if you both miss it, there may be an offering in that lane; journal about your why. Plus a two-self decision filter he says informs almost every decision he makes: make sure 90-year-old you has no regrets and 12-year-old you would be proud.

The market moment

  • ~100,000 songs uploaded every day. Saturation is the baseline.
  • Story is now as important as, if not more than, the music. Alba's estimate: the brand — "the movie" — is 70–80% of a project's success.
  • Social media became "interest media." Around 2024 the algorithms shifted from discovery mode to optimizing for identity, niche resonance, predictability, return viewership and depth of connection. Post performance now depends on value delivered and engagement, not follower count — someone with 500 followers can get as many impressions as someone with 50,000. "The playing field is more even than it's ever been."
  • The AI split. If your identity rests on a style or genre, or is surface-level, AI is coming for you. If you can define your story, connect with like-minded humans, and hold clarity on your point of view, you're bulletproof. "AI doesn't live. AI doesn't suffer and AI doesn't evolve." Corollary: the more abundance, the more valuable story, identity and meaning become — once AI content is everywhere, finding something real "will be like finding gold."
  • "Storyteller" is now a real, often multiple-six-figure job title at big companies, because their data says storytelling is how to stand out in oversaturation.
  • Fat tie, skinny tie (from Alba's dad). The American working man's tie: 50s fat, 60s skinny, 70s fat, 80s skinny, 90s fat. Why? "People have to sell ties." Trendsetters do the opposite of what's popular and then tell the next generation that's the way; every generation defines itself against the one before.

Expanded Read that last one as an instruction: whatever your scene has done for five years is what the next cohort will reject. Position against it now and you're early instead of late.

8. Exercises

# Exercise Time Output
1 Five Billboards 45–60 min Five raw phrases, contradictions allowed
2 Belief ideation + edit to 6–12 2 hrs + 1 hr next day Belief doc: header, sentence, rationale per belief
3 Archetype check + six-part stress test 45 min Annotated list; anything failing two tests gets rewritten or cut
4 Elevator pitch (template → 3 sentences / 30–60 sec) 60–90 min One pitch + one short story-bio
5 World alignment map — 10 labels, 10 artists, 5 venues/nights, 5 brands you want to sit next to, 10 you don't 60 min Two-column "adjacent to / not adjacent to" sheet
6 "Who's coming over for dinner" — 2–3 personas via the eight questions 90 min Persona sheets with a "where they hang out" line each
7 Superpower audit — unwatched / 10-friend survey / wins / powerful 3 hrs across a week (the survey takes days) Four journal entries
8 Pattern read + 5-year test with a third party 60 min One named category + a paragraph of justification
9 Scene gap map — 10 artists, the 5 things they all do, your breaks 60 min "What everyone does" list + 3 chosen pattern breaks
10 Five flavors — place, biography, behavior, demeanor, reference set 60–90 min Five flavors with a sentence of evidence each
11 Sound Steps 1–3 — past list, present list, recipes 2 × 90 min Two lists + 10+ written recipe combinations
12 The sound chart (Step 4) — all ten categories 2–3 hrs One page, printed, taped where you produce
13 Commitment declaration — 12–24 months, or 40–50 demos at 10–20% release, ~90% arrangement consistency 15 min Dated written commitment handed to one accountability person
14 Reverse-engineer three artists through the same ten categories 2 hrs Three filled charts + what they share
15 Taste download trip — museum, gallery, vintage store, art books, a show in a genre you don't make; no application in mind Half a day, monthly 20+ references filed by category, sourced outside your genre
16 Rebrand decision memo (only if a scenario fits) 60 min One page: which scenario, what changes, what stays
17 Pre-mortem — every scenario that could make you quit 45 min A list with one written response per scenario

9. What "done" looks like — Phase 2 artifacts

Done means a stranger could read one folder and describe your movie, your position and your sound without you in the room.

Two questions to check everything against before Phase 3:

Does the soundtrack match the movie? Could someone paste these beliefs onto another artist and have them still work?
