If the first is no or the second is yes, go back. Art direction, content and campaigns all inherit whatever you leave unresolved here.

phases.goal: An art direction deck and brand bible a stranger could execute from — themes, colour, type, photography, motion, styling, logo, stage and the asset list.
phases.intro: The brand should look how the story feels. Everything here is a translation of decisions you already made, which is why it comes last — you cannot costume a movie you have not written. Two clocks are running: the 2-second scan that decides yes or no, and the 60-second scan every booker, label and playlist editor gives your digital world.

items.h: You have a character, a belief system, a set of foes, a plot, and a signature sound. Phase 3 turns all of it into something a stranger can see in two seconds. This is where most artists start, and starting here is the single most common reason a project looks expensive and means nothing.

1. Why the look comes after the story

"The brand should look how the story feels."

Chris Alba says this twice in the Fred Again Art Direction Playbook and calls it the core secret of fifteen years of work. Your visual identity isn't decoration on the music. It's the translation layer that takes an invisible internal story and gives an audience a way to feel it before you've said a word.

Why visuals-first fails. You can't costume a movie you haven't written — how could you style the characters if you don't know what the movie is about? Every visual decision is an answer; if the question doesn't exist, the answer is arbitrary. Building without blueprints is hammering wood with no idea what you're doing; struggling artists are "freestyling the process," deciding from whatever inspired them that morning. The Brand Story Pyramid runs story at the bottom, beliefs in the middle, aesthetic on top, built bottom-up — an aesthetic with nothing under it is what the Skrillex episode calls "facades built on sticks." And the biggest visual-identity mistake named on the channel is choosing visuals because you think they're cool; the filter you want is "Does this support the story we're telling right now?"

Framing beats quality. Virgil Abloh's candle: the same dented candle is art in a white gallery and trash in a garage. "I could design the candle… or I could just design the room." The wine study Alba cites — over 5,000 people, expensive-labeled wine preferred roughly 90% of the time, with brain scans showing taste regions lighting up harder — proves packaging changes the experience of the thing itself.

Two clocks are running. The 2-second clock: what is it, what's the story about, what does it look like, what does it mean for me, how do I feel, do I care, does it meet a need, am I interested in the story — then yes or no. Each encounter is "an at-bat"; strike out enough and they're gone permanently. The 60-second clock: every fan, booker, label and playlist editor scans your digital world and decides in 60 seconds or less. Cult will sometimes spend half a year building a brand purely to win that minute.

Expanded Phase 3 has one job: make the first minute of contact do the work of a conversation you'll never get.

2. The Art Direction Method

Every Art Direction Playbook runs the same spine. Fred's episode is built on five numbered keys — call it The 5-Key Art Direction Method (that name is this playbook's; Alba just numbers them). Dom Dolla's runs the same spine across seven keys, expanding the execution end. Skrillex's wraps it in a house metaphor. Mau P's nests it inside a 10-step rebrand as Step 7.

Key Question What it produces
Key 1 Who are you? Archetype blend (in percentages) + belief/value system
Key 2 What's your story? Plot (one leading) + brand story summary / elevator pitch
Key 3 What are the brand themes? 3–5 pillars every visual decision drafts off
Key 4 How does the story match the look? The art direction guidelines deck
Key 5 How do you present the brand? Execution standards + non-deviation rules

Key 1. Carl Jung's archetype wheel. The audience subconsciously asks "What is this? Who is this? Do I care?" Humans sort each other by perceived primary motivation, so a clear archetype bonds fast. One ideal, two fine, never more than three. Always name a dominant, in percentages — 70/30, or 70/25/5; the channel's usual shape is two at 80/20 (or 90/10), sometimes a third at 5–10% "spice." Then 6–12 beliefs, each starting "We believe…" or "We do not believe…"

Key 2. Booker's seven plots: overcoming the monster, rags to riches, voyage and return, the quest, comedy, tragedy, rebirth. Mixing allowed; one must lead. Then the story summary, framed as "what would be on the back of the DVD" — three sentences or less, 30–60 seconds spoken.

Keys 3 and 4 are sections 3 and 4 below. Key 5 is execution: a great script, a great director and a great crew can still make a bad movie. Write what you always do and what you never do, then commit to a window.

The same method elsewhere. Dom Dolla's 7 Keys: who are you (archetype + plot) → the look (signature) → consistency → photo/video art direction → typography and illustration → color → digital presence. Skrillex's House: The Land (what genre is the movie?) → Blueprints (archetype; Rebel + Creator) → Foundation (beliefs; his are "the rules of cool") → Floor Plan (plot; the quest) → Materials (themes, then references, then mood board) → Front Door (logo, press photos, content videos, rollout) → The Rooms (consistency across every touchpoint, where superfans are made).

The order is not negotiable. Archetype → beliefs → plot → story summary → themes → visual identity → execution. Fred's episode flags the gate: "there's one more crucial step needed before you begin art directing," and that step is themes.

3. Brand themes — the hinge

What they are. 3–5 story pillars every visual decision drafts off. Not adjectives you like — the emotional load-bearing ideas of your movie, short enough to hold in your head on set. Alba calls this the shortest section of the deck and the most important, because art direction, copy, voice and content all draft off it. If a decision can't be traced to a theme, it doesn't go in the deck.

How to derive them. Read back your archetype, beliefs, foes and plot, and compress the recurring emotional ideas into one or two words each. Expanded Test: if you deleted a theme, would at least three visual decisions lose their justification? If not, it's a preference.

The clearest translation. Guillermo del Toro's Frankenstein (Jacob Elordi, Oscar Isaac): the theme is the life/death cycle, so the shape language everywhere is circles — circular lab, circular window, round chandelier lights, rounded cave doors, round electrical tubes, halo coils. No scene is there by accident.

Artist Themes / pillars
Fred Again Connection; Real & Raw; Humanity; "Excitement lives in the moment"; Relatability. Pillars: Fred as relatable creator; real candid images; photo/video in the moment and in action; minimal clean graphic design; photo and video do the storytelling.
Mau P Freedom and attitude, instinct over formula. Pillars: his likeness; 2000s nostalgia; unpolished "stolen" images and video; luxury street fashion. Five flavors: honoring the underground and his city; the sacred studio his late father built; controlled chaos; the quiet storm; reference the past, not the future.
Skrillex Freedom, creativity, cool — carried into visual and sonic language before any mood boarding.
Dom Dolla Elevated taste as the weapon against scene mediocrity; cool-but-relatable; restraint.

Pillars vs. themes. Themes are story-level; visual brand pillars are the ingredients those themes license — "the ingredients you're going to cook the visual brand with." Both the Fred and Mau P decks put a pillars page early, because pillars are positive constraints: once they're on the table, you cook with those and nothing else. Fred's deck also embeds three on-set arbiters: Does this feel human? Does this feel now? Does this feel real? Write your own three.

q.label: Write your 3-5 brand themes by compressing the recurring emotional ideas in your archetype, beliefs, foes and plot.
q.help: Called the shortest section of the deck and the most important, because art direction, copy, voice and content all draft off it. Each theme is one or two words, short enough to hold in your head on set. Not adjectives you like — load-bearing ideas. Test: if you deleted a theme, would at least three visual decisions lose their justification? If not it is a preference, not a theme.
q.eg: Fred Again's five: Connection; Real & Raw; Humanity; "Excitement lives in the moment"; Relatability.

q.label: Convert the themes into 4-6 visual brand pillars — the ingredients you will cook the visual brand with.
q.help: Themes are story-level; pillars are the concrete ingredients those themes license, and they act as positive constraints: once they are on the table you cook with those and nothing else. The mechanism to copy is del Toro's Frankenstein — theme is the life/death cycle, so circles appear everywhere: circular lab, round window, rounded cave doors, halo coils. Theme in, visual language out.
q.eg: Mau P's four: his likeness; 2000s nostalgia; unpolished "stolen" images and video; luxury street fashion.

q.label: Write your three on-set decision questions — your version of "Does this feel human? Does this feel now? Does this feel real?"
q.help: Fred's deck embeds these three as arbiters that settle arguments on set without you having to re-explain the brand. Write your own three, keep them short enough to say out loud mid-shoot, and tape them above your desk. If a decision cannot be traced back to a theme through one of these questions, it does not go in the deck.
q.eg: Does it feel stolen? Would it have existed if the camera was not there? Would my 12-year-old self think this is cool?

q.label: Collect 100+ references from outside your genre and mostly from the past, then cut to the minimum that conveys each category.
q.help: Sourcing rules are strict: outside your genre bubble, often outside music entirely, and from the past rather than the current moment. Do not use other artists as references, especially not artists in your lane. Be careful with Pinterest — so many people use it that everyone ends up homogenized. Hunting grounds: films and shows, art books, old magazines, old album covers, architecture, runways, museums. Minimum 1500px on the long edge, because a screenshot of a screenshot tells a photographer nothing about grain or highlight roll-off. The most common mood board failure is too many elements: if one image conveys a category, use one.
q.eg: Skrillex referenced Justice's Cross cover for single-shape minimalism and Anthrax's sharp-lined punk logo — not other DJs.

items.h:
4. The mood board / art direction deck

Not a Pinterest wall — a working document that turns story into instructions a contractor can execute without you. Fred's framing: you're building a sandbox for the artists you hire. "Remember they're artists themselves, but you've now given them a sandbox they can exist in." And: "the more specific you can be, the better" — none of them will be bummed on more information.

The Fred Again deck (14 pages):

  1. Archetype blend — the split plus a written explainer of how the archetypes interact
  2. "What the movie is all about" — the DVD-back story summary
  3. Is the artist the face of the brand? — does the likeness lead, or do the visuals lead
  4. Brand beliefs
  5. Visual brand pillars — the ingredients
  6. High-level mood board — each reference annotated to call out the specific element, plus a written brief
  7. Environments pages (usually several) — "the sets": day vs. night, urban vs. nature
  8. Color palette / color story — separate palettes for photo coloring, video coloring, overall brand, hero/pop colors
  9. Photography art direction — a lead write-up, one page per style, plus a composition page
  10. Video art direction — mirrors photography one-for-one, plus a dedicated camera movement page
  11. Execution examples — how the direction was brought to life
  12. Layout style — the design language for flyers, tour ads, single art, billboards
  13. Typography
  14. Styling

The Mau P deck (16 pages): title (logo only) → contents → archetype (early, written as prose so any contractor grasps it instantly) → visual pillars → overall mood board with "main ingredient" images highlighted → photography style 1 → photography style 2 (selfie art direction) → posing page (guides built with 40–50 poses to pull up on shoot day) → execution examples → 2000s nostalgia board → IRL short-form video → long-form video → textures → fonts → handwritten element → one combined application: a show flyer using all six brand elements at once (likeness, rebel-ruler attitude, styling intention, on-camera-flash realness, rebel pose and crop, typography plus handwriting).

Cult's decks have run 40 to 50 pages of references. Required categories: overall universe, photography or illustration style, motion, colors, fonts, styling. Every element should have a reference.

Sourcing. Look outside your genre bubble — often outside music entirely — and to the past rather than the current moment; looking where others aren't is what makes an identity unique. Do not use other artists as references. The best references are things you grew up with, which makes them authentic rather than trending. Hunting grounds: films and shows, art books, old magazines, old album covers, architecture, runways, museums. Pinterest warning: so many people use it that everyone ends up with the same references.

How many. Fewer than you think. The most common mood board failure named on the channel is too many elements, which confuses you and your collaborators. If one image conveys a category, use one. Test: show the boards plus the story to someone who's never heard of you — they should understand the vibe.

Common mistakes: un-annotated references (a photo with no callout is a Rorschach test); no written brief; boards built from artists in your lane; no "we never do this"; mood boarding before the story exists.

Expanded How to actually build one

Tools. Figma (free tier, infinite canvas, easy annotation, PDF export) is the best default; Keynote or Slides if you prefer fixed pages; Milanote or Eagle for the messy collection stage. What a contractor receives should be a PDF — renders identically everywhere, opens on set with no login.

Format. 16:9, 1920×1080 per page. One idea per page. Big image, small caption. Page title in a consistent position so the deck reads as a system.

Resolution. References at minimum 1500px on the long edge — a screenshot of a screenshot tells a photographer nothing about grain, skin texture or highlight roll-off, which is exactly what you're referencing. Keep full-resolution originals for the next hire.

Page anatomy. (1) the image, (2) a one-line callout of the specific element, (3) two or three bullets of instruction, (4) a "not this" where useful.

Briefing. Send the PDF ahead of the call, never during. Walk the pillars page first and the references second — they need the why before the what. Give them the three feeling-objectives. Then hand over the sandbox: where they have freedom (usually composition and moment) and where they don't (palette, styling, lens language). Ask what they'd add. You hired an artist; the board is the boundary, not the storyboard.

5. The visual vocabulary

Color. Color makes people feel something instantly and subconsciously, which is why it's central to filmmaking. Before a single frame is shot, a film has a palette. Decide: overall brand palette, per-campaign palette, photo coloring, video coloring, hero/pop colors. Consistency in color is non-negotiable regardless of the palette you choose. Fred: golden warmth, sky blues, black and white — never neons, never super-saturated, never dark/moody/synthetic. Dom Dolla: dark and muted, heavy blacks and grays, so color pops when it appears. Titanic: warm as the love grows, cool as it dies. Tyler: Don't Tap the Glass primary red/yellow/blue, Chromakopia green. Rezz: red, black, teal, purple. Tactic: Google "color palettes from movies" for swatches pulled from iconic films.

Typography. One of the most overlooked pillars. Fonts carry deep subconscious associations, and one bad font choice can make all your visuals feel cheap. Dom Dolla's ratio: typography plus what it's paired with — illustration or photography — is 80% of your visual identity. Decide: primary typeface, pairing mode, handwritten element or not. Fred: minimal Helvetica-style plus handwriting styled like a scribble or something finger-written on a phone. Mau P: minimal sans-serif plus a handwritten page — "quiet visual interruptions." A-Trak's brother built their direction by asking what the polar opposite of the cheesy prevailing DJ-world typography would be, then distorting a stiff reference: Swiss typography with kinetic motion tricks.

Photography style. Decide: how many distinct styles (Fred has three, Mau P two), composition rules, posing, who shoots. Fred's three: blur (momentum, accident, documentary); on-camera flash (disposable-camera '90s–2000s nostalgia — "the image already has history"); iPhone capture (a language we read as honest) — with black and white as a treatment inside the iPhone style, for when a shot should feel timeless and more artistic rather than as a fourth style of its own. Framing rule: closeness, eye level, shared perspective — never frame the artist above the audience. Wide shots with a small subject shift the story onto the environment. Mau P: flash candid, subject centered, wide-angle pulling in the environment, mid-motion, "almost voyeuristic," never over-posed. John Summit: flash again — "you almost want it to look stolen." Universals: documentary over editorial, presence over performance, imperfection over control; images that feel like "stolen fragments of life." Selection can be curated; the feel must be 100% real.

Wardrobe and styling. Decide: the signature, the silhouette, the never. The Halloween Costume Test (called the ultimate brand test): if someone dressed as you, what would they wear, could they assemble it easily, would we recognize it instantly? Fisher, James Hype, Anyma, John Summit, The Weeknd's After Hours era, Steve Aoki, neon-green-era Billie Eilish and Tyler all pass. Fred: hoodies, sweats, t-shirts, vests, muted, minimal graphics, no heavily-graphic luxury pieces — "the clothes should never wear Fred" — and no sunglasses ever, because eyes are "the truest form of human connection." John Summit: open shirts and the headphone band forward. Mau P: glasses and a track jacket. Note: everyman brands are harder to style than rebel or ruler brands — find your signature elsewhere.

Logo and wordmark. A-Trak's durability tests: would this work as a sticker? On a chain? Small on the bottom back of a record? As a sticker on a light pole you walk past at 3 in the morning? "The best logos work in all these derivatives." His own mark, by graffiti artist Gory, has been in use since 2014. See also: Justice's cross, made by two guys who started as graphic designers; Dust La Rock's Fool's Gold identity, logo plus every cover for the label's first five years; Illenium's phoenix, the plot rendered as a mark.

Set design and staging. Decide: is the artist or the visual the focus, scale vs. intimacy, what you refuse. John Summit at the O2: no giant time-coded LED show; large-scale lighting, some visuals and lasers, John as the focus, and real dancers who dance like audience members feeling the music rather than doing pop choreography. Skrillex: logo and lighting only — when everyone built CGI productions he went basement-set and human. Anyma: the opposite pole, hyper-detailed characters at the Sphere. Alok at Coachella 2025: 50 real figures in identical outfits, silver gloves, specific masks, time-coded choreography. Cheap framing ideas the channel names: put your setup on the floor in the center of the audience; run a strobe and smoke machine on foot pedals; monochromatic outfits matched to color-coded instruments, White Stripes style. Also: playing your own city once a year makes it an annual moment; every couple of weeks kills urgency.

Lighting. Lives inside photo/video art direction: a high-energy performer shoots with motion blur, a cinematic brand uses high contrast and deep shadow. In the Anderson .Paak x Fred Again Eagle Rock session a cinematic camera was used, then graded golden-warm so it still felt real.

Motion and video language. Decide: styles (mirror your photo styles one-for-one), camera movement, short-form vs. long-form. Fred's: slow-motion candid (moving blur), nostalgic camcorder footage, iPhone video. Camera movement gets its own page. The rule: avoid tripods — "sticks." Static cameras freeze and distance the viewer; handheld puts the audience in the bumpy ride. You want slight swing, imperfect framing, reactive movement, human pacing. "The camera should feel like a person in the room, not a machine observing it." References: Spike Jonze — Fatboy Slim's "Praise You" (1998, an amateur flash mob outside a movie theater, stolen from life), Pharcyde's "Drop," and Her. The proof: in Fred's viral new-song video the camera starts pointed up at him from the decks; right before the drop the operator grabs it and dances with him. "That subtle camera move was likely the difference between a good video for social and a viral moment." Mau P: short-form IRL selfies, set capture, travel; long-form referencing the Aziz Ansari standup trailer shot by Spike Jonze and 2000s rave mini-DV grain. John Summit: crowd iPhone footage.

Cover art systems. Treat every release and every run of tour dates as a campaign with its own concept feeding the greater story — with bigger artists that's where the conversation starts. Anti Up (Chris Lake × Chris Lorenzo): "vintage UK rave meets contact sheets" — a yellow sticker popping on black-and-white assets, contact-sheet layouts from pre-digital film proof sheets, a photocopy texture over the photography, a clean logo paired with a prominent mark (the Queen's crown). Mau P: a noise/grain overlay. John Summit's "Comfort in Chaos": one visual world (John in a suit at "Summit CPAs," cubicle, old computer) applied to album cover, tour flyer, DSP default images, banners and social posts.

Live show visuals. How your performance frames the audience is live brand context. Multisensory encoding is real: music plus crowd sound plus visuals plus merch on the body creates a far stronger memory trace than the same song under a social video.

q.label: Define your colour system: overall brand palette, photo grade, video grade, and hero or pop colours — plus the colours you never use.
q.help: Before a single frame is shot, a film has a palette. Consistency in colour is non-negotiable regardless of which palette you pick, so the 'never' list matters as much as the palette. Fred: golden warmth, sky blues, black and white — never neons, never super-saturated, never dark or synthetic. Dom Dolla: dark and muted, heavy blacks and greys, so colour pops when it appears. Rezz: red, black, teal, purple. Tactic given: search colour palettes pulled from iconic films for swatches.
q.eg: Brand: bone, oxide red, near-black. Photo grade: warm shadows, no crushed blacks. Never: neon, gradients, chrome.

q.label: Choose your typography: primary typeface, what it pairs with, and whether you use a handwritten element.
q.help: One of the most overlooked pillars and, on Dom Dolla's ratio, typography plus what it is paired with — illustration or photography — is 80% of your visual identity. One bad font choice can make all your visuals feel cheap. Fred: minimal Helvetica-style plus handwriting styled like a scribble or something finger-written on a phone. Mau P: minimal sans-serif plus a handwritten page, described as quiet visual interruptions. A-Trak's direction came from asking what the polar opposite of the cheesy prevailing DJ typography would be, then distorting a stiff Swiss reference with kinetic motion.
q.eg: Primary: a condensed grotesque, all caps, tight tracking. Paired with photography only. Handwritten element: yes, marker on tape.

q.label: Define your photography: how many distinct styles, the composition and framing rules for each, and your posing approach.
q.help: Fred runs three styles, Mau P runs two. Fred's three: blur for momentum and accident, on-camera flash for disposable-camera 90s-2000s nostalgia where the image already has history, and iPhone capture, which we read as honest — with black and white as a treatment inside the iPhone style rather than a fourth style. The framing rule is load-bearing: closeness, eye level, shared perspective, never frame the artist above the audience. Mau P: flash candid, subject centred, wide-angle pulling in the environment, mid-motion, almost voyeuristic, never over-posed, with a posing page built from 40-50 poses. Universals: documentary over editorial, presence over performance, images that feel like stolen fragments of life.
q.eg: Two styles: on-camera flash candid, and a 35mm wide documentary style at eye level. Never a lit studio portrait.

q.label: Define your video language: styles mirroring your photo styles one-for-one, plus a dedicated camera movement rule.
q.help: Camera movement gets its own page, and the rule is avoid tripods — sticks freeze and distance the viewer while handheld puts the audience in the bumpy ride. You want slight swing, imperfect framing, reactive movement, human pacing; the camera should feel like a person in the room, not a machine observing it. The proof cited: in Fred's viral new-song video the operator grabs the camera and dances with him right before the drop, and that subtle move was likely the difference between a good social video and a viral moment. References named: Spike Jonze on Fatboy Slim's "Praise You" and Pharcyde's "Drop"; 2000s rave mini-DV grain.
q.eg: Three: slow-motion candid, mini-DV camcorder grain, phone video. Camera always handheld, always at the subject's height.

q.label: Run the Halloween Costume Test: list the exact fit someone would assemble to be you, then write your signature, your silhouette, and your never-wears.
q.help: Called the ultimate brand test — if someone dressed as you, what would they wear, could they assemble it easily, and would we recognise it instantly? Passing examples: John Summit's open shirts and headphone band forward, Dom Dolla's mustache, Mau P's glasses and track jacket, Fisher, Anyma, The Weeknd's After Hours era, neon-green-era Billie Eilish. Fred's rules: hoodies, sweats, muted, minimal graphics, no heavy luxury logos because the clothes should never wear Fred, and no sunglasses ever because eyes are the truest form of human connection. Signatures only become signatures through repetition, and everyman brands are harder to style than rebel or ruler brands.
q.eg: The costume: black work jacket, white tee, wired earbuds around the neck, one specific pair of glasses. Never: shorts, logos, hats.

q.label: Describe your logo or wordmark and record the result of the four durability tests.
q.help: A-Trak's tests: would it work as a sticker, on a chain, small on the bottom back of a record, and as a sticker on a light pole you walk past at 3am? The best logos work in all these derivatives. Actually print it and try them, then write keep, revise or kill. Reference marks: Justice's cross, made by two guys who started as graphic designers; Illenium's phoenix, which is the rebirth plot rendered as a mark; A-Trak's mark by graffiti artist Gory, in use since 2014.
q.eg: A single-shape mark like Justice's cross — works at record-spine size and reads from across a dark room.

q.label: Define your live and stage presentation: is the artist or the visual the focus, scale versus intimacy, and what you refuse to do.
q.help: How your performance frames the audience is live brand context, and multisensory encoding means music plus crowd plus visuals plus merch creates a far stronger memory trace than the same song under a social video. Poles: Anyma with hyper-detailed characters at the Sphere versus Skrillex with logo and lighting only; John Summit at the O2 with no giant time-coded LED, John as the focus, and dancers who move like audience members rather than doing pop choreography. Cheap framing ideas named: put your setup on the floor in the centre of the audience, run a strobe and smoke machine on foot pedals, monochromatic outfits matched to colour-coded gear, White Stripes style. Also decide frequency — playing your own city once a year makes it an annual moment; every couple of weeks kills urgency.
q.eg: Floor setup in the centre of the room, two work lights and a smoke machine on foot pedals, no screen. Home city once a year.

items.h:
6. Case studies: the story → theme → visual chain

Fred Again — Everyman/Creator on a Quest

Story. South London, ordinary upbringing despite high-society surroundings. At 16 he made music with his neighbor Brian Eno, who taught curiosity, listening, and treating music as a living thing rather than a formula. Marlborough College, where the focus was emotional impact, not image. Then years behind the scenes for Ed Sheeran, Rita Ora and Demi Lovato — number ones, learning to "disappear inside the work." He stepped out because hiding felt like hiding.

Archetype and plot. 70% Everyman / 30% Creator — "just an ordinary person, your friend Fred," plus the obsessive maker. Result: artistry without distance. Plot: Quest dominant, Voyage and Return as subplot.

Beliefs driving the look. Real life is where the art lies. We do not believe perfection makes things better — chasing it removes the cracks, the off-timing, the breath in the voice. We do not believe the artist should stand above the audience. Intimacy can scale. "Scale what's real."

Theme Visual decision
Real & Raw Blur, on-camera flash, iPhone capture; "stolen fragments of life"; no AI visuals ever
Humanity / no pedestal Eye-level framing, closeness, shared perspective; never above the audience
Connection No sunglasses ever
Excitement lives in the moment No tripods; handheld, reactive; the operator who grabbed the camera and danced
Relatability Hoodies, sweats, muted colors; "the clothes should never wear Fred"
All of it Golden warmth, sky blues, black and white — never neon, never synthetic

Proof. The Boiler Room CDJ incident: an audience member knocked the CDJ off; Fred laughed, restarted the song, and jumped with the person instead of having security remove them. The rooftop set from a friend's London rooftop — framed not as an impromptu idea but as a masterclass in on-brand execution, versus an industry listening party shot with cinematic cameras. What they don't do: add AI visuals, wear loud luxury brands after success, add pyro, jump on a genre trend.

Skrillex — Rebel/Creator, and the art of doing less

Story. Pop-punk and metal, then UK underground bass, French touch, LA's underground electro scenes. He merged scenes instead of committing to one; from early on he wasn't mimicking heroes, he was forming a point of view.

Foundation — the Rules of Cool. Success is attracted, not chased. If everyone heads one way, look the other direction. Don't chase hits; move culture. Mix above-ground, underground and in-between. Attach yourself to cool things and people. Be real. Be yourself.

The chain. Rule 2 is the visual identity. When everyone else built huge LED walls and CGI productions, Skrillex went real, basement-set, no big graphics — "the opposite of big: raw, human, intimate." His Scary Monsters-era references were Excision and Downlink's robotic 3D bass art, French touch via Daft Punk, Justice and Ed Banger, the Justice Cross cover for its single-shape minimalism, deadmau5's glowing-light themes, and Anthrax's sharp-lined punk logo — a merge of scenes rendered as artwork, matching a merge of scenes rendered as sound.

The Soma rollout. Album dropped June 5 with no warning. No label campaign, no press run, no pre-saves, no track breakdowns. A few days prior he posted the title and full 13-track tracklist to Instagram Stories, gone in 24 hours — that was the announcement; Reddit and Discord lit up on their own. Cover: a minimal photograph, no titling, no bright colors. Profile images switched to a mirrored, broken-glass logo. "Juro" with Young Miko came six weeks earlier with a visualizer of live and hangout footage, apparently shot on a DSLR. Instead of a 200-show world tour, a small number of key performances. Stage: logo and lighting only. The inversion to steal: everyone else asks "how much promotion can we do?" His team asks "how little can we do, and how much impact can that have?"

The warning: do NOT copy the Stories-only announcement as a new artist. He can do it because of roughly 17 years of brand equity and superfans who amplify one post. Take the principle, not the tactic.

Dom Dolla — the cool everyman who looked like a major artist first

Story. The cool everyman — confident but relatable, the guy you'd grab beers with; if he were a product he'd be selling relatability. Plot: rags to riches meets overcoming the monster — local DJ to global headliner, layered with a fight against the noise and mediocrity of the typical EDM scene, using higher standards of styling, branding and taste as the weapon.

Key Decision
The look The mustache plus casual elevated styling. "He wears brands, but the brands don't wear him." Passes the Halloween test.
Consistency Instagram, Spotify banners, YouTube thumbnails, tour posters and live staging all read as one vibe. The result is brand gravity — fans recognize it with no logo present because the feeling is consistent.
Photo/video Every image reads as a still from a real moment. Deliberate mood, scene, posture, context.
Type + illustration Illustration style + texture layer + defined font per campaign — fresh but familiar. 80% of the identity.
Color Dark and muted, heavy blacks and grays, color used sparingly so it pops.
Digital presence The grid has rhythm and curation; Spotify and YouTube feel cut from the same cloth. "Dom's fans don't just stream the music, they subscribe to the story."

He "didn't just look like a major artist, he became one." Sometimes just looking the part gets both fans and the industry to believe in you.

Mau P — the rebrand that changed the price

Before. Maurice West: Dutch big room, polished, hero archetype, aligned with Hardwell, W&W, Martin Garrix. Big festivals, small fanbase, never felt organic.

After. 80% rebel / 20% ruler. Master concept: freedom and attitude — rejecting formulas, trends and genre expectations, instinct-led. Plot: overcoming the monster, the monster being a system limiting creative freedom. "He doesn't join the system, he defines what's cool within it." World re-alignment out of big room into the world of cool: Defected, Repopulate Mars, Fisher, Chris Lake adjacency.

The chain. Rebel + 2000s nostalgia + "stolen" realness + luxury street fashion became the four pillars, and every deck page after serves one: on-camera flash candid, subject centered, wide angle pulling in backstage, streets, travel, textured architecture; selfie art direction as a second style; a 40–50 pose library; a 2000s nostalgia board; mini-DV grain for long-form; a noise texture layer; minimal sans-serif plus handwriting. The final page stacks all six elements into one show flyer.

Behavior as art direction. Early on he played "Drugs from Amsterdam" in sets smoking a cigarette with sunglasses on — something Garrix, Hardwell or Maurice West would never be caught doing. The "Mau P is dancing" Coachella moment — trolled for being too cool to dance, he put himself on the dance cam as a rebel troll-back — was 100% planned, not improvised. His Coachella 2025 set video executes the whole board: Spike-Jonze handheld, 2000s camcorder, on-brand styling.

Result. From a few thousand dollars per show to six figures plus. A Google image search of the two brands shows almost polar opposites. It was "not a new logo, a new story and position in the culture."

7. The Brand Bible

Compile everything into a brand guide / brand bible so promoters, contractors and labels can absorb story, position and visual rules quickly.

Page structure (from the Chris Lake × Chris Lorenzo deck): cover → table of contents → biography → personality, voice and tone → brand themes → mood board pages → logo → logo usage dos and don'ts → icon → icon dos and don'ts → brand colors → fonts → design elements → brand example page → press photo pages.

Who receives it: contractors creating assets; promoters at the clubs and festivals you play; labels, management companies and potential brand collaborators, so they know your story and what can and can't be done with the brand.

Why build it before you're big. Alba was a talent buyer for almost fifteen years. When an artist sent a brand guidelines deck, "it immediately made them more expensive in my mind" — it proved seriousness, and on the assumption that how you do anything is how you do everything, it suggested they could sell tickets. Cult has gotten songs signed to major labels for brand-new clients purely on a pitch deck with a strong brand story and compelling mood boards.

8. Asset production

The launch list. Skrillex's Front Door names the minimum: logo, press photos, content videos, rollout strategy. The agency-origin episode names the recurring set every release demands — the "treadmill of assets": press photos, single art, music videos, tour flyers. Mau P's Step 8 adds the crew: photographers, videographers, graphic designers, motion artists. Level-1 minimum kit: name, vibe, bio, one-sheet/EPK, and a visual that goes with the brand.

The order:

  1. Deck first. Nothing gets shot until format, script, shot list, editing style and visual language are defined. "At Cult, we don't shoot a single frame of video or photo that doesn't have these elements defined beforehand."
  2. Logo and wordmark — run the four durability tests.
  3. Press photos plus a first content video, from one production.
  4. Single art and layout system — once photography exists, the layout language has something to hold.
  5. Flyers, banners, DSP default images, Spotify Canvas — applications, not new decisions.
  6. Music video / tentpole piece — last; the most expensive thing to get wrong.
  7. Brand bible — assets must exist before they can be organized into it.

The super shoot. On a major artist they were doing far too many small shoots and consolidated into "super shoots" — many items in one production. Same rule at your scale: don't shoot one thing, shoot as many things as possible that day. Dial in pre-production, have scripts and shots ready before capture, and "get a ton of meat off the bone."

Who to hire. The highest-leverage hire for a smaller artist is a "predator" — producer, director, videographer, photographer and editor in one. Find them on social: identify 8–10 candidates in your city and DM for rates; same for illustrators and designers. Portfolio strength is the whole game — ten photographers given the same mood board return ten different results. The #1 mistake in twenty years is hiring the wrong people to execute the vision, either from no budget for the right people or from moving too fast without vetting; a perfect script with the wrong CGI team crumbles. Ask a designer whether they'll teach you as you go as part of the engagement; the confident ones will. Hire on love of the vision and demonstrated strength, not title or résumé.

Budget and quality. "Not more expensive, more creative." Paranormal Activity cost under $20,000 and made $193 million by showing night-vision footage of audiences reacting instead of scary scenes. Nolan started with a $6,000 feature, Following. OK Go's treadmill and Rube Goldberg videos reached millions and neither was expensive — they took effort and choreography instead. Lutezi Music shoots in his own New Orleans — buses, vintage stores, street corners, burger shops — for millions of impressions. The flip side, from Mau P: "if it feels expensive, even if it isn't expensive," perception of brand and music changes. And the governing line: you know deep down what your best is; releasing something you know isn't it does nothing.

9. Consistency and non-deviation

Consistency is mostly about what you don't do. Real consistency is boundaries — knowing what your brand is and, more clearly, what it's not. On a collaborative video shoot, one artist suggested a shot with fake acid tabs on their tongues; the other said within seconds, "No, sorry. I don't want to do that. It's not my brand." No drama, straight to the next shot. That's the power of clarity. At the top this hardens into two phrases used with real conviction: "this is what we always do" and "this is what we never do." Write both lists.

Timeframe. Commit for at least 24 months before you judge it (the masterclass says 12–24). Artists commonly abandon a concept after weeks, and if you switch after three months you may never learn what was possible.

The pre-mortem. Before launch, write out every scenario that might make you quit, pause or abandon the new identity. Naming the problem solves half of it; your brain starts pre-solving. Planning for the storm before it comes.

The three ways artists go wrong: never defined who they are, their story, principles, visual identity or marketing plan; defined it but don't stick to it, chasing the next shiny object, "so desperate for success they've forgotten who they are"; or hired the wrong collaborators and rushed, shipping a mediocre brand.

It isn't a cage. The overarching story stays intact while eras change. Kanye ran College Dropout, 808s, Yeezus and Pablo as different movies in one franchise — the through-line is how he cooks. Tyler decides each era's art direction before any content or campaign. You're locking the point of view, not the palette forever. One caution from the John Summit teardown: watch your side ventures — his label name "Experts Only" reads as elitist, closer to a ruler brand than the everyman brand it sits under. Roughly 95% of the rest lines up, which is the goal.

q.label: Write your asset list in production order, with who shoots each one.
q.help: The order is fixed: deck first (nothing gets shot until format, script, shot list, editing style and visual language are defined), then logo and wordmark, then press photos plus a first content video from one production, then single art and the layout system, then flyers, banners, DSP default images and Spotify Canvas as applications rather than new decisions, then the music video or tentpole piece last because it is the most expensive thing to get wrong, then the brand bible. Consolidate into super shoots — do not shoot one thing, shoot as many things as possible that day and get a ton of meat off the bone. For crew, find 8-10 candidates in your city on social and DM for rates; the highest-leverage hire is a 'predator' who is producer, director, videographer, photographer and editor in one. The named #1 mistake in twenty years is hiring the wrong people to execute the vision.
q.eg: Super shoot day 1: 12 press stills across two styles, 4 content videos, Canvas loops, single art plates. One predator hire.

q.label: Write your two lists: "this is what we always do" and "this is what we never do" — ten items minimum each.
q.help: Consistency is mostly about what you do not do; real consistency is boundaries. The worked moment: on a collaborative shoot one artist suggested fake acid tabs on their tongues and the other said within seconds, "No, sorry. It's not my brand" — no drama, straight to the next shot. At the top this hardens into two phrases used with real conviction. These become the non-deviation rules in the brand bible. Fred's never list includes AI visuals, loud luxury brands, pyro, and jumping on a genre trend.
q.eg: Always: eye-level framing, handheld, one imperfection left in. Never: AI visuals, festival recap edits, sunglasses, pre-save campaigns.

q.label: Run the pre-mortem: write every scenario that might make you quit, pause or abandon this identity, with one written response each.
q.help: Do this before launch. Naming the problem solves half of it because your brain starts pre-solving — planning for the storm before it comes. Be concrete about the real ones: six months of flat numbers, a friend's project taking off first, money running out, a track that works but is off-brief, boredom with your own sound at month nine. The failure this guards against is the biggest mistake named in the whole playbook: starting over every time it gets hard, because the climb gets hardest right before the elevation kicks in.
q.eg: Scenario: nine months in, no traction, and an A&R asks for something off-chart. Response: make it, shelve it, revisit at the 18-month mark.

q.label: Write the date you launch this identity and the date, at least 24 months later, when you are allowed to judge it.
q.help: Commit for at least 24 months before you judge it; the masterclass floor is 12-24. Artists routinely abandon a concept after weeks, and if you switch after three months you may never learn what was possible. Put both dates on an actual calendar. This is not a cage — the overarching story stays intact while eras change; you are locking the point of view, not the palette forever. Max Styler ground for roughly 15 years before the full fruits.
q.eg: Launch 1 April 2026. Locked until 1 April 2028. No judgement, no restart, no new name before that date.

items.h: 10. Exercises

11. What "done" looks like

Phase 3 is done when you can hand a stranger a folder and they can execute your brand without you.

When those exist you stop making visual decisions and start making visual applications. You've answered thousands of future questions once.

Then don't touch it for two years.

phases.goal: A working content machine: 4-6 defined buckets, one repeatable property, one primary platform, a 30-day calendar and a tracking sheet.
phases.intro: Content is the only part of your brand most people will ever touch, so it comes fourth — after the story, the position and the look, never before them. What you are building here is a machine, not a habit: buckets and formats as the mechanism, a calendar as the distribution model, and an analysis block as the feedback loop. Every answer below should be something you could hand to a photographer, an editor or a label and have them execute without asking you what you meant.

items.h:
You have the character, the position and the look. Phase 4 is where the audience arrives — because content is the only part of the brand most people will ever touch. Alba's framing: daily content is the primary room, "where most people first find the project." Everything else is downstream.

So build a machine, not a habit. Inputs (the story work you've done), mechanism (buckets, formats, calendar), distribution model (the algorithm), feedback loop (analysis). Miss one and it stops turning.

1. Why content comes fourth — and what happens to people who start here

The channel is blunt: you cannot judge or plan a single post without knowing the whole movie. Content is the scene. Without the film, you're shooting scenes with unconsidered characters and unintentional cinematography, hoping something coheres.

What the sources say about starting here:

  • "Posting to post." The named failure: a random studio clip, a club video, a meme, a copy of another artist. No world building, no character, just moments.
  • "An incredible movie with no script." Without brand story, mission and content strategy you're "blindly shooting in the dark."
  • "A confused audience doesn't grow." Artists stall at touring level from unclear story or no one to execute; both end the same way.
  • "If you neglect brand foundations, you're likely not getting very good results with the content" — said before any tactic is given.
  • Content without identity actively hurts you with the algorithm. Inconsistent format, style, brand or story confuses the classifier, the post goes to the wrong people, and it dies shortly after its test group.
  • Metrics without connection is observed, not theoretical. Alba names artists with "insane numbers and consistent viral posts but nobody buys tickets."

Expanded The mechanical reason, not just the philosophical one: every content decision — what to shoot, how to caption, whether to keep a take — is a filter question. Filter on "is this cool?" and you make thousands of unconnected decisions. Filter on "does this support the story we're telling right now?" and the same thousands all point one direction. Alba names that swap as the Level 4 brand shift; Fred Again's team is the proof — the more upfront definitional work, the easier the thousands of downstream choices.

Your two standing filters from here on: Does this fit the movie (archetype, plot, position, visual language)? Does it serve the reason people actually follow me? "The best ideas are cool ideas with purpose." A bad idea is a cool idea with no story purpose — a scene that looks great and takes you out of the film.

2. How the algorithm actually works

2a. The business model underneath it

Platforms are ad businesses. More time on platform = more ads = more revenue. The algorithm's job is retention, which means "the algo wants your piece of content to be a hit." It isn't a gatekeeper deciding whether you deserve reach; it's a matching service that gets paid when it guesses right about you.

2b. The distribution path, step by step

  1. You post.
  2. It goes to a test group made mostly of non-followers. Your follower count is not the input. After an algorithm change Alba flags from "a few months back," performance depends on value provided and engagement earned — someone with 500 followers can get as many impressions as someone with 50,000. "The playing field is more even than it's ever been."
  3. The test group is selected from your past posts plus existing account data — the algorithm already has a hypothesis about who you are and who you're for.
  4. It logs the response.
  5. It matches the video against taste profiles. Consumer-side version: like one cute dog video, get blasted with that breed.
  6. Good signals → distribution expands. Bad or confusing signals → the post dies shortly after the test.

The core claim: "the algorithm isn't pushing your music, it's trying to match identities." Being specific doesn't mean one genre — it means narrowing brand and niche enough that the classifier knows who to hand you to.

The niching formula given: [brand archetype] + [genre fusion] + [world/space the brand lives in] + [feeling]. Three worked examples:

Too broad Narrowed
"DJ producer who makes dance music" Everyman merging melodic house with yacht rock; brand lives in a perpetual quest to vacation across the world; "brand is good times, soundtrack is good vibes"
"A band that makes metal" Rebel/Hero blending modern metalcore with cinematic film score and apocalyptic world building; feels like surviving the end of the world, empowered while everything crumbles
"Typical female pop artist" Lover/Rebel blending glossy pop with emotional honesty plus pop-punk; documenting life in real time, DIY, relationships, confidence, insecurity — real, raw, rebellious

2c. The signal hierarchy — every signal and how to engineer it

The data points logged: watch or no-watch, watch duration, repeat watches, share of session time spent on your content, how many of your videos they watched, likes, comments, saves, shares.

Ranked by how much work each does for you, with the engineering method:

Signal Why it's weighted How you engineer it
Shares A share brings a new person onto the platform — the single most valuable event to an ad business Build in a reason someone would pass it to one person or broadcast it (full taxonomy in §5)
Comments Proof of discussion, and discussion holds sessions open Design for comments a human would actually type — not fire emojis and hand claps
Saves Signals durable future value, not a momentary reaction Make it useful, inspiring, study-worthy, or something they'll want to share later
Watch time / completion Direct measure of retention, the platform's actual product Hook, curiosity loops, delayed payoff, no dead space
Repeat watches Multiplies watch time from one viewer Easter eggs, twist endings, fast pacing, seamless loops
Likes Cheapest signal, but volume matters Give people a reason to like that has nothing to do with the song

The five reasons people save: I'll need this later; this inspires me (inspiration library); I want to watch this but not now; I want to study this deeper; I'll share this later.

The ten reasons people like a post that have nothing to do with the song: the overall visual (styling, attitude, lighting, presence pulling you into the artist's universe); the viewer sees themselves in it; relatability; "this is impressive" (technical execution, not the song); "this is a vibe" (cinematic, nostalgic, peaceful, fun); an act of support; agreement with a stance; alignment with their taste and identity (subconscious); it was entertaining as a concept; aspiration — "I want a life like this."

This is the core mistake, stated plainly: most artists only give the audience one reason to like a post — the song. The reframe to run before every shoot: would someone like this even if they didn't love the song?

Concrete engineering tactics:

  • Comment farming via DM gate. For a free bootleg remix or unreleased track: "comment [word] and I'll DM you the link." A good song produces thousands of comments and thousands of DMs, lifting your overall engagement score.
  • Opinion bait. Text-on-screen headline stating a real stance — e.g. "The house music of today sucks, I miss 2000s house music." Agreement and disagreement both count as discussion. Safe-but-real stances given: pro-analog/anti-AI, or the inverse — being one of the first producers behind AI artists. You don't need political or religious hot takes. The warning attached: artists today are "soft in what they stand for" because they fear upsetting people, and that suppresses discussion and therefore reach.
  • Shareability headline overlay. Instead of just performing the song, open with "I think I just found the song I'm walking down the aisle to," then perform. Instantly shareable to engaged couples, married couples, their friends.
  • Relatable-environment swap. Instead of playing the track straight, put yourself in a setting your audience lives in — a wide-open field, a vintage store, a car with friends — and layer a situational headline: "When I want to listen to ___ but my friends want to hear ___ and it's an aux cord fight," with your track underneath.
  • Mini music video. Unique cinematography + clever storyline + world building drives "I discovered this first" status shares. Doesn't need to be expensive; needs to be well thought out and well executed.

2d. Why inconsistency kills reach

Inconsistent format, style, brand or story leaves the algorithm "confused", so it shows the post to the wrong people. Inconsistency isn't neutral — it's negative. Every off-brand post degrades the profile the platform has built for you, which degrades every future test group.

The other half: "Consistency and just posting to post is not what's winning." Volume alone is dead. What's rewarded is consistency of identity, not of upload count.

2e. Why "the algorithm is on your side"

It's paid to make your post a hit; it no longer requires an existing audience to give you distribution; and it's an identity matcher, and identity is the one thing you fully control. Alba's caveat, kept honestly: he "personally doesn't love that this is where we are." Play the game as much as you choose to.

3. Brand as network, platform as channel

The Food Network model

Treat your brand as a network and each platform as a channel. The Food Network runs many shows across many channels unified by one identity — all things food. Different content per platform is fine as long as every channel ties back to the network's larger identity and point of view.

The historical proof is MTV: one music-video channel that expanded into reality, game shows, scripted drama, animation and stunt comedy, spawning MTV2, MTV Brazil, MTV UK, MTV Hits and VH1 — over 60 channels at its peak — with programmers matching shows to each channel's offering. Same with the niche cable channels: Cooking Channel, ESPN, Comedy Central, Sci-Fi. You may not know the show, but you always know the category.

How to decide what goes where

Rule 1 — Go deep, not wide. Unless you're already a mainstage global headliner, choose ONE place to make and distribute content, focus there until it's working, then expand. Expand presence only as the team and marketing effort grow.

Rule 2 — Go where your people are. The questions: If I were a fan of this project, what platforms would I be on? Where are like-minded people digitally hanging out? Where does my target community spend most of its time? Younger audience = one set of platforms; midlife audience = another. The named client mistake: targeting Gen Z with Instagram posts plus Facebook ads — they're not there.

Rule 3 — Don't make broccoli. "Chopping up broccoli just gives you smaller broccoli." Don't cut one asset into pieces and scatter them across every platform. Each platform has a native style and a native audience. Make native content. The good example: Paul McCartney doing selfie videos on TikTok breaking down Beatles stories — not dances, not acting young, just using the platform's native style to tell his stories.

Rule 4 — Sub-channels. Instead of dumping live clips, studio footage, new music, rants, skits and music-video clips onto one page, split your strongest formats onto separate subpages. Subpages grow faster because the algorithm knows exactly what to do with them. The kicker: when someone engages with a subpage, the platform will likely serve them your other channels next — very often your main page. Reported result from Cult clients using this hyper-curated approach: 10,000–20,000 new real followers with fewer than 50 posts, in a couple of months.

Expanded For a solo artist with no audience, the practical read is: one main account is your network's flagship channel, and you earn the right to a second channel by making the first one work. A subpage isn't a hedge, it's a specialisation — it should have one format and one reason to exist.

q.label: Name your ONE primary platform and defend the choice: if you were a fan of this project, where would you be, and where does your target community actually spend its time?
q.help: Rule one is go deep, not wide — unless you are already a mainstage global headliner, pick one place to make and distribute content, make it work, then expand as team and budget grow. Treat your brand as the network and each platform as a channel, Food Network style. Answer with the platform plus the demographic evidence for it; the named client failure was targeting Gen Z with Instagram posts and Facebook ads, because they are not there.
q.eg: TikTok. My 18-27 melodic house listeners live there; the DJ mix accounts they follow all index there, not on Facebook.

q.label: Write your native-content rules for that platform: what native looks like there, what you will NOT do on it, and — if you want a subpage — its single format and single reason to exist.
q.help: Do not make broccoli: chopping one asset into pieces just gives you smaller broccoli, so each platform gets content made in its own language. The model is Paul McCartney doing selfie videos breaking down Beatles stories on TikTok — not dances, not acting young. A subpage is a specialisation, not a hedge: one format, one reason to exist, and the algorithm rewards it by serving your other channels to anyone who engages. Cult clients using this hyper-curated approach reported 10,000-20,000 real new followers with fewer than 50 posts in a couple of months.
q.eg: Native: handheld, on-camera flash, talking straight to camera. Never: reposted 16:9 festival recaps, dance trends, lyric graphics.

items.h:
4. What to actually post — the bucket system

4a. The nesting hierarchy (this is the whole system)

Brand → Era → Chapter → Campaign → Content bucket → Content property → Individual post.

Every single level has its own guiding idea — one central concept that organises it. A post ties to a campaign, which ties to a chapter, which ties to an era, which ties to the brand.

Level What it is Timespan
Brand The movie: story, position, visual identity, pillars The life of the project
Era A chapter of the same overarching story. Sometimes album/EP-tied, often just "another sandbox housing the guiding idea" — most artists live in a singles world Months to years
Chapter Usually a song campaign or key moment, with its own vibe, aesthetic and guiding idea Typically 1–2 months
Campaign The targeted story for one offering — release, tour, drop, collab Weeks
Bucket A recurring content category that creates scenes in the movie Ongoing
Property A repeatable, owned series inside a bucket Ongoing
Post One scene One day

Era examples: Tyler, The Creator — Chromakopia (all things green, military-inspired, metaphorical) vs. Don't Tap the Glass (primary colours, leather, dancing, fun). Same artist, two eras. Peggy Gou — three eras with no albums, only EPs and singles: underground all-vinyl techno/house sets with matching visuals; then melodic accessible house in a world of colour introducing her fashion and art taste; then pop-crossover plus large brand work, with the Nike collab as its own chapter promoted heavily for a couple of months. Kanye — College Dropout, 808s, Yeezus, Pablo: same artist, same story, different looks and campaigns.

The zoom-out test (the stated "formula for unlimited content ideas"). For any single post, ask upward: What's the format? What's the scripted idea for that format? What platform, and is that where my like-minded demographic hangs out? Which bucket does it fit, and how is that bucket tied to the campaign and brand? What's the current campaign? What's the current era? What's the overarching movie — who are the characters, what's it all about? If you can climb that ladder from any post, your system works.

4b. Buckets follow archetype

Buckets are the styles and formats that show the audience your movie, and they're determined by who your character is:

  • Hero brand → challenge, failure, overcoming adversity, stakes, struggles, wins and losses, values.
  • Rebel brand → chasing freedom, doing things your own way against the status quo.
  • Everyman/Everywoman → relatable stories; "I'm just like you, but living the life of a music artist."
  • Creator brand → ultra-creative, point-of-view-driven work; the art itself must carry the emotional charge.
  • Lover brand → love, sex, passion, heartbreak.
  • Jester brand → if they follow you for entertainment, 95% should be high-level, share-worthy comedic content so funny it has to be sent to a friend.
  • Explorer brand → an in-studio track breakdown "doesn't really do much to forward the story of an Explorer."

The reverse warning, verbatim in spirit: a rebel brand dancing in the studio to your latest song may not convey what you're rebelling against. And the exception that proves it — an Everyman brand with real dance culture in their world doing the latest dance trend absolutely fits. The same tactic passes or fails depending on the relationship.

4c. Two fully worked bucket sets

Explorer archetype + quest plot, album recorded in locations worldwide with international collaborators: the act of travel; adventure stories; unique places visited; world cultures; world foods; performances in unique locations. The audience follows you like a travel show — where will they go next?

Rebel archetype + rags-to-riches plot, DIY-punk mixtape, campaign themed on old security-camera footage, aggressive high-energy sound, meant to incite revolution: "started from the bottom now we're here" stories; "can't tell me nothing" rebel moments; mock security/surveillance tapes; "I don't have a label, I have a message"; "this isn't a mixtape, it's a revolution"; high-energy performance clips; pop-ups in random locations that feel like underground boxing gyms.

4d. A working six-bucket example (Mau P)

  1. Photo shoots — a mix of curated studio and candid on-camera-flash street. (Because Mau and his likeness are the brand — unlike Eric Prydz, whose brand is the visuals.)
  2. Selfie images — bathroom, car, plane. Makes the artist feel like a real person; "dueling middle fingers up" is on-brand for a rebel.
  3. Show footage — not general recaps. Only significant show moments that showcase attitude and energy.
  4. Music videos, elaborate show announces, unique Spotify Canvas videos — "if it feels expensive, even if it isn't expensive," the perception of the brand and the music changes.
  5. Lead with one defining track — less is more. Concentrate marketing on key records instead of a barrage of bootlegs, edits and mixtapes.
  6. Content that lets the internet do the work — edits, memes, track IDs, hype threads, shared clips.

4e. Content properties — the highest-leverage thing in this whole phase

A content property is a repeatable, owned series: same format, same setup, same style every time; only the subject matter changes. This is the TV-show mechanic applied to a feed.

Property Format Result
Wookie — "Beats I Can't Release" Plays two versions of himself: producer at the desk, and a passerby in a different outfit who overhears the track, is unsure, then falls in love as the build and drop hit; they dance together Went viral, repeated, viral again — done ~200 times. The single format changed his career trajectory; original owners later officially released several of the remixes
Vinyl Nights Cinematic record-listening sessions — pulls out a record, puts it on, sits back, listens. Identical shots every time, only the song changes ~700,000 followers in a few months
The Steve Aoki jump Mid-jump photos in key locations worldwide, later with other DJs, celebrities and public figures — all versions numbered A static recurring property spanning a career
Emma Films herself on her phone making music; setup, composition and framing near-identical every time Cited as a model of format discipline
Charlie Puth Same selfie video format teaching how music is made, music theory, music psychology Displays mastery, feels authentic, makes the audience curious what music he'd make — with the flagged risk that leaning too far into tutorials makes people come to you only for tutorials

4f. The format library

Named content property/format types, with what each is for:

Format What it is Best for
Man/woman-on-the-street interview Strangers answering a question Awareness, comedy, hot-take fuel
Vlog walkthrough of a day Often sped up with captions or voiceover Relatability, everyman brands
Hot takes Bold or contrarian opinion to spark discussion Comments, point-of-view broadcasting
Blind listen A fan, stranger or friend reacting to something for the first time; their like/dislike is the content Music-forward proof without self-promotion
Cinematic voiceover + B-roll Story scored with your own music Camera-shy creator archetypes
Day-in-the-life with challenges Structured around a task Hero brands
Acts of kindness Hero brands
Motivational posts Hero brands
Failure-themed posts Something that went wrong Hero brands — these "historically perform really well" because the audience comes to the hero's aid

Format-selection questions: How does this tie to my current campaign? Is it aligned with me, my personality, my story? Would it resonate with my community? Is it doable with my current resources?

4g. The three-part mix

What the bigger artists Cult works with actually run:

  1. Content for the current campaign
  2. Ongoing content properties tied to the overarching brand story
  3. One-off posts that fit neither but strengthen the brand

Balance storytelling posts against awareness-oriented posts. Don't try to go viral with every post — the audience still needs to learn who you are. And don't get so lost in storytelling that you forget awareness. Half of total effort should go to marketing and telling people about the work.

q.label: Write your 4-6 content buckets. For each: name, a one-line definition, why it exists (which part of your story it advances), three example post ideas, and target frequency.
q.help: Buckets are recurring content categories that create scenes in your movie, and they are decided by your archetype: Hero buckets are challenge, failure, stakes and wins; Rebel buckets are freedom and doing it your own way; Explorer buckets are travel, unusual places, world cultures and performances in unique locations; a Jester should be roughly 95% high-level share-worthy comedy. Cap it at 4-6 — enough rotation to fill a month, few enough that the algorithm still knows who you are. Test every bucket with one question: does this forward my character's motivation? An in-studio track breakdown does nothing for an Explorer, and a Rebel dancing in the studio to their new song conveys nothing about what they are rebelling against.
q.eg: Mau P's six: photo shoots, selfie images, significant show moments only, expensive-feeling videos, one lead track, and content that lets the internet do the work.

q.label: Design your one content property: the repeatable series where the setup never changes and only the subject changes. Name it, list the fixed elements (location, framing, wardrobe, edit style), the one variable element, and how you would shoot ten of them in a single day.
q.help: This is the highest-leverage unit in the whole phase — the TV-show mechanic applied to a feed. Wookie's 'Beats I Can't Release' ran about 200 times and changed his career; Vinyl Nights (identical cinematic record-listening shots, only the song changes) hit roughly 700,000 followers in a few months; the Steve Aoki jump is numbered mid-jump photos worldwide. Commit to at least 30 posts (the Phase 5 version says 50) before you are allowed to judge it. If the setup drifts between entries, it is not a property.
q.eg: Fixed: same corner of the studio, same lamp, same handheld angle, same cold open. Variable: which unreleased track plays.

q.label: Set your three-part mix: what share of your posts serve the current campaign, what share are ongoing content properties, and what share are one-off brand-strengthening posts?
q.help: This is what the bigger artists actually run. Balance storytelling posts against awareness posts — do not try to go viral with every post, because the audience still has to learn who you are, and do not get so lost in storytelling that nobody hears about the work. The stated rule: half of total effort goes to marketing and telling people about the work. Give real percentages or a per-week count, not adjectives.
q.eg: Per 12 posts a month: 5 campaign, 5 property, 2 one-offs. Half my working hours go to marketing the work.

items.h:
5. The virality psychology

Governing metaphor: "Brands are movies, content is the scenes." The question before you make anything: Why would somebody share a scene from your movie?

The warning that opens the topic: "I honestly think that often artists and companies focus too much on trying to go viral." Understand why people share instead of chasing the outcome — and note that going viral for the wrong reason can be actively damaging, because it attracts the wrong audience.

5a. Two different kinds of sharing

A) Person-to-person (direct, to one friend/family member/coworker) — 8 triggers:

  1. "Isn't this crazy" — out of the ordinary; can be crazy good or crazy bad; shared with one or a few people to co-sign the craziness.
  2. "This is entertaining / fascinating / cool" — described as one of the main ones.
  3. "I feel cool sharing this" — a flex; the share confers status on the sharer just for finding it.
  4. "This is us" — reminds them of a shared relationship or experience.
  5. "We should try this / doesn't this look fun" — flagged as especially useful for show announces: sell the event as an experience and people share the trailer.
  6. "Remember this" — nostalgia; a shared moment or bond; I wonder if you'd have the same memory.
  7. "We both love this" — "a really big one for fans and when you're building community"; deepens a bond over shared love.
  8. "This reminds me of you" — deepens connection by showing you thought of them.

B) Sharing to your own audience (broadcast) — 5 triggers:

  1. Belief alignment — thought-provoking content or inspirational quotes; part of the reason is showcasing their own identity.
  2. Entertaining / fascinating / cool — they think their audience will enjoy it too.
  3. "This is coming up, everyone should be aware" — an event, release or drop; signals identity and alerts followers.
  4. "Isn't this crazy" — so notable it must be told. This is the Purple Cow slot.
  5. "My followers might find value in this" — value-based content out-shares purely expression-based content.

The flat list from the algorithm video overlaps and adds: shock and awe; "this is so me"; "this is so you"; "this is so us"; "this made me feel something"; "we should talk about this"; status — "I found it first, I think this will help you"; social currency — "this makes me look interesting by sharing it" (usually subconscious); agreement — "finally someone said it."

Expanded Notice that almost none of these are about you. They're about what sharing the thing does for the sharer — their relationships, their identity, their status. Design accordingly: the post is a tool you're handing someone to say something about themselves.

5b. The Purple Cow

Seth Godin's principle: driving past a field of ordinary cows you don't stop; a purple cow makes you pull over and tell everyone. Build purple-cow moments so "people end up becoming your marketing vehicle." Alba's related word: remarkable means "to remark about," not "incredible." You want fans texting "Have you seen this yet?" / "This is crazy" / "This is so good, I think you'd like it."

The canonical case: Alice Cooper at Wembley Arena (10,000 cap), 50 tickets sold two weeks out. Manager Shep Gordon shot a press photo of Cooper nude with a snake wrapped around him, mounted it as a billboard on the side of a truck, and paid the driver to deliberately break down in Piccadilly Circus — instructed not to move the truck even if arrested. Hours-long jam, driver arrested, wall-to-wall coverage. The show sold out.

Cheap-but-remarkable precedents: "Smile" placing people with creepy smiles at key US events until major outlets did the awareness lifting; Paranormal Activity trailering night-vision footage of audiences reacting rather than scary scenes — under $20,000 budget, $193 million worldwide; OK Go's treadmill video (2006) and Rube Goldberg machine video (2010), neither expensive, both demanding effort and choreography. The principle: "Not more expensive, more creative."

5c. The shareable content formula (order matters)

Shareable content concept + What makes this authentic to my brand + How can I present this in a creative, unique way vs. how I saw it / how it's been done

  • Part 1 goes first. Research what's currently getting shared and find a concept that inspires you. Ripping a viral concept wholesale is "totally fair game."
  • Part 2: run it through your brand's identity filter.
  • Part 3: push it further than the version you saw. "That's the fun of all of this" — and it's where the merit is.

Related stacking method from the algorithm video — "remix the concepts." Take one good concept and layer three elements: (1) shot in a unique or atypical way (not necessarily expensive), (2) built to spark conversation via a polarizing opinion, (3) a built-in shareability trigger. Result: far greater reach potential, and it reads as more creative than chasing a trend.

Apply all of this beyond social posts too: pop-ups, merch, product drops, releases, big moments, show announces.

5d. Pre-post checklist

Run this in the ideation phase, before you make the thing — the sources are explicit that engagement is designed at concepting, not bolted on afterward.

6. Hooks and structure

6a. The three structures, reconciled

The channel gives three labels for what is essentially one three-act skeleton. Use whichever vocabulary fits the piece.

Model Beats Use when
Hook → Lean-in → Story → Punchline Stop the scroll → open a curiosity loop → deliver the core content → close the loop with a shareable payoff The default for all short form. Named as the universal structure
Setup → Curiosity → Tension → Payoff Longer short-form, story-driven posts, mini music videos
Hook → Conflict → Climax "A three-act play or a three-act movie" Scripted shareable concepts — they write mini scripts for these

Self-test attached to the first model: Would I stop and watch this? Would I be curious? Would I lean in and stay till the end? Would I engage with or share this?**

6b. Retention mechanics

  • Hook first. Always.
  • Open curiosity loops early. Once a loop opens, the viewer is primally wired to see it close — that's the cliffhanger holding you through the ad break.
  • Re-hook every 5–10 seconds in short form.
  • Delay the payoff to the very end.
  • Cut anything that doesn't drive the story forward. "No dead space, no filler."

Hook examples given: "I can't believe this happened" (curiosity). "I think I just found the song I'm walking down the aisle to" (shareability). "The house music of today sucks, I miss 2000s house music" (opinion). "When I want to listen to ___ but my friends want to hear ___ and it's an aux cord fight" (relatable situation).

6c. Rewatchability — four methods

  1. Hidden elements / Easter eggs that only surface on rewatch.
  2. A twist ending that makes people rewatch through the new lens.
  3. Move fast — fast enough that watch 2 or 3 reveals more. Warning: not so fast the concept is incomprehensible.
  4. A seamless loop with no clear stopping point.

6d. New but familiar

The memory principle behind why remixed structures work: the brain loves patterns and rewards surprise. It constantly predicts what's next; meeting expectations feels good, breaking them slightly lights it up. Rom-coms are the illustration — identical beats, but this one's set in space. "You don't need to reinvent the wheel, just remix it. The brain will remember both the shape and the surprise."

q.label: Write one of your upcoming posts as a full mini script on Hook → Lean-in → Story → Punchline. Mark every re-hook and mark where the payoff lands.
q.help: This is the universal short-form structure: stop the scroll, open a curiosity loop, deliver the content, close the loop with a shareable payoff. Re-hook every 5-10 seconds, delay the payoff to the very end, and cut anything that does not drive the story — no dead space, no filler. Add one rewatchability mechanic: a hidden Easter egg, a twist ending, fast pacing, or a seamless loop. Self-test: would I stop, would I be curious, would I stay to the end, would I share it?
q.eg: Hook: 'I think I just found the song I'm walking down the aisle to.' Re-hook at 0:06. Payoff: the drop lands on the last frame.

q.label: Which three share triggers will you deliberately engineer, and what is one post concept for each?
