q.help: There are eight person-to-person triggers (isn't this crazy; this is entertaining; I feel cool sharing this; this is us; we should try this; remember this; we both love this; this reminds me of you) and five broadcast triggers (belief alignment; entertaining; everyone should know this is coming; isn't this crazy; my followers will find value in this). Value-based content out-shares expression-based content, and 'we should try this' is flagged as especially useful for show announces. Write a concept for all 13 first if you can, then keep the three best — most will be bad, which is the point.
q.eg: 'We both love this' — a numbered series of records only my scene would recognise, one per week.

q.label: Take one post that is currently just 'here's my song' and rewrite it to hit at least three of the ten reasons people like a post that have nothing to do with the song. Then answer in writing: would someone like this even if they didn't love the song?
q.help: The ten reasons: the overall visual, seeing themselves in it, relatability, 'this is impressive', 'this is a vibe', an act of support, agreement with a stance, taste and identity alignment, entertainment as a concept, and aspiration. The core mistake is giving the audience exactly one reason to like a post — the song. Show the before and the after, and name the three reasons you are now hitting.
q.eg: Aux-cord fight in the car with friends, track underneath: relatability, 'this is us', entertainment — three reasons before the song.

q.label: What real stance will you take on record — the opinion you will state on screen that starts an argument in your comments?
q.help: Agreement and disagreement both count as discussion, and discussion is what holds sessions open. You do not need political or religious hot takes; the safe-but-real examples given are pro-analog/anti-AI or the inverse, being one of the first producers behind AI artists. The warning attached: artists today are soft in what they stand for because they fear upsetting people, and that suppresses reach. It must be a stance you would defend in a room, and it should come from the same origin as your foe hierarchy.
q.eg: 'The house music of today sucks, I miss 2000s house music.'

items.h:
7. The content calendar

7a. The nested calendars

From the Mau P rebrand playbook, Step 9:

  1. 12-month high-level calendar — tentpoles and milestones; choreographed "moments" for the brand.
  2. 6-month detailed calendar.
  3. 30-day day-by-day map across all platforms.

Sitting above it: the results-setting cascade. Write the results you want in the next 12 months (aggressive but realistic), rank them, circle the top 3. Repeat for this month — the month's top items must ladder into the year's top 3. Repeat for this week. Repeat daily, weekends included. Calendar commitments: one 2-hour self-review every 3 months and 1 hour per week to time block the coming week (Sunday night, or first thing Monday if travelling).

7b. Build order — do it in exactly this sequence

  1. Define story / brand.
  2. Define the current era and chapter.
  3. Define the current campaign.
  4. Create your content buckets page.
  5. Lay out this month's tentpoles as placeholders — new music, new art, show announces, shows already played that need post-show content. A song release might occupy 10 total posts / 10 calendar blocks.
  6. Fill the remaining days by pulling from the buckets.
  7. Time block the making of the content, not just the posting.

The order matters: tentpoles go down first as placeholders, buckets fill the gaps second. And the operating law: "If it's on the calendar, it usually gets done." If it's not on the calendar it slides down the priority list. The standard to hold yourself to: you should never be in the "I haven't posted in a while, I should post something" position. Great companies and artists never wonder what they're posting this week.

7c. Planning horizons — where you should sit

Tier Horizon
Biggest artists 24-month strategy plan of tentpole moments
Big/pop teams 4–6 months ahead
Mid-tier 1–2 months — "not a terrible strategy, but it'll definitely keep you in the middle"
Newer artists Often no plan at all — forget to post, then rush lackluster content

Tentpole cadence benchmarks: a major artist runs at least one, often two "bomb" moments per month. A touring artist runs only 5–6 major strategic moments per year. Big artists still leave room to work in-the-moment events into the calendar.

7d. Volume — decide which game you're in

The two poles, both cited as legitimate: Alex Hormozi ≈ 350 pieces of content per week across multiple platforms. At the other pole, Alba points to an artist who posts only a few times a year and still pulls millions of views per video (the name is garbled in the transcript, so don't go looking for it). Neither is right or wrong — decide whether you're in a quantity game or a quality game.

The counterweight from the failure-modes video is the gym analogy: post one day a week, get one-day-a-week results; go seven days a week for multiple hours, maybe two-a-days, and you get seven-day-a-week two-a-day results. Marketing is the same as the gym — you get out what you put in. But it's listed as a separate failure from quality: consistency without quality accomplishes nothing, and quality without consistency also fails. The named common failure is knowing something isn't your best and putting it out anyway just to have something out.

And from the next-phase video, the modern correction: "You don't necessarily need a lot. You need good." High quality doesn't mean expensive — it usually means more time ideating, editing and refining.

Expanded For an artist with no audience, resolve the tension this way: pick a volume you can hold at your quality bar for six months, and let the bar — not the ambition — set the number. Three excellent posts a week beats seven you'd be embarrassed by, because the algorithm reads the bad ones as data about who you are.

7e. Batching

  • Super shoots. The cost lever discovered on a major artist: they were doing far too many small shoots — one photo/video capture per single moment — and consolidated into "super shoots" capturing many items in one production.
  • Don't shoot one thing. When you shoot with your content person, "don't shoot one thing — shoot as many things as possible in that day." Dial in pre-production; have scripts and shots ready before capture so you "get a ton of meat off the bone."
  • The banking method. A real client rhythm: 3 months in the writing process creating 6 months' worth of music, then 3 months making content for that 6-month stretch. Banking music and banking content buys you another 6 months to create the next batch.
  • Other client rhythms: two weeks generating demos → bring 1–2 to a finished place → pick one → next two weeks making content for it. Or the weekly split: Mondays/Wednesdays/Fridays music, Tuesdays/Thursdays/Saturdays content.
  • Content runway. Alba launched Neighborhood Art Supply with 12 weeks of videos shot and edited before posting anything, precisely because the agency was too busy to make videos weekly in real time.

7f. Planning around releases and tours

  • Build a work-back from the release date: start at the end and place strict dated deadlines on everything that must finish before it. His own launch work-back ran launch date → 12 weeks of content banked → handles and distribution set up → videos edited → videos shot → artists coordinated → pitch deck built → brand finalised → mood boards and ideation → vision meetings. Planned as 4 months, took 5 — without it he estimates 8 or 9.
  • A release is a campaign, and a campaign is a chapter — typically a 1–2 month span with its own guiding idea. Treat every release and every run of tour dates as a campaign: What's the campaign? What's the concept? How does it play into our story?
  • Tour content has a shelf life. "Turn and burn quickly." Don't play a big festival and post about it four months later.
  • Show frequency is itself framing. Playing your city once a year makes it a special annual moment; once a month or every couple of weeks kills urgency ("I'll catch them on the next one") and lowers perceived value.
  • Action-inducing events. Manufacture the deadline if you don't have one. Alba's own hack with a modest following: post "new remix coming this Friday" with no remix started and no idea what he'd remix. Those quick-turnaround bootlegs became the most-awareness work he ever did — tens of millions of plays, support from artists he respected, international bookings. The requirement: the deadline can be made up, as long as someone or something actually holds you accountable. The counter-story: an EP for Mad Decent with no deal and no deadline that he restarted repeatedly and never released.

q.label: State your weekly volume target and the quality bar it must clear — the number you can hold for six months without embarrassment.
q.help: Both poles are legitimate: Alex Hormozi runs roughly 350 pieces a week, and there are artists posting a few times a year pulling millions of views. Decide which game you are in. Consistency without quality accomplishes nothing and quality without consistency also fails, so let the bar set the number, not the ambition — three excellent posts a week beats seven you would be embarrassed by, because the algorithm reads the bad ones as data about who you are. Write the number plus one sentence defining the bar.
q.eg: 4 posts/week. Bar: scripted, shot to a shot list, edited on a separate day — nothing posted the same day it was shot.

q.label: Fill the 30-day plan header, then map all 30 days: era and its guiding idea, this month's chapter/campaign and its guiding idea, primary platform, buckets in rotation, tentpoles, posts allocated to the release, and day-by-day bucket / format / concept / hook / share trigger / capture status.
q.help: Build it in this exact order: era, chapter, campaign, buckets page, then lay this month's tentpoles down as placeholders (release, show announce, art drop, post-show content), then fill the remaining days from the buckets. A song release might occupy about 10 posts. Also calendar the making, not just the posting: shoot days, edit blocks, a caption block, the Sunday one-hour planning session and the monthly analysis block. If it's on the calendar it usually gets done; the diagnostic you are trying to eliminate is ever thinking 'I haven't posted in a while, I should post something.'
q.eg: Era: 'late-night driving'. Chapter: single release Mar 14. Tentpoles: art drop D5, announce D9, release D14, post-show D22.

q.label: Plan one super shoot: a single day producing 20+ assets. List every bucket and property needing footage in the next 60 days, then the locations, wardrobe changes, shot list per setup, and three feelings per block.
q.help: The biggest cost lever found on a major artist was consolidating many tiny shoots into super shoots. When you shoot, don't shoot one thing — shoot as many as possible that day, with pre-production dialled so you get a ton of meat off the bone. Never shoot without format, script, shot list, edit style and visual language defined first. Before the shoot write three objectives you want fans to feel (confident, relatable, powerful) and build the board to deliver them through lighting, styling, set pieces, poses and wardrobe. Include the booked date.
q.eg: One Saturday, three setups: loft (property x10), street on-camera flash (x8), car selfies (x6). Feelings: restless, warm, unbothered.

items.h:
8. The next phase of social media

8a. What changed

Old algorithm (roughly 2020–2023, "discovery mode"). Platforms wanted to flood feeds with new creators, so they rewarded volume, consistency, clips, randomness, novelty, trend chasing and short bursts of virality.

The shift (2024 onward). Platforms now have enough creators and enough content. What they need is longer attention and retention of returning users, because ad revenue scales with time on platform. The name for it: "interest media" instead of social media. The question changed from "what did you post?" to "what does this person care about consistently?"

The five things platforms now optimize for:

  1. Identity
  2. Niche resonance — what do you care about, and from which niches?
  3. Predictability — you always seem to do this
  4. Return viewership — you'll watch it again
  5. Depth of connection — were you into it this time?

Sharing is also prioritised, because a share brings a new person onto the platform.

The consequence most artists haven't absorbed: showing more variety and depth now makes reach WORSE, not better.

The parallel framing from the women-in-music video: the shift is from social media to interest media, where algorithms favour connection over aesthetics — and it isn't altruism, better performance produces better data which produces wider distribution.

8b. The TV show model

Consistent style and format, point of view, message and world — "the same but something new and different." Characters have arcs and drama, but you don't sub out Kramer or move Jerry to a new apartment. The neuroscience shorthand: repetition = memory = identity. Humans bond when they can predict you, recognise patterns, and know what you stand for.

Genres you can borrow from TV: scripted drama/sitcom; reality (voyeur, fly-on-the-wall POV); game and competition shows; edutainment; animated/cartoon/anime/claymation/AI; comedy (standup specials, stunt comedy, clip shows).

The 6 steps to build your series:

  1. Lay out objectives and mission — what should this content do, and how does it help tell the brand's story?
  2. Define the brand — foundation clear first, otherwise you're shooting in the dark.
  3. Define content buckets, ideate series inside each bucket, then assign each series a home platform based on the new algorithm plus demographics.
  4. Deep research — references from modern platforms and old movies, sitcoms, dramas, game shows, reality shows, talk shows, challenge shows. "The more diverse you make your taste and references, the more unique your art will be." Most artists skip this step entirely.
  5. Make the content — pre-production first. Format, script, shot list, editing style, visual language all defined before shooting. "We don't shoot a single frame of video or photo that doesn't have these elements defined beforehand."
  6. Analysis — Does it feel real (not "look real")? Does it come from a truthful place? Send it to people whose opinion you value. Is it unique, or an exact copy?

8c. Time = bond

The thought experiment: one awesome 30-second meeting versus ten 20-minute hangouts (three hours total). You bond with the second person. The brain doesn't distinguish digital hangouts from real ones — which is why research indicates younger generations feel more bonded to their favourite live streamer than to their favourite movie actor.

Practical consequences: consider long-form offerings alongside short-form. "Short form is really only there so that you can get to long form" unless you have a ton of short form. And: one or two viral moments won't sell hard tickets. Virality ≠ bonding.

8d. AI's role

The stated split: if your artist identity is built on a specific style or genre, or is surface-level with no depth, AI is coming for you. If you can define your story, create connection with like-minded humans, and hold deep clarity on your point of view, you're bulletproof.

The historical pattern given — printing press, cable TV, social media, now AI — resolves the same way each time: the more abundance, the more valuable story, identity and meaning become. With cable, the flood forced creators to get sharper, more specific and more personal, producing HBO, FX, AMC and the golden age. With social, the breakouts weren't the most polished or even the most consistent — they had a lens, a world view and audience trust.

What that means operationally:

  • Don't make for the algorithm. Make for a specific person — including a specific past version of yourself.
  • The specificity heuristic: "The more specific around your taste you get, oddly, the more universal it becomes. The closer it is to you, the closer it gets to them."
  • Expect the reflex. The predicted default audience response going forward is subconsciously asking "I wonder if this is AI." Real, human, imperfect footage now reads as a signal, which is why the on-camera flash, camcorder and handheld iPhone languages of Phase 3 matter more, not less.
  • AI on the design side is usable, but an all-AI, no-human identity likely won't connect. "The more human something is, the better chance it has of connecting with another human."
  • Adapting doesn't mean changing your point of view. It means being willing to take your art into the new world. Adapters last; non-adapters aren't as active today.
  • The payoff prediction: once AI content is everywhere, finding something real "will be like finding gold."

8e. What you must do differently, now

  • Stop posting scattered clips. Program repeatable shows on dedicated channels.
  • Think like a channel manager or small studio owner, not a person with an account.
  • Don't confuse the algorithm — one page should not carry every style of content.
  • You don't need dozens of content types. Find core formats and unique angles and make those as high-quality as possible.
  • Reframe the word: content is "communication." Treat each platform as a language — learn the language and you can speak your story in it. Committing to communication is called "100% the difference between a local artist and one that can sell out a stadium."

9. Content production workflow for a solo artist

9a. The eight-step sequence (identical at every level)

A stadium act and a bedroom artist run the same sequence — only the number of bodies changes.

  1. Get clear and define results — "before you hire anyone or make anything, you need to know what result you're actually chasing."
  2. Vision — the overarching vision, the story, the era, what's going on with the character now.
  3. Production planning — what we're shooting, who we need, locations, formats, budget, timelines, required assets.
  4. Capture and execute.
  5. Post — editing, colouring, graphics, sound, captions, cutdowns, photo selects, formatting. "A lot of content is either won or lost in post, because it's where the story actually gets shaped."
  6. Distribution plan — the content calendar; where each item goes and why.
  7. Operations — follow the calendar, hold deadlines, approvals, file organisation, budgets, who owns what. "This is where a lot of artists and their teams will drop the ball."
  8. Analysis and postmortem.

At come-up level two functions must exist: making the content and managing the flow of the content. You personally own two roles: project manager (define the creative, then build the system for capturing and distributing it) and data analyst (time-blocked study of performance).

9b. Your single highest-leverage hire: the predator

Industry term for one person who is Producer + Director + Shooter + Photographer + Editor in one body — the highest-leverage hire for smaller artists and the come-up artist's first investment priority. When you shoot with them, shoot everything you can that day.

To find one, or any photographer/videographer: find 8–10 candidates in your city on social, DM them for rates. Same for illustrators and designers. Portfolio strength is what matters — ten photographers given the same mood board return ten different results.

9c. Capture habits and equipment

  • Never shoot without pre-production. Format, script, shot list, editing style, visual language defined first.
  • Before every shoot, write three objectives you want fans to feel (e.g. confident, relatable, powerful), then build mood boards conveying those feelings through lighting, styling, set pieces, poses and wardrobe.
  • On-camera flash — imperfect, reads like a stolen shot from an old point-and-shoot. The workhorse of "real."
  • iPhone capture — a visual language we all read as honest.
  • Camcorder / mini-DV grain — nostalgia, history baked into the image.
  • Crowd iPhone footage — for shows, fly-on-the-wall beats a hired cinematographer for realness brands (John Summit's model).
  • Avoid tripods ("sticks") — static cameras freeze and distance the viewer; handheld puts the audience in the ride. "The camera should feel like a person in the room, not a machine observing it."
  • Selfie capture — bathroom, car, plane. Cheap, on-brand for relatability and rebel brands alike.
  • Noise/grain texture overlays for vintage feel; minimal sans-serif type plus handwritten elements.

The framing that makes all of this sustainable: stop treating shoots as a task; treat them as world building. Each shoot adds a page to your brand's visual story.

9d. Repurposing rules

  • Don't make broccoli. Native content per platform, not one asset sliced up.
  • Do bank and reuse the capture. A super shoot produces many finished pieces; that's different from cutting one finished piece into fragments.
  • Cutdowns and clips are a real job. At touring level it's a junior assistant's whole role. Solo, it's a scheduled block, not something you do "while" doing something else.

9e. A realistic solo rhythm

Group similar tasks so "your brain is playing in the same sandbox." Don't bounce call → creative work → call → errand. Alba's own template as a model: Monday deep creative work, zero calls; Tuesday/Wednesday calls and admin; Thursday pre-production; Friday productions; weekends family and recharge.

Music-system cadence options you can mirror for content: daily (2 hrs new creation / 2 hrs finishing / 2 hrs moving works-in-progress forward), weekly (Monday create, Tuesday finish, Wed–Thu move things downfield), or monthly (week 1 create, weeks 2–3 flesh out, week 4 finish).

The two guardrails: be careful about putting finishing at the bottom of the totem pole — artists who prioritise finishing over creating have far greater output. And the capture rule for off-plan inspiration: spend 15–20 minutes getting the bare bones down, save it, return to the plan. "Yes, but not right now, is better than saying no."

Named tools: color-coded Google Calendar paired with Asana for project management — tasks live in Asana and find their way into the calendar by priority. Granularity: 30-minute blocks mornings and evenings, 15-minute increments during the day (15 forces compression). 15-minute meetings instead of 30. Post on Indeed with a listing like "Music group seeks marketing director" if you need a marketer. Spotify Canvas as an underused brand surface. The channel's free assets, all comment-gated with no signups: "cult calendar" (content calendar template, plus suggest a future video topic), "cult content scorecard" (a content-idea framework that scores whether you've layered the elements raising algo metrics), "cult playbook" (art direction playbook with blank slides).

The 80% rule to keep you sane: "if I accomplish 80% of what I laid out for the week, that week is a win."

10. Measurement

Content analysis is the last step of the system and "a lot of artists miss it." Time-block it — this is the data-analyst role you personally own.

What to track

Track Why
Shares Highest-value signal to the platform; direct evidence you built a reason to pass it on
Comments — and what they say Read the sentences. Are people discussing what you wanted discussed?
Saves Durable value; predicts return viewership
Watch time / completion, and where people drop Tells you if the hook worked and whether the middle sagged
Repeat watches Rewatchability mechanics working or not
Per-format performance over time Which properties deserve to become staples
Follower growth attributable to a format Whether a subpage or series is compounding
City-by-city behaviour Where demand is concentrating for routing later — "one strong city is worth more than five weak ones"
Ticket, merch and stream numbers The only three questions the business side actually asks: how many tickets can you sell, how many people buy merch and how much, how many are listening

What to ignore

  • Follower count as a gate. It no longer determines distribution.
  • Fire emojis and hand claps. Not the comments you're designing for.
  • One bad post. A single crowd is not a verdict.
  • Vanity metrics divorced from bonding. Artists with insane numbers and no ticket sales are the cautionary case.
  • Virality as a goal. Going viral for the wrong reason attracts the wrong audience.

How to read a post's performance

Ask in this order:

  1. Did it get out of the test group? If reach collapsed almost immediately, the problem is usually clarity — the algorithm didn't know who to show it to.
  2. If it reached people but they left fast, the hook or the pacing failed.
  3. If they watched and did nothing, you gave them no reason to comment, save or share — an ideation failure, not an execution one.
  4. If it performed but the wrong people came, check whether the post contradicted the reason your actual audience follows you.

Then the alignment questions, which matter as much as the numbers: Does this feel aligned to me and my story? Am I chasing performance or purpose? Am I telling my story or just getting views? Is this the best I can make with the resources I have? Am I connecting with the right audience — are we truly bonding?

When to change course

  • Change the format, not the brand. Formats are experiments; the movie is not.
  • Give a property real reps before killing it. Wookie ran his format ~200 times. Alba's commitment threshold for a brand direction is at least 24 months, and for a creative concept 12–24 months. The named failure is starting over every time something gets hard — new plan, new name, new brand, new sound. "The climb gets hardest right before the elevation kicks in."
  • Watch the strikes rule. If content contradicts the reason someone follows you, "the brain will allow for a few strikes, but too many and they're over it."
  • Reassess weekly if goals keep slipping. Chasing inspiration over the plan is allowed — but if it happens constantly and weekly results slip week after week, reassess and reschedule. "If all you're doing is digging for potential gold and not hitting other results, you may need to reassess."
  • Run a 2-hour self-review every 3 months and a full postmortem after every campaign: what worked and why it may have worked.

q.label: List exactly what you will track in your monthly analysis block, and what you are deliberately ignoring.
q.help: Track shares, comments and what they actually say, saves, watch time/completion and where people drop, repeat watches, per-format performance over time, follower growth attributable to a format, city-by-city behaviour (one strong city is worth more than five weak ones), and ticket, merch and stream numbers. Ignore follower count as a gate, fire emojis and hand claps, one bad post, vanity metrics divorced from bonding, and virality as a goal. Name the sheet, the day of the month, and the length of the block.
q.eg: Shares, saves, comment sentences, completion %, per-format table, top 10 cities. Ignoring: follower count, emoji comments.
q.time: 30 min to set up, 60 min monthly

q.label: Write your commitment window: how long you will run this brand direction and this creative concept before you are allowed to judge them or change course.
q.help: The stated thresholds are at least 24 months on a brand direction and 12-24 months on a creative concept, with a property given real reps before it is killed — Wookie ran his about 200 times. When something is not working you change the format, not the brand: formats are experiments, the movie is not. The named failure is starting over every time it gets hard — new plan, new name, new brand, new sound. Write it as a dated commitment you would show someone.
q.eg: Brand direction locked through Aug 2028. Concept locked 18 months. Property judged only after 30 posts.

items.h:
11. Exercises

4.1 — The Bucket Board. 60–90 min. Output: a one-page content buckets document. From your archetype and plot, write 4–6 buckets. For each: name, one-line definition, why it exists (which part of the story it advances), three example post ideas, target frequency. Test every bucket: does this forward my character's motivation?

4.2 — Property Hunt. 45 min + ongoing. Output: three candidate repeatable series. Take your strongest bucket. Design three formats where the setup never changes and only the subject changes (Vinyl Nights, Beats I Can't Release, the Aoki jump). For each: the fixed elements (location, framing, wardrobe, edit style), the variable element, and how you'd shoot ten in one day. Commit to one for 30 posts before judging it.

4.3 — The Zoom-Out Audit. 30 min. Output: pass/fail on your last ten posts. For each, climb the ladder: format → concept → platform → bucket → campaign → era → movie. Any post where the ladder breaks confused your algorithm profile. Count them — that's your inconsistency tax.

4.4 — Ten Reasons to Like. 30 min. Output: a reframed shot list. Take one upcoming post that is currently "here's my song." Rewrite it to hit at least three of the ten reasons people like a post that have nothing to do with the song. Then answer in writing: would someone like this even if they didn't love the song?

4.5 — Share Trigger Mapping. 45 min. Output: 13 post concepts. One concept for each of the 8 person-to-person triggers and each of the 5 broadcast triggers. Most will be bad. Keep the three best and run them through the shareable content formula.

4.6 — Mini Script. 30 min each. Output: three scripted shorts. Write each kept concept on Hook → Lean-in → Story → Punchline. Mark every re-hook (5–10 seconds apart) and the payoff (the very end). Add one rewatchability mechanic.

4.7 — Platform Assignment. 30 min. Output: your channel map. If I were a fan of this project, what platforms would I be on? Pick one primary. Note what native content looks like there and what you will not do on it. If you want a subpage, name its single format and single reason to exist.

4.8 — The Work-Back. 60 min. Output: a dated reverse schedule. Pick your next real release or moment. Start at the date, work backwards, hard dated deadlines on every dependency. Attach a stake — money, time or embarrassment — and an accountability person who will actually follow through.

4.9 — Super Shoot Plan. 90 min. Output: a one-day shot list producing 20+ assets. List every bucket and property needing footage over the next 60 days. Consolidate into one day: locations, wardrobe changes, shot list per setup, three feelings per block. Get a ton of meat off the bone.

4.10 — The 30-Day Content Plan. 2 hours. Output: a filled calendar. Use the template below — tentpoles first, then buckets.

Header — fill before the grid:

  • Era: ____________ Guiding idea: ____________
  • Chapter/campaign this month: ____________ Guiding idea: ____________
  • Primary platform: ____________
  • Buckets in rotation: 1 ____ 2 ____ 3 ____ 4 ____ 5 ____
  • Tentpoles this month (release / show announce / art drop / post-show): ____________
  • Posts allocated to the release (target ~10): ____________
  • Weekly volume target: ____ posts/week at quality bar: ____________

The grid — repeat for 30 rows:

Day Bucket Property/format Concept (one line) Hook Share trigger Platform Capture status Posted Result
1 ☐ shot ☐ edited ☐ scheduled

Production blocks — put these on the calendar too:

4.11 — Postmortem. 60 min, monthly. Output: a written assessment. Rank the month's posts by shares, then comments, then saves, then completion. Write what worked and why it may have worked. Answer: am I chasing performance or purpose? Decide one thing to keep, one to kill, one to test.

12. What "done" looks like

Phase 4 is complete when these artifacts exist and are in use:

You'll know the engine is running when you never again think "I haven't posted in a while, I should post something." That thought is the diagnostic. Its absence is the goal.

phases.goal: A named community with a ranked enemy, a defined fan ladder, a first purchase that means something, and one real-world room to build it in.
phases.intro: Building community around your brand is described as the single biggest growth lever available to you — bigger than playlisting, bigger than track breakdowns. Roughly 100,000 songs are uploaded every day, so nobody is waiting for yours; what makes people stay is a shared belief, a shared enemy and enough time spent with you to bond. Answer these as decisions, not as descriptions: what you are against, what your people are called, and what the first thing they can buy is.

items.h: You have a character, a position, a sound and a content system. None of it counts until strangers show up. Alba's framing: "building community around your brand and music is the number one way to grow your artist project." Not playlisting. Not track breakdowns. Community. The raw conditions: ~100,000 songs uploaded every day. Nobody is waiting for yours.

1. The fan ladder

Expanded The channel never draws one named ladder — it gives the rungs in pieces across a dozen videos. Every claim below is his; the ladder shape is assembled.

Rung What they are What moves them up What you supply
Stranger Never encountered you A pattern break. The brain filters out average and flags only difference Distinctiveness. "Being better than someone isn't enough. You need to be different"
Scroller Saw one post; decided in under 2 seconds Surviving the 8-question subconscious sequence: What is it? What's the story about? What does it look like? What does it mean for me? How do I feel? Do I care? Does this meet a need? Am I interested in following the story? Framing. Each encounter is "an at-bat" — enough strikeouts and they're off you permanently
Casual listener Likes a song, no relationship Repetition, spaced. Repeated exposure over time moves you into long-term storage; myelin wraps the pathway. "It's not brainwashing, it's neuro-reinforcement" Cadence. A show dropping one episode every few months can't build an audience even if it's incredible
Fan Watches the movie, not just the soundtrack Time. One great 30-second meeting vs. ten 20-minute hangouts — you bond with the second. "The brain doesn't distinguish digital hangouts from real ones." Plus emotional intensity: a director needs two hours to make you cry, the right song does it in 10 seconds Story, presence, vulnerability, enough episodes that they can predict you
Superfan Has converted "I like this" into "I am this" A point of conversion that costs something — first ticket, first merch — plus belief alignment. When a brand holds beliefs deeply and sticks to them, movements form A belief system, a named community, symbols, rituals, things to buy that mean something
Evangelist Does your marketing, unpaid Remarkability — literally "to remark about," not "incredible." Plus status: sharing you has to make them look good Purple-cow moments worth texting about: "Have you seen this?" "This is crazy." "I think you'd like it."

Two governing rules:

  • You can't skip rungs. Superfans "can only be created after the house exists." "One or two viral moments won't sell hard tickets" — he works with artists who have insane numbers and consistent viral posts but nobody buys tickets.
  • Some rungs are dead ends. A follow driven by attraction or by "wise friend who advises me" will "time out or won't convert" — migrate those people to another connection type before expecting a purchase. Watch the teacher trap too: lean too hard into tutorials and they come only for tutorials.

q.label: Diagnose why people follow you: name your top two reasons from the seven, cite what ten real followers told you, then audit your last 20 posts against it and count the strikes.
q.help: The seven reasons are attraction, aspiration, 'we are the same', raw entertainment, 'I feel cool following this person', weird/different/intriguing, and the wise friend who advises me. People usually follow for several at once, and multiple reasons form a stronger bond. This becomes your second idea filter alongside the movie — the best ideas are cool ideas with purpose. Two warnings: follows driven by attraction or 'wise friend' tend to time out or not convert, and the teacher trap means leaning too far into tutorials gets you an audience that only wants tutorials. Contradict the follow reason and the brain allows a few strikes, then they're gone.
q.eg: 'We are the same' plus entertainment. Ten replies said 'you sound like my group chat.' 4 of 20 posts were strikes.

q.label: Write your fan ladder plan: one specific move you will make to move people up each rung — stranger → scroller → casual listener → fan → superfan → evangelist.
q.help: Each rung moves for a different reason. Strangers move on a pattern break, because being better than someone isn't enough, you need to be different. Scrollers decide in under two seconds and every encounter is an at-bat. Casual listeners move on spaced repetition. Fans move on time — ten 20-minute hangouts beat one great 30-second meeting — plus emotional intensity. Superfans move on a point of conversion that costs something plus belief alignment. Evangelists move on remarkability and status. You cannot skip rungs: superfans only exist after the house is built, and one or two viral moments will not sell hard tickets.
q.eg: Casual → fan: a weekly long-form episode, same night every week, so they accumulate hours with me instead of seconds.

q.label: Design your point of conversion: the cheapest first thing someone can buy that means something. Name the item, the run size, the price, and the story the price is based on.
q.help: Paying converts a spectator into a participant — the buyer has said so with their wallet, and merch makes them a walking billboard, which only happens if they believe your work is worth representing. Make it limited, wearable and priced on story rather than on blank cost (a printed tee lands around $8-15 and sells direct at $35-45; venue sales usually give up a 10-25% merch cut). Other conversions that count: the first ticket, a numbered edition, vinyl. Give people something countable so they can rank themselves — Swift fans count shows attended like army stripes.
q.eg: 50 numbered screen-printed shirts, $40, printed live at the first show — the number is the date you joined.

q.label: Write two personas — 'who's coming over for dinner'. For each: what kind of person, their interests, their cultural icons, what cultures they're in, their job, where they're from, what they struggle with, what they care about.
q.help: The principle is go to the people, don't make the people come to you — which is impossible without knowing who they are. All eight questions, minimum two personas, and be specific enough that you could name the three accounts they already follow and the three rooms they already go to. The named failure is targeting Gen Z with Instagram posts and Facebook ads. Specificity is the whole point: the closer it is to you and to one real person, the more universal it becomes.
q.eg: 24, line cook in Chicago, into A24 films and thrifting, struggles with 60-hour weeks, goes to a Thursday warehouse night.

items.h:
2. The ONE method that makes fans obsess

Source: "The ONE Method That Makes Fans Obsess Over You Forever."

The claim. Humans bond fastest through shared belief or shared conflict — and what you stand against is more powerful than what you stand for. The moment the audience understands the enemy your brand fights, emotional alignment forms; if they stand against the same thing, it deepens into us-versus-them. It's tied to the primal survival need to belong.

His evidence stack: Independence Day (the second aliens attack, all inter-country fighting stops — politics, borders and differences vanish under one common enemy); sports and city rivalries running generations, where you can feel hostility toward a stranger from a rival city; political parties and religions, often stronger on what they oppose; punk rock and fashion subcultures, bonding through rejection of the mainstream; Harley-Davidson, selling rebellion and freedom rather than motorcycles; Apple, which built one of the strongest tribes ever standing against the "evil big brother" computer companies (IBM, HP) and later Mac vs. PC — a campaign entirely about identity: Apple young, cool, artistic, progressive; PC older, lame, nerdy, corporate.

The method: the Brand Foe Hierarchy. Not a list — a ranked totem pole, big boss at the top, smaller easier bad guys below. Star Wars is the model: the Empire, then the Emperor, then Darth Vader, then a general, then a stormtrooper. All obstruct the hero; some are harder to beat. The ranking gives you a difficulty curve — you win small battles publicly while the big boss stays unbeaten for years.

Hierarchy #1 — a HERO brand (doing hard things, going toward challenge to make the world better), 6 up to 1:

  • 6. Haters and trolls — not a big boss, but on the wrong day it lands. "Fully stormtrooper vibes." Built right, your fans handle these themselves.
  • 5. Not being seen / being overlooked — an idea, not a person. Most people feel the world doesn't see who they really are.
  • 4. Staying on the path — the distractions of the world; straying from purpose is easy, so fighting for focus is a foe.
  • 3. The physical demands of the pursuit — pushing to your limits, burning the candle at both ends.
  • 2. Time — his example: American football contains roughly 10 clocks (game clock, play clock, timeout clock, two-minute warning), all making time the antagonist.
  • 1. The shadow self / the ego / your inner thoughts — the big boss and possibly the most relatable villain alive.

Hierarchy #2 — a REBEL brand (against societal norms, the status quo, what they tell you you're supposed to be):

  • 6. Rule followers — not attacking you, but they make freedom harder to find.
  • 5. Fake people who edit themselves to fit social rules — other rebels dislike them too, so it creates strong POV alignment.
  • 4. Dopamine culture — people on autopilot in an invisible prison built for them.
  • 3. The regulators — those who tell you who you're supposed to be, out of their own fear.
  • 2. Self-censorship — "you versus you," through a rebel lens.
  • 1. Established systems — corporations, gatekeepers, people controlling everyday freedom for their own gain.

Enemies don't have to be people: superficiality, fake social-media lifestyles, bullies, corporate culture, the status quo, real musicianship vs. AI music, time, your own mind.

Six artist foe sets: Rage Against the Machine — corporate greed, political corruption, government oppression, economic inequality, media manipulation, blind obedience, social injustice. John Summit — the over-serious world of dance culture, fake cool-guy energy, wasted potential, the boring corporate nine-to-five. Chappell Roan — shame around self-expression, conservative expectations, industry pressure to play it safe, people who judge you for being weird or emotional. Blackpink — being underestimated, told to stay quiet, traditional gender expectations, industry control over identity, criticism of ambitious women. Jimmy Buffett — entirely non-political escapism: corporate culture, the man, your boss, material obsession, the idea you're alive only to work; he created "it's 5 o'clock somewhere." Anyma — humanity vs. technology: digital disconnection, emotional numbness, artificial identities, fear of technology replacing human soul. It works because those fears already exist; the brand gives an existing feeling an artistic format.

The rules. Never invent an enemy because it's good for the brand. Six is the worked example; never exceed 10. All battles must come from a singular origin. Once art-directing against the list, never deviate — express the same foes in varied forms. The foes should drive 100% of brand and content strategy. Don't be everything to everyone — "you end up becoming nothing to no one." A well-built tribe polices its own trolls. And archetype comes first: a hero list and a rebel list are different lists.

He models it live: he makes this content on a Saturday, he says, because he stands against the big corporations, big tech companies and gatekeepers that make it hard for artists to reach their audience — then asks whether you now feel differently about him than about "another guy on YouTube giving music marketing advice."

q.label: Write your brand foe hierarchy: six ranked foes with the big boss at #1 and the easiest, smallest foe at #6.
q.help: Humans bond fastest through shared conflict, and what you stand against is more powerful than what you stand for. Build it like Star Wars — Empire, Emperor, Vader, a general, a stormtrooper — so you can win small battles publicly while the big boss stays unbeaten for years. Six is the worked example and you must never exceed ten. All foes must come from one authentic origin, they must be emotionally real in your fans' daily lives, and enemies do not have to be people (time, superficiality, dopamine culture, self-censorship, the corporate nine-to-five, AI music). Never invent an enemy because it is good for the brand. Archetype decides the list: the hero list runs haters → not being seen → staying on the path → physical demands → time → the shadow self; the rebel list runs rule followers → fake people → dopamine culture → the regulators → self-censorship → established systems.
q.eg: John Summit's set: the over-serious world of dance culture, fake cool-guy energy, wasted potential, the boring corporate nine-to-five.

q.label: For each foe, list three ways to dramatize it in content without ever naming it directly.
q.help: Once you are art-directing against the list you never deviate — you express the same foes in varied forms, and they should drive 100% of brand and content strategy. Anyma dramatizes humanity versus technology through emotional numbness and artificial identities; Jimmy Buffett dramatized 'the man' and the idea you're alive only to work through pure escapism and 'it's 5 o'clock somewhere.' Each entry should be a concrete scene, setting or format — something you could shoot — not a slogan.
q.eg: Foe: dopamine culture. (1) Phone-in-a-drawer studio session. (2) Silent walk B-roll. (3) A set with no phones allowed.

items.h:
3. The psychology of belonging

Need to Belong theory — Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary, 1990s: the drive to form strong lasting relationships is as fundamental as hunger or thirst. It explains families, friend circles, clubs, online communities and fandoms.

The wiring: surviving alone was nearly impossible, so acceptance meant survival and rejection could mean death. The brain evolved dopamine and oxytocin rewards for connection and pain systems that punish rejection; Eisenberger and Lieberman (2003) found social rejection activates the same brain regions as physical pain. Measured harms of non-belonging: higher depression, higher anxiety, shorter lifespan; the widow or widower who dies months after a spouse; health collapse shortly after retirement from lost purpose. In Maslow's hierarchy — physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem, self-actualization — belonging sits in the middle, and without it the top two are harder to reach. His conclusion: "the game you're in is more biological and psychological than creative."

In-group / out-group, and the enemy. The insider logic is one line: "they don't believe what we believe." That's why defining the enemy is Step 1 of building a belief system, before archetype and before beliefs — a group needs an edge to exist. The price is explicit: "to have super fans you're also going to have super haters." If nothing creates clear opposition, you built a mailing list, not a group. Taylor Swift is the demonstration: when media attacks her, Swifties defend hard because "while they're defending her, they're subconsciously defending themselves." If she loses, they lose.

Initiation rituals and points of conversion. Entry requires a transformative ritual that signals commitment and sets a hard in/out boundary. It has to cost something.

His example What it does Your equivalent
Gang initiation Irreversible; you can't quietly un-join The tattoo — Party Favor's fans have tattooed lyrics from "Be Okay" and "Caskets"
Fraternity/sorority pledge, rush week Visible effort before acceptance Being there early: "I was at the 200-cap show"
Army boot camp — "turns civilians into soldiers" You exit a different category of person The first show: paid, physical, multisensory, unrepeatable
Country club application plus sponsorship by an existing member Entry gated by an insider vouching A friend putting someone on — the "you have to hear this" text. Why word of mouth differs structurally from an ad
Buying the first product, ticket or merch item Paying converts spectator into participant Exactly this — the one he names for brands, and the cheapest to build

Two supporting mechanics: earned stripes (Swift fans count shows attended "like army stripes" — give people something countable and they'll rank themselves inside your world), and the purchase as conversion (music is devalued because subscription framing makes it feel free; buying vinyl and CDs turned casual listeners into fans who "said so with your wallet").

Identity conversion: "I like this" → "I am this." A well-defined belief set converts a casual liker into someone who adopts the brand as personal identity — that's what produces lifelong superfans, and Alba argues the belief system matters more than the product. The physical marker is merch: someone willing to be a walking billboard is telling the world they identify with you, which requires believing your work is best-in-world enough to represent. "Artists who can sell merch are on a different level." Same logic in Travis Scott merch and Rolex (nobody needs a watch to tell time in 2025 — "you are a better version of yourself with a Rolex on than without"). The memory version: fans link the artist to social belonging, one of the brain's strongest emotional systems, and the identity they wear becomes a "neural badge." Memory communities: Swifties, Little Monsters, deadmau5 fans in mouse ears.

4. Building a cult following

The model — the House (from the Skrillex art-direction video). Superfans, not music, hold up the biggest brands, and they're manufactured by architecture:

  1. The Land — the emotional/cultural territory. "If it were a movie, what genre is it?"
  2. The Blueprints — the archetype (Skrillex = Rebel + Creator).
  3. The Foundation — the belief system, a rulebook that settles every creative argument. Skrillex's centre is freedom, creativity and cool, so his rulebook is "the rules of cool."
  4. The Floor Plan — the plot (Skrillex = the quest; album literally called Quest for Fire).
  5. The Materials — themes, then visual and sonic language, then mood boards.
  6. The Front Door — logo, press photos, content, rollout.
  7. The Rooms — where superfans are made. They're inside; the job is staying consistent and executing the same story across every touchpoint: music, visuals, live show, content, merch, moments, everywhere your people already hang out.

At zero audience, steps 1–6 are your work. Step 7 is the rest of your career. "When your brand becomes their brand, you have a super fan." And: "one house can become a whole city."

Community mechanics.

  • Name the fanbase. Little Monsters, Swifties, Illenium's Illenials, Slipknot's maggots. The shift is precise: "I like Taylor Swift" becomes "I'm a Swiftie." One is a preference, the other is a noun you can be.
  • Standing questions of a community leader: How are you showing up for your people? What rituals do you do together? What are the symbols? How do you showcase like-minded taste?
  • Symbols and insider language. The Justice cross, one of music's most recognizable logos, from artists who began as graphic designers. Buffett's "it's 5 o'clock somewhere." Mouse ears. The Halloween Costume Test — if someone dressed as you, what would they wear, could they assemble it easily, would we recognize it instantly? He calls it "the ultimate brand test," and it's the same test as insider language: a symbol works only if a fan can wear or say it without explaining it.
  • Decide your distance deliberately. John Summit's beliefs include "we do not believe in fans, we believe in friends." Fred again..'s include the artist should not stand above the audience on a pedestal — enforced down to camera framing: never frame the artist above the audience. When someone knocked the CDJ off at Boiler Room, Fred laughed, restarted the song and jumped with them instead of calling security. Compare Gesaffelstein, a ruler brand keeping distance on purpose, or Justice, whose beliefs include mystique over exposure. Both work. What kills you is being accidentally neither.
  • Ritualize the recurring. The Steve Aoki jump — mid-jump photos in key locations worldwide, later with other DJs and celebrities, all versions numbered.
  • Ask for word of mouth out loud. 12th Planet closed his set at Control with "my name is 12th Planet, tell all your friends about me."

The ethical line. These are manipulation-adjacent tools, and the channel draws the line in three places. (1) Authenticity is the boundary — you may not invent an enemy or adopt beliefs you don't hold; the Unique Test kills borrowed beliefs, the Time Test kills convenient ones. (2) Extremity is optional — Rage Against the Machine puts politics at the centre; Jordan Brand is explicitly apolitical, "greatness and style, not politics." Both honest. (3) Your brand is part of you but not all of you — you're directing a movie, not exhibiting every side of yourself. That's curation, not deception: you don't show all of yourself to the barista or your grandparents either. On framing he's blunt: luxury scarcity "can absolutely be argued that it's manipulation, but it's storytelling, experience, and framing." Expanded The practical line: framing that raises how much someone feels from real work is craft; framing that substitutes for the work fails on contact with the first show.

q.label: Name your fanbase. Write the name and the sentence a fan would say using it.
q.help: The shift is precise: 'I like Taylor Swift' becomes 'I'm a Swiftie' — one is a preference, the other is a noun you can be. Named precedents: Little Monsters, Swifties, Illenium's Illenials, Slipknot's maggots. The test is whether someone would use it unprompted in a bio or a comment without explaining it. It should come out of your land, your foes and your beliefs, not out of a rhyming dictionary.
q.eg: Deadmau5 fans in mouse ears; Buffett's Parrotheads with 'it's 5 o'clock somewhere.'

q.label: Write three symbols, two rituals you always do, and two phrases of insider language.
q.help: The standing questions of a community leader are: how are you showing up for your people, what rituals do you do together, what are the symbols, how do you showcase like-minded taste. Symbols must pass the Halloween Costume Test — if someone dressed as you, could they assemble it easily and would we recognise it instantly — and insider language works only if a fan can say it without explaining it. Rituals should be things you repeat and number, like the Steve Aoki jump, or say out loud, like 12th Planet closing with 'my name is 12th Planet, tell all your friends about me.'
q.eg: Symbol: the Justice cross. Ritual: numbered mid-jump photos in every city. Language: 'it's 5 o'clock somewhere.'

q.label: Decide your distance from the audience deliberately: are you on their level, or above them — and what rules enforce it?
q.help: Both work; what kills you is being accidentally neither. John Summit's belief is 'we do not believe in fans, we believe in friends.' Fred again..'s belief that the artist should not stand above the audience is enforced down to camera framing — never frame the artist above the crowd — and when someone knocked the CDJ at Boiler Room he laughed, restarted and jumped with them. Gesaffelstein keeps ruler distance on purpose; Justice hold mystique over exposure. Write the choice plus two or three enforceable rules (framing, replies, DMs, backstage, how you talk).
q.eg: On their level. Rules: never framed above the crowd, reply to every comment for 60 minutes after posting, no VIP-only content.

items.h:
5. How to build an audience of millions

Step 1 — diagnose why people follow you. Most artists "blindly make things and share things." The seven reasons, all sitting on Maslow:

  1. Sexual/romantic attraction — they imagine themselves with you; pre-programmed mate-finding wiring that persists even in committed relationships.
  2. Aspiration — "I want my life to be like this person's." Not necessarily wealth; can be kindness, power, status, lifestyle.
  3. "We are the same" — your reflection, confirmed biases, "I feel like we would be friends." Strong and durable.
  4. Raw entertainment — funnier, more controversial, more creative than the rest of the noise.
  5. "I feel cool following this person" — a status shift; people use artists to define identity.
  6. Weird / different / intriguing — the brain flags novelty and follows to see if the interest holds.
  7. The wise friend who advises me — everyone casts themselves as the hero and seeks "their next Sensei, Jedi Master, or person to get them out of the Matrix."

People usually follow for several reasons at once, and multiple reasons form a stronger connection than one. For artists it all rides on top of also liking the music.

Step 2 — use it four ways. Deepen the connection (lean into the actual reason). Better use your time (if they're there for entertainment, spend your interaction time producing entertaining moments). Add it as a second idea filter — with the movie defined and the follow-reason defined, you have two filters to kill ideas: "the best ideas are cool ideas with purpose." A bad idea is a cool idea with no story purpose, like a scene that looks great but takes you out of the film; he claims this saves years. Apply it to content strategy — "the specific organization of the stories and content concepts that will accompany your music."

His archetype × follow-reason mixes: a Jester followed for entertainment should be roughly 95% high-level, share-worthy comedy. A Hero followed for "we are the same" makes content about doing hard things because they're right. A Magician (Prince) followed for weird-yet-intriguing showcases the weirdness. A Lover followed for attraction leans into love, soft flirting, sexuality. A Rebel followed for "we are the same" must not do the latest dance trend to their new song — while an Everyman whose fans share dance culture absolutely should. Same tactic, opposite verdict, decided by the relationship. The strikes rule: contradict the follow reason and "the brain will allow for a few strikes, but too many and they're over it."

The compounding mechanics.

  • Time equals bond — the 30-seconds-vs-3-hours test above. Research he cites: younger generations feel more bonded to their favourite live streamer than their favourite movie actor, purely on hours spent.
  • Repetition = memory = identity. People bond when they can predict you, recognize patterns and know what you stand for. "This is brand architecture 101."
  • The platform tailwind. Around 2024 algorithms shifted from discovery mode into "interest media," optimizing for identity, niche resonance, predictability, return viewership and depth of connection instead of volume and novelty. Because performance now depends on value and engagement rather than follower count, someone with 500 followers can get as many impressions as someone with 50,000. "The playing field is more even than it's ever been."
  • The channel/studio model. Stop dumping every content type on one page. Split your strongest formats onto separate subpages — they grow faster because the algorithm knows what to do with them, and when someone engages with a subpage the platform will likely serve them your other channels, very often your main page. Think like a channel manager, the way MTV went from one channel to over 60 at its peak.
  • Documented results: several Cult clients grew new channels by 10,000–20,000 real followers with fewer than 50 posts in a couple of months. Vinyl Nights — cinematic record-listening sessions, identical shots every time, only the song changes — reached ~700,000 followers in a few months. Wookie's "Beats I Can't Release" was repeated ~200 times and changed his career; rights owners eventually officially released several of the remixes.

Five growth levers that don't need money. Stand on existing stages — fully original first offerings struggle because there's no prior reference in the viewer's mind, so the brain files them as "this doesn't matter to us." Shorten the runway with an official remix, bootleg, sampled song, cover, a trusted label or channel, or attaching to reputable people; he says this is the 0→100 path for ~90% of the big electronic artists he watched (Porter Robinson's "Say My Name" is the exception that proves the rule). Nothing beats word of mouth — "not more expensive, more creative." Paranormal Activity ran a trailer of night-vision footage of audiences reacting rather than scary scenes: budget under $20,000, $193 million worldwide. Go to the people; don't make the people come to you — requires personas, the exercise they nickname "who's coming over for dinner" (what kind of person, what interests, whose cultural icons, what cultures, what jobs, where from, what they struggle with, what they care about). His named client mistake: targeting Gen Z with Instagram posts and Facebook ads. Stack the odds — many simultaneous avenues, never one; "cool people know cool people," so attach people with their own followings to every launch, because trust transfers. Digital is good, experiential is better — in-person bonds harder, and real-life events self-select for real fans.

The timeframes. 24 months minimum on a new brand before judging it. 12–24 months locked into the concept. 6 months on one narrow guiding idea for the music. 12–24 months or 40–50 demos per signature-sound season. Five or six full cycles before a breakthrough, invoked alongside "10,000 hours" and "10-year overnight success." ~15 years for Max Styler, a client since he was 18. ~200 repetitions of one format for Wookie. Planning horizons: 4–6 months ahead for big artists, 1–2 months mid-tier, none for new artists; 24-month strategy plans at the top. His warning: "the climb gets hardest right before the elevation kicks in." The biggest mistake is starting over whenever it gets hard — new plan, new name, new brand, new sound. Path-switchers "circle around slightly above base camp and end up back where they started." "Commitment is the attribute that wins every time."

6. Live shows and IRL

Why shows convert harder than anything digital. A concert is multisensory encoding — music plus crowd plus visuals plus physically wearing merch — creating a far stronger memory trace than the same song under a social video. It's the boot camp initiation: paid, effortful, shared. And it's the purest form of time-equals-bond. It's also where the industry ranking lives: the business hierarchy is how many tickets can you sell, how much merch do people buy, how many people are listening. What does not count: how long you've been doing this, how nice you are, how easy you are to work with, how hard you work. "Headliners headline because they move the most tickets."

The local-to-headliner path (from the 5 Levels):

  • Level 2 → professional: you pull a few hundred people locally, repeatedly, not as a one-off. Learn cash flow and monthly burn; separate look gigs from income gigs. "A lot of artists confuse busy with progress."
  • Level 3 → touring: small soft-ticket rooms (rooms with built-in audiences) or support slots where a bigger act shares their fans. The agent enters at 10–20% of gross performance fee; if a promoter offers $2,500, a good agent raises it — you make more, they make more. Touring is reading demand signals, not going everywhere: "one strong city is worth more than five weak ones." Graduation: people pay to see you in cities you don't live in — "not because it's free… because they chose you."
  • Level 4 → headliner: execution speed, expert calendar management ("what they don't do is often more important than what they do"), systems, leadership, data. Graduation: your name alone anchors the show; "the system now bends around you."

The John Summit arc

Expanded — accuracy flag The video titled "Local Artist to Headliner in 36 months" contains no month-by-month timeline. "36 months" is a packaging claim in the title only; the video is an eight-principle teardown. Anyone selling you a 36-month schedule from it invented it. The actual content, in full:

  1. An artist brand is a movie, not just a person. His early brand was effectively a social-media reality show — working on music, post; funny mood, post; drunk after a party, post. "Ultra extreme realness, full transparency, but from a defined perspective." Positioning: "your fun friend John" — the buddy from college somehow becoming one of the biggest artists in the world, deliberately not the too-cool guy at the party. Fan psychology: "one of us is making it." Good music is table stakes — "a great soundtrack still needs the movie in order for people to care."
  2. Origin story and villain. Accountant by day, dance-music lover by night, turned DJ-producer, then quit the accounting job. The accountant fact is what people lead with when putting a friend on to him — "that's storytelling at its finest." Villain: the pretentiousness of the typical too-cool DJ-producer. Archetype: Everyman. Superpower outside the music: ultra-relatability and honesty on a level plane with strangers worldwide.
  3. The story must keep moving. Extreme change, high contrast: accountant → producer → touring DJ → one of the biggest artists in dance music. Plot: rags to riches, a Cinderella story where "the audience feels like they win the more John wins."
  4. The look needs a signature. Everyman brands are harder to style than rebels or rulers, who can go extreme on fashion. His signatures: open shirts and the headphone band positioned forward — signatures only through repetition. The Halloween/impersonation test applies: comedy videos of people dressing as Fisher, James Hype, Anyma or John Summit work because each has recognizable visual signatures.
  5. Consistency is more about what you DON'T do. Real consistency is boundaries. On a collaborative video shoot, one artist suggested a shot with fake acid tabs on their tongues; the other said within seconds, "No, sorry. I don't want to do that. It's not my brand." No drama, straight to the next shot. "That's the power of clarity." He also flags a real misalignment — the label name Experts Only can read as we only want experts, closer to ruler than everyman (the prior name, Off The Grid, leaned explorer; his understanding is it changed over a trademark issue). Verdict: ~95% of the rest of the brand lines up.
  6. Clear art direction turns content into a brand. Photography that looks real, almost "stolen" — on-camera flash, imperfect, like an old point-and-shoot. Video largely iPhone footage shot by people in the crowd. Tour flyers candid. Live show: no big time-coded visuals like Anyma — large-scale lighting, lasers, John as the primary focus; at the O2 Arena in London the show is mostly him rather than giant screens. His big moment brings out real dancers behind and above him — crucially not pop choreography; they dance like audience members feeling the music, and he dances too.
  7. Campaigns are scenes in the larger movie. The "Comfort in Chaos" / Control-Escape campaign: a guy in a 9-to-5 escaping into dance music. Visual identity is John in a suit in an accounting office called "Summit CPAs," in a cubicle with an old computer — applied to album cover, tour flyer, default images on digital platforms, banners, social posts. The "Lights Go Out" video opens with him bored in a warehouse office while other accountants make CPA calls; the music forces them into a trance that pulls them out of their jobs into freestyle dancing, ending in an explosive party. "Every part of the campaign is run through one controlling lens."
  8. The brand that got you here may not take you there. What happens when the hero wins? "Once a character in a story reaches the goal, the story then becomes boring." He's mid-transition: Everyman → Hero. Evidence: far fewer drunken rants, more exercise and running content, showing his kind side, giving his team flowers. Precedents: Calvin Harris went rebel → hero in the 2010s; Martin Garrix went everyman → hero. Formula: new harder challenges + new villains = continued brand interest and growth.

Summary judgment: the team built a "brand magnet." Diagnostic: "You don't need a massive team. You just need clarity, intention, and consistency."

What to do about shows now, with no audience

The best case study is Alba's own zero-audience promoter story.

Attempt 1: mid-20s, small-town kid, no promo experience. He copied the local model — booked a venue, put himself on the lineup, printed flyers, went out every night for weeks handing out thousands outside clubs. Result: ~10 people outside his friend group; about 40 total in a 150-cap venue. Diagnosis: strangers had no reputation with him and no relationship — like being invited to a stranger's house.

Attempt 2: an art show with music in the downtown LA warehouse loft he shared with SCI-Arc architecture students — already gallery-like, with a rooftop deck. He stacked it with people who carried relationships: a dozen local artists with small followings, 24 DJs across multiple rooms including two known headliners, local DJs with residencies around LA, bartenders and barbacks with their own friend groups, a local clothing company doing live screen printing with limited shirts, and a paid flyer feature in LA Weekly. Break-even: 150 people at $8. Everyone promoted on their own socials. Result: almost 800 people. That became the template for every event after, and eventually a residency at the Avalon Theater doing 1,000+ almost every week. Even when a headliner could sell it out alone he kept every channel running out of paranoia — and says the paranoia kept him sharp.

Your moves, plus the show-framing tactics from the framing video:

  • Don't book a show and hope — build a room where everyone on the bill brings someone. Artists, DJs, a visual artist, a clothing brand doing something live, people with small followings of their own.
  • Play your city rarely. Once a year makes it an annual moment; once a month or every couple of weeks kills urgency ("I'll catch them on the next one") and lowers perceived value.
  • Frame the room cheaply: request your setup on the floor in the centre of the audience instead of on stage; bring a strobe and smoke machine on foot pedals; wear monochromatic outfits matched to colour-coded gear, White Stripes style.
  • Perform like you're already a headliner. He watched a newly signed artist play the back room at Dim Mak Tuesdays to maybe 50 people — platinum blonde, big sunglasses, matching sequins, carried onstage by four shirtless guys, insane energy on a tiny stage. That was Lady Gaga: "she was performing at the Grammys even though the audience was small." Same lesson from Dada Life giving full champagne-and-bananas energy at 3 a.m. to a couple hundred people in a 2,000-cap room. Belief is infectious.
  • But be a good opener. His explicit PSA: this does not mean playing headliner-level music out of the gate. Being a good support act is a lost art; setting the tone is crucial. "Be aware of where you are and be the best in that space… don't blow it out early."
  • Sell shows as an experience. "We should try this / doesn't this look fun" is flagged as especially useful for show announces.
  • Do experiential at any size — a small pop-up or a unique listening party counts. And let the internet do the work when a moment is remarkable enough: the Smile campaign placed people with creepy smiles at events across the US and let media do the awareness lifting.

q.label: Plan one IRL moment inside 90 days where every participant brings their own people. Name the date, the venue, everyone on the bill, the break-even math, and who promotes.
q.help: This is the zero-audience playbook: attempt one was flyering every night for weeks and getting about 40 people into a 150-cap room. Attempt two was an art show with music stacked with people who carried relationships — a dozen local artists, 24 DJs across multiple rooms including two known headliners, bartenders and barbacks with their own friend groups, a clothing company doing live screen printing with limited shirts, and a paid flyer feature in LA Weekly. Break-even was 150 people at $8; almost 800 came. Digital is good, experiential is better, and real events self-select for real fans. A pop-up or a listening party counts.
q.eg: Break-even 150 at $8. Bill: 6 DJs, 4 visual artists, a screen printer, a coffee brand — 11 promoters instead of one.

q.label: Set your show frequency in your home city, and list the cheap framing tactics you will use to make a small room look like a headline show.
q.help: Playing your city once a year makes it an annual moment; once a month or every couple of weeks kills urgency ('I'll catch them on the next one') and lowers perceived value. Cheap framing given: request your setup on the floor in the centre of the audience rather than on stage, bring a strobe and smoke machine on foot pedals, wear monochromatic outfits matched to colour-coded gear. Perform like you're already a headliner — Lady Gaga played a 50-person back room like the Grammys — but be a good opener: know where you are in the night and don't blow it out early.
q.eg: Home city twice a year, both self-promoted. Floor setup in the round, two pedal strobes, all-white fit matched to white gear.

q.label: Name the existing stages you will stand on in the next 12 months: which official remix, bootleg, sample, cover, label, channel or collaborator gets you a prior reference in the listener's mind?
q.help: Fully original first offerings struggle because there is no prior reference, so the brain files them as 'this doesn't matter to us' — standing on an existing stage is described as the 0-to-100 path for roughly 90% of the big electronic artists watched, with Porter Robinson's 'Say My Name' as the exception. Stack the odds: many simultaneous avenues, never one, and attach people with their own followings to every launch because trust transfers — cool people know cool people. Name specific tracks, labels, channels and people with dates, not categories.
q.eg: Two bootlegs of records my scene already loves, one official remix pitch, one co-hosted night with a residency DJ.

items.h:
7. Exercises — Phase 5

What "done" looks like: a stranger who spends 60 seconds with you can say what you're against, not just what you sound like. You can name your community and your people use the name unprompted. There is one cheap thing to buy that makes someone feel they joined something. You know the top two reasons people follow you and can defend it from real replies and DMs. One series exists with 50 entries and a recognizable format. You've run at least one room where the crowd wasn't just your friends.

phases.goal: The numbers, rights and revenue picture a label or agent will ask for, plus the 12-month plan and the specific ask you are making.
phases.intro: The business side asks three questions and only three: how many tickets can you sell, how many people buy merch and how much, and how many people are listening. Tenure, niceness and how hard you work do not appear on that list. This section is general information, not legal or financial advice — get a music lawyer before you sign anything — but every number here should be true, current, and something you can say from memory.

items.h:
General information only — not legal, tax or financial advice. Terms vary by territory, contract and negotiation. Get a music lawyer before you sign anything.

The channel's blunt version: "how many people can you bring to the party?" Everything here is downstream of that.

1. The revenue map

Stream How it works Roughly when Unlocked by
Live performance fees A promoter or talent buyer pays you to play. His real numbers: he booked Steve Aoki for $1,000 and Skrillex for $300 in the early 2000s; Hollywood offers in the 2010s ran $1,500 to $100K by draw; mid-tier is $2K–$5K; $20K+ is where lifestyle questions arrive; $100,000+ marks the top tier; Cult clients get $25K–$100K+. Party Favor started at $100 gigs Level 1 onward Draw. Nothing else
Self-promoted shows You take door risk and upside. Alba's break-even was 150 people at $8 Immediately Willingness to organize and stack the bill
Streaming Per-stream royalties via distributor or label Immediately, tiny Volume. Subscription framing makes music feel free
Merch Highest-identity item you sell. "Artists who can sell merch are on a different level" Once superfans exist A belief system worth wearing
Products / experiential Pop-ups, limited drops, listening parties, physical goods Mid Community. "It is easier to build recurring revenue from products than from streams"
Brand partnerships Brands pay for trust, community, taste and cultural relevance, not fame. Peggy Gou: Nike (Air Max ambassador), Ray-Ban, Louis Vuitton, Alpha Industries, Don Julio. RAYE: Dyson, Nintendo, H&M, Audemars Piguet Earlier than most think — brands are "aggressively hunting," so even smaller followings get real offers An audience that "listens, buys, shares, and identifies with the lifestyle"
Remixes / commissions Paid official remixes. Alba became a go-to remixer for Interscope, Def Jam, Capitol on 48-hour to one-week turnarounds Level 1–2 Being fast and good; one relationship (his came via Skrillex → Dave Rene)
Production / writing for others Fred Gibson produced and wrote for Ed Sheeran, Rita Ora, Demi Lovato before stepping out Level 1–3 Craft plus rooms
Sync licensing Music in film, TV, games, ads. He recommends it to hack memory centres via context, including mood playlists like "late night drives" Any time Owning your rights and a clear identifiable sound
Publishing royalties Income from the composition First release Registration — most beginners never do it
Masters income Income from the recording First release Owning them. "Own your masters" is Lesson 9
Label / imprint Your own label as a brand asset (Fool's Gold, Experts Only) Level 3+ Audience trust that transfers to other artists
Teaching / tools Alba's second business is knowledge; Curt Cameruci moved from records to making production tools Any time Expertise others want
Investing Save your money or invest in real estate, or both. Many top artists bought multifamily real estate when money arrived Once income is real Not blowing it

The number to internalize: a friends' band with 20–30k followers all-in has an average annual spend per fan of $300, and the band alone is described as an eight-figure business. You don't need to be a household name to be a millionaire artist. "One highly connected fan community can easily outperform a much larger but disconnected audience."

q.label: Build your revenue map: mark every stream Live / Dormant / Not yet available, with the actual amount it earned in the last 12 months — then write the one thing that unlocks the next dormant stream.
