q.help: The streams are live performance fees, self-promoted shows, streaming, merch, products and experiential, brand partnerships, remixes and commissions, production or writing for others, sync licensing, publishing royalties, masters income, a label or imprint, teaching or tools, and investing. Each is unlocked by something specific: live fees by draw and nothing else, merch by a belief system worth wearing, brand partnerships by an audience that listens, buys, shares and identifies with the lifestyle. It is easier to build recurring revenue from products than from streams, and a band with 20-30k followers all-in averaging $300 annual spend per fan is described as an eight-figure business.
q.eg: Live $4,200 (live) · Streaming $310 (live) · Merch $0 (dormant — unlock: the 50-shirt numbered drop) · Sync (not yet).

q.label: Run the rights audit: for every released track, who owns the master, are the splits agreed in writing, and are you registered with a PRO as a writer (and publisher, if self-publishing) with every work registered?
q.help: Every song is two pieces of property — the composition and the master — generating different money and licensable separately. Own your masters is Lesson 9 and not owning them is called the biggest regret of more artists than can be counted. Agree splits in the room, in writing, on the day; unagreed splits are the most common cause of catastrophic disputes. A PRO (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, PRS, SOCAN, APRA, GEMA) is cheap and takes an afternoon; if you have released music and never joined one, money is sitting uncollected. Fully self-owned tracks are also far easier to place in sync. Fix any 'no' this month and note the date you fixed it.
q.eg: 6 tracks, all masters mine, 2 with unsigned co-producer splits (fixing this week). BMI writer registered; publisher side not yet.

q.label: Set your pricing: your current show fee and the fee you're holding for, your break-even show size, your merch prices, and the framing levers you're using to justify them.
q.help: Framing moves real value — in the wine studies, subjects preferred whichever glass was labelled expensive roughly 90% of the time, across over 5,000 people. The holding story is the pricing lesson: an agent said 'not enough and not yet' twice before accepting $12,000 plus a headline slot, but the framing was backed by real marketing, press and ticket demand — holding out with nothing behind it is just being unavailable. Reference points: mid-tier is $2K-$5K, $20K+ is where lifestyle questions arrive, $100K+ is the top tier. Levers: show frequency, billing, scarcity and numbered runs, packaging ('if it feels expensive, even if it isn't'), the company you keep, and the brand deck — as a talent buyer of almost 15 years, receiving one 'immediately made them more expensive in my mind.'
q.eg: Current $500-750 local. Holding at $1,500 outside my city. Break-even self-promoted: 150 at $8. Shirts $40, 50 numbered.

q.label: Calculate your monthly burn, how many months you survive with no income, and whether the day job stays.
q.help: Cash flow literacy is not just how much comes in but when it comes and goes, and how long you survive if things slow. Quit the day job only when music is your primary income and the thing driving your quality of life — once survival stress enters, the stress does not make good music, and compromised art fails, so you can move backwards. Arnold Schwarzenegger is the model: laid brick, invested in multifamily real estate, and was a millionaire before he ever acted, so he could refuse roles that would damage his brand. Also flagged: a professional with only one big income source can drop a level fast.
q.eg: Burn $2,900/mo. Runway 3 months. Day job stays until music clears $3,500/mo for six straight months.

q.label: What is your 12-month financial goal, broken down by revenue stream and by quarter?
q.help: Write results, not goals — a result either happened or it didn't. Break the total into the streams from your revenue map, with a quarterly figure for each, so the plan shows which stream you are actually betting on. Anchor it to the unit economics you know: your break-even show size, your merch margin, your average fee. Aggressive but realistic is the stated standard, and the number should ladder directly into the 12-month plan in the next group.
q.eg: $34,000: live $22k (24 shows avg $900), merch $7k (two 50-piece drops), remix commissions $4k, streaming $1k.

q.label: Write the five press talking points you want in every interview this era.
q.help: Write talking points before every interview and podcast — don't go in blind, and keep it candid. Interviews are a storytelling and plot-setup tool, so each point should carry a piece of the movie: the origin fact people repeat when they put a friend on to you (John Summit's is the accountant job), the foe, the era's guiding idea, the thing you refuse to do, and the current chapter. Five short lines you could say out loud, not paragraphs.
q.eg: 'I quit accounting at 26.' 'Dance music got too serious.' 'Everything is shot on a point-and-shoot.'

items.h:
2. Industry mechanics explained Expanded

The channel uses these terms and defines almost none. Everything marked Expanded is standard industry knowledge added so the terms are usable; the channel's own claims are labelled.

Two copyrights, always. Expanded Every song is two pieces of property. The composition (melody, chords, lyrics), controlled by songwriters and their publisher. The master (the specific recording), controlled by whoever owns the recording. They generate different money, are licensed separately, and can be owned by different people. Someone can cover your song without permission (compulsory mechanical licence in the US); nobody can use your recording without clearing the master. Channel claim: "Own your masters. It's your original art. If you made it, you should own it" — the biggest regret of more artists than he can count.

Splits. Expanded The agreed percentage each contributor owns. Two split sheets per song: one for the composition (anyone who contributed to the writing) and one for the master (artist, sometimes producer via producer points, sometimes a label). Agree them in the room, in writing, on the day. Unagreed splits are the most common cause of catastrophic artist disputes.

Royalty types. Expanded

Royalty Triggered by Collected by Paid from
Mechanical Reproduction of the composition — downloads, physical units, the composition half of a stream Publisher / mechanical body (the MLC in the US) Composition
Performance Public performance of the composition — radio, TV, venues, composition half of a stream Your PRO Composition
Master royalties Use of the recording — streams, downloads Distributor or label Master
Neighbouring rights Public performance of the recording (mostly non-US) Neighbouring rights collectors Master
Sync fee One-off negotiated licence pairing music with picture Publisher and master owner Both — you generally need both sides cleared

A PRO Expanded is a Performing Rights Organization — ASCAP, BMI or SESAC in the US; PRS (UK), SOCAN (Canada), APRA (Australia), GEMA (Germany). Register as a writer (and separately as a publisher if you self-publish), register every work, and they collect performance money for you. If you've released music and never joined one, money has been sitting uncollected. It's cheap and takes an afternoon.

Distributors vs. labels. Expanded A distributor (DistroKid, TuneCore, Symphonic, UnitedMasters, the label-services arms of majors) gets your recording onto platforms. Flat fee or small revenue share; you keep your masters; no marketing, no advance, no A&R. A label invests money and people — recording, marketing, radio, video, playlist relationships — in exchange for owning or controlling the masters for a term and a much larger share. Channel claim: none of the five levels require a label. "What they require is leverage and an audience." The typical industry ladder is "fading into the distance." Cult has gotten songs signed to major labels for brand-new clients purely on a pitch deck with a strong brand story and mood boards — the deck was the leverage.

Label deals, 360 deals, advances, recoupment. Expanded An advance is not a fee — it's a prepayment against your future royalties. Recoupment means the label recovers its recoupable costs (advance, marketing, video budgets, sometimes tour support) out of your royalty share only, not theirs. That's how an artist can be "successful" and unrecouped for years — and recoupment isn't repayment: once recouped, the label typically still owns the masters. A 360 deal takes a percentage not just of recordings but of touring, merch, publishing, endorsements, sometimes acting; the stated rationale is that the label builds the brand that makes those valuable. The risk is giving away a share of live and merch — the two things this channel says actually pay. Term and options matter as much as percentages: "one album with four options" is a deal the label can extend and you can't exit. The question to hold: what is being bought, for how long, and what happens when the term ends? Reversion (masters returning to you after a set period) is negotiable and routinely ignored by artists staring at the advance number.

Sync licensing. Expanded Pairing music with visual media — film, TV, ads, games, trailers, social campaigns. You need clearance on both composition and master, which is why fully self-owned tracks are far easier to place and often preferred by music supervisors. Fees run from a few hundred dollars for small indie placements to six figures for national campaigns, and a sync often also generates ongoing performance royalties when the show airs. Channel claim: sync is its own department on the major-artist org chart, and he recommends syncing into "movies, TV shows, video games, social content, and mood/style playlists" as a memory strategy as much as a revenue one.

Booking agents. Channel claim: agents typically take 10–20% of gross performance fee depending on agency services. If a promoter offers $2,500, a good agent raises the fee — "you make more, they make more." You can book yourself, but a good agent expands the markets you can reach and adds brand reputation. He puts the agent's arrival at Level 3. Expanded "Gross" means commission comes off the whole fee, before your costs. Agents are generally exclusive by territory and paid on deals they source and deals routed through them. They live on deal flow, so they sign artists who can already sell tickets — which is why the agent arrives after the audience, never before.

Management. Channel claim: the manager usually arrives at Level 2, "typically a friend who believes in the project." Alba recruited a close friend with zero management experience purely on personality fit; they worked together for years with a lot of success and the friend went on to manage other successful artists. His warning: most artists forget the role entirely or wait for a manager to "reveal themselves once the music pops off," and many hold little respect for it because it doesn't look creative. "That's a huge miss. A good manager is often the difference between a mid-level artist and a top-tier one." Expanded Standard commission is 15–20% of gross artist income, usually across most streams, sometimes with carve-outs (recording costs, session work, pre-existing deals). Get the term, commission base, carve-outs and the sunset clause (declining commission after you part ways on deals signed during the term) in writing before real money moves. A business manager is a different job — accounting, taxes, bill payment, reporting — usually 5% or a flat fee. Channel warning: it is "staggering" how many stories he's heard of business managers stealing from artists — "it happens far more than you'd think." Vet hard and keep your own eyes on statements.

Merch margins. Expanded A printed tee costs roughly $8–15 landed depending on blank quality, print method and quantity. Sold direct-to-fan online at $35–45 you keep most of the gap minus processing and shipping. Sold at a venue you typically pay a merch cut of 10–25% of gross (sometimes negotiable, often waived in small rooms), plus a seller. Print-on-demand removes inventory risk and most of the margin. Channel claim: merch is not primarily a margin business, it's an identity business — the wearer becomes a walking billboard, which only happens if they believe your work is best-in-world enough to represent.

q.label: What are your current monthly listeners and total streams, per platform, as of today's date?
q.help: Give the raw figures with the date attached and the trend over the last six months (up, flat, down, and by how much). Streaming is the smallest revenue line you have and subscription framing makes music feel free, but it is the third of the three questions the business side asks, and every conversation starts here. Include your top five cities and top five countries if the dashboard shows them — city-by-city concentration matters more than the total, because one strong city is worth more than five weak ones.
q.eg: Spotify 4,120 monthly listeners (up from 900 in Feb); 61k all-time streams; top cities Chicago, Detroit, Berlin.

q.label: List your follower count on every platform you're active on, with the 90-day growth number for each.
q.help: Follower count no longer gates distribution — after the algorithm change, someone with 500 followers can get as many impressions as someone with 50,000 — but a label will still ask, so have it exact and dated. What matters more is which platform is compounding and off which format, so note next to each number the format driving the growth. Include any subpage separately.
q.eg: TikTok 6,800 (+3,100 in 90 days, all from the property); IG 2,340 (+180); YouTube 410 (+60).

q.label: How many people are on your email list and any SMS/direct list, and how often do you actually contact them?
q.help: This is the audience you own rather than borrow — at scale there are people whose entire job is owning the audience instead of renting it from a platform. Give the size, the growth rate, the open rate if you have it, and the collection mechanism (show sign-ups, DM gate, download gate). If the number is zero, say zero and write the one step that changes it this month; the comment-gate mechanic — 'comment [word] and I'll DM you the link' for a free bootleg — is the cheapest list-building move in the playbook.
q.eg: 312 emails from show sign-ups, 41% open. No SMS yet. Adding a comment-gated bootleg DM funnel in March.

q.label: How many shows have you played in the last 12 months? List them with venue, capacity, your draw, your fee, and whether it was a look gig or an income gig.
q.help: Headliners headline because they move the most tickets, so this table is the most load-bearing thing in the section. Separate look gigs from income gigs explicitly — confusing busy with progress is a named failure. Note which were soft tickets (rooms with a built-in audience) or support slots versus hard tickets people bought specifically to see you, and flag any city outside your home town where people paid to see you, because that is the graduation marker into touring level.
q.eg: 9 shows. Best: 210 paid at a 300-cap room, $600, income. 4 support slots, look gigs. No out-of-town hard tickets yet.

q.label: What is your best-performing release, with its numbers — and why do you think it worked?
q.help: Give the track, the date, the streams, the saves, the playlist or share sources, and what it did for anything downstream (followers, bookings, DMs). Then the harder half: why it may have worked. The instruction is to write what worked and why it may have worked, not just to rank. Also say whether it is on-brief for your current sound and story or an outlier you would not make again — leading with one defining track beats a barrage of bootlegs and edits.
q.eg: 'Night Shift', Sep 2025, 38k streams, 2.1k saves. Worked because the hook was in the first 4 seconds of every clip.

items.h:
3. The single method to make millions

The method is the Kobe Bryant "one choice": identify what would make you great, map a plan that transforms you into it, and make one big non-negotiable choice with extreme commitment and organized execution.

Kobe's regimen as cited: wake at 3, train 4:00–6:00 a.m., home, breakfast, 9:00–11:00, relax, 2:00–4:00, 7:00–9:00. "By year five or six it doesn't matter what kind of work they do in the summer, they're never going to catch up." What Alba emphasizes is the question: Kobe was surprised that many NBA players' dream had already come true just by making it, and they only wanted to stay. Kobe asked a better one — "How can I be the best in the game?" Long-game thinking about becoming the best version of himself, not a hack to beat other players. And the one choice constrained everything: he couldn't stay out late, couldn't eat food that didn't fuel training, couldn't attend every event for friends and family.

The critical nuance: only sitting in the studio all day is like Kobe using four-a-days on only his three-point shot — you become an incredible three-point shooter with the rest of your game missing. He used the extra sessions to round out the whole game.

The 5 key aspects of the music artist game:

  1. The music itself — crucial, must be there, but it's "just shooting." One aspect.
  2. Story, branding and positioning — consistent story and position, content that makes people interested in you outside the music. Concretely: script writing, scene writing, copywriting in your voice, becoming a master storyteller.
  3. Producing — not music production. Everything that goes with the project: executing the vision and bringing it to life. "That's why movies have producers — it's a skill set all its own."
  4. Awareness (advertising) — the psychology of human behaviour, how platforms work, how you show up in your fans' world, whether they'd find enough value to share it. Then: what do you do with awareness once you have it, and how are fans nurtured?
  5. Quality control — high quality visually and sonically. Many artists are consistent but low-quality; you can tell a post was thrown together — "posting to post."

How to attack each. Music: his own "one year, one focus" system. He assumed it would take at least 5 years, more likely 8, to get really good at producing EDM, and gave each year a single focus. Year 1: synthesis and sound design — YouTube all year, sessions with mentors he considered great sound designers, plus sectioned-out time just to twist knobs applying what he'd learned. Year 2: drums — a full year learning to record, design and build strong dance drums. Theory, songwriting and structure came later, deliberately, because sound design and drums were what he loved in the music he was into. Story and brand: if your brand is comedic (like Dillon Francis), take comedy writing courses, read books on how jokes are built, and schedule practices watching comedic films and analyzing which jokes worked. Don Diablo taught himself graphic design because he wanted a visual, design-led brand. Read books on story, branding and script writing — Alba, 20 years in, still does. When hiring a designer or creative director, ask up front whether they'll teach you as you go: "some creatives will absolutely be weird about this, but the good ones and the confident ones may be more than happy to teach." Awareness: study advertising tactics and marketing trends, read or take classes on the psychology of advertising and consumer behaviour, work with mentors from the advertising world — and vet them. Quality control, twofold: study greatness — "you have to know what quality is first to be able to control it" — sitting with the greats asking "Why does this move me? What's great about this?" (that's Kobe watching Jordan tape); and self-exploration, because artists are "broken with jagged edges, soft underbellies," and that sensitivity skews self-critique both ways — holding a finished piece for weeks saying "it's just not there yet," or shipping something weak out of desperation for a hit that affects upcoming gigs. His prescriptions: therapy, meditation, journaling, a life coach, self-help reading. "Taste is everything, but you have to be confident in your taste."

Supporting evidence. Skrillex, pre-fame, ran session after session with established electronic artists worldwide, spending his own money to travel and learn — after working with Noisia his music "felt like it changed light years"; instead of a vacation he spent the same money on a trip to Europe to learn. Jerry Seinfeld has written every single day for 40+ years. Alba's little brother lost 100 pounds in a year, 290 to 190, off one choice: intermittent fasting, tried for a couple of months, then stuck with.

The caveat, stated twice: art isn't sports — but both reward extreme commitment if you want to be the best in the world. Top artists don't complain about what it takes, and "it's never over for them." They're driven for themselves, not for fans — "it's a one-on-one game, you versus you." And: "if you think there's a door closing on you, you're probably the one closing the door."

4. Framing and pricing

Framing is "the borders around an idea" — the setup an idea sits inside. Virgil Abloh's version: the same dented candle is art in a white gallery and trash in a garage, so "design the room, not the candle."

Evidence that framing moves value. The wine studies: subjects told one glass was $100/glass and one $10/glass rated the expensive one better roughly 90% of the time — and when both glasses were secretly different $10 wines, they still preferred whichever was labelled expensive. Brain scans showed taste and experience regions lighting up more under expensive framing. Run on over 5,000 people. They don't just say it tastes better; they experience it as better. Apple puts hidden weights inside iPhone boxes because the mind associates weight with value, and runs a slow unboxing against competitors' cardboard and styrofoam. Gentle Monster builds eyewear stores as art museums with large installations; glasses are inspected, deep-cleaned, then given an elaborate boxing ritual — "not real value, not cost. Story-driven framing value." Luxury retail ritual: being told an item is out of stock but available across town — making it harder to earn changes your relationship to it. Basquiat and Banksy: graffiti carried up to a year in prison in early-'80s New York, but the same act framed as fine art put Basquiat in prestigious galleries; the illegality became framing for coolness.

Types to use deliberately. Pre-framing — the audience arrives primed: known IP, known director, "based on a true story." It's why studios greenlight sequels. Your versions: a trusted label, a co-sign, a known collaborator. Scarcity framing — limited drops; price reflects story and meaning, not production cost. Value framing — environment, packaging, ritual. Emotional framing — composition matched to emotional state: La La Land shoots the early encounters at medium distance like strangers, the Griffith Observatory dance in glowing close-ups, and the breakup and epilogue in wides that isolate them; The Notebook does the same — carnival meeting at medium distance, rain reunion in tight close-up, arguments wide.

What you can charge. The holding story is the clearest pricing lesson on the channel. From his talent-buying days: an artist with viral bootleg remixes. Alba offered a few thousand — the agent said "not enough and not yet." Months later he doubled it; declined again. Four months later he offered $12,000 plus a headlining slot for the debut — accepted. The next day the artist announced a Vegas residency at XS, and the debut LA show sold 2,000 tickets. His own caveat matters: the framing was backed by real marketing, press and ticket demand. Holding out with nothing behind it is just being unavailable.

Lever Move
Show frequency Play your city once a year and it's an annual moment; once a month kills urgency and lowers value
Billing Festival billing size and set times are literal value signals — worth fighting for
Scarcity Limited runs and numbered editions; price for the story, not the blank
Packaging "If it feels expensive, even if it isn't expensive," perception of brand and music changes
Company you keep Attach to cool things and people; collaborations set the room you sit in
The deck As a talent buyer of almost 15 years, when an artist sent a brand guidelines deck, "it immediately made them more expensive in my mind"
Press prep Write key talking points before interviews and podcasts; don't go in blind, keep it candid

The counterweight: "it doesn't matter how good the product is if it's packaged wrong" — but awareness spend cannot rescue a product people don't feel.

5. The 7 habits of millionaire music artists

The dance-music edition. Each habit comes from a firsthand story.

1 — Be yourself. Story: a studio session with Skrillex, fusing intricate dubstep and drum-and-bass sound design with pop and big-room elements. Asked who he was making it for, he said himself — hoping others would like how different it was. Pop-punk background, love of glitchy aggressive sound design, came up around Ed Banger, Justice and indie dance. It wasn't trying to fit in, so by default it stood out; it confused people at first, and when Alba played early Skrillex at Avalon "the dance floor didn't know how to dance to it." Lesson: every trend you chase is already on its way out. Being yourself doesn't mean ignoring the audience; it means trusting that your uniqueness is your biggest advantage, and audiences can feel when something isn't true. Tactic: lay out what you loved past and present — what music were you into as a kid, what scenes still give you that feeling, what's missing from the modern scene? Make your own recipe, then filter constantly: "Is this me? Does this represent the things I care about?"

2 — Be intentional. Story: Chris Lake made big room and electro house that fit the festival circuit; Alba booked him repeatedly at Control in the early 2010s. Around 2014 he began shifting brand and sound toward something more underground and high-taste, completely distancing himself from big room. It didn't catch quickly. In 2017 he appeared on the Howse compilation curated by Skrillex, beginning the new era, built over eight years into a successful community — a rare case of changing sound without changing name, grooming a new audience to understand it. Lesson: unintentional means reactive. The best artists don't just release music, they release statements — mixdown, cover art, content, videos and collaborators as one strategy. Tactic: journal — what career do I really want, what rooms do I want to play, what do I want my music to represent when people talk about me in 5 or 10 years? Then commit: start with the end in mind and reverse-engineer everything toward it.

3 — Make content like a pro athlete practices. Story: James Hype, a Cult client, in Alba's opinion one of the best at content. He doesn't rely on music to carry the weight — he documents tours and sets, shows routines, breaks down setups, interacts with fans, crafts one narrative around the music. High volume, never random: "the content version of a four-day workout for an Olympian." Fans call him "La Machina," the machine — and he'll tell you he built it over years of tiny efforts. He films after a few hours of sleep in three days. Lesson: content is modern visibility — "if no one sees you, they'll never hear the music." Post when it's ugly. Post when it's late. Post when it's uncomfortable. Tactic: start with ONE small habit you can hold for 6 months — even walking to the mailbox daily. Once locked, stack another. Create high stakes if you don't do it. And: don't add habits until the current ones are locked. People get "discipline drunk" and end up with 30 morning-routine items before they can start any.

4 — The brand is everything. Story: in the 2010s, booking Hollywood shows meant submitting offers to agents; for his venue size, offers ran $1,500 to $100K by draw. He submitted an anniversary offer for Dada Life, and around the same time an offer for another artist he'd been in the studio with — a super talented producer with Beatport hits. Pound for pound in the studio they were the same level. One offer was 20 times higher. Dada Life didn't just play music, they put on a show: time-coded visuals, champagne sprays, banana costumes in the crowd, inside jokes, a personality, a world. The other guy had great sets. They were just DJ sets. Lesson: "Your music is the soundtrack, but what about the movie?" Branding sets the room, gives context, controls "the emotional frequency that your name broadcasts." Movie-trailer heuristic: within about 60 seconds you know if it's horror, comedy, drama or action. Your profile should be no different.

5 — You're an entertainer. Story: Steve Aoki, whom Alba toured with early, understood his brand was spectacle — stage diving, raft riding, cake tosses, mic work, crowd surfing. Every performance became a moment. "Whether you loved it or hated it, you knew about it." Lesson: great music gets someone to listen once; a memorable performance gets them back, brings friends, and gets talked about for weeks. Tactic: for bigger posts, shows and press, run four filters — What will make this entertaining? What will make it memorable? Why would people talk about this? If I had no idea who this artist was, would this pique my interest?

6 — Be a leader. Story: a meeting with Alison Wonderland to build a brand around a collaboration. Mid-meeting she stood up, said everyone at the table was way too tall (everyone was 6 foot or over), and did the rest standing and walking around the table. Subtle — but the energy changed. "There was a clear captain in that moment." She collaborates, but her point of view drives visuals, tone, content and music. Lesson: leadership isn't doing everything — it's owning the results, knowing priorities, managing time, choosing collaborations carefully, holding the line when something doesn't align. It also means structure: are projects on a timeline, do you have monthly goals, are you tracking content, outreach, creative growth, are you someone your team would want to follow? "Most artists stall not because of a lack of talent, but because of a lack of direction. There's a leadership gap." Tactic: study leadership, but mostly "get straight in your own head." Therapy is great for this. "You can't lead anything by making excuses."

7 — Sharpen your creative saw. Story: A-Trak, from turntablism and battle roots to collaborations with legends and newcomers, stays sharp because he's always seeking — galleries, other genres, old and new visuals, design, architecture. He doesn't wait for inspiration; he cultivates it. Lesson: creativity is a muscle needing tension, fuel and rest. Go to a lo-fi jazz show and a metal show, watch international films, study old album covers, hang out with fashion designers, ask photographers and filmmakers about process. "The more inputs you have, the more interesting your outputs become." Grow it in discomfort too — writing sessions, collabs you're not comfortable with, sharing ideas with non-musicians. "In a scene moving this fast, your originality is your best currency." Tactic: Alba grew up in small towns with few reference points until he moved to California and started travelling; he became "addicted to curiosity" and now studies art like most guys study sports — runways, museums, design books, books on story. Over 10, 20, 30 years that builds "a vast ocean of references." "That's all art really is — using tools, referencing, and remixing, making new recipes out of the ingredients you've collected." The three drivers of a unique perspective: discovery, creation, and sharing.

Closing warning: most artists won't take these seriously, like the tiny percentage of aspiring athletes who go pro. "Most of the time, the only thing standing between an artist and their next level is fear, habits, or mindset."

6. Twenty years of industry knowledge

Twelve lessons, grouped.

Craft. (1) Make it for you first, and keep it fresh. "If you aren't excited, they aren't excited." He cites Rick Rubin: put the audience last. In sessions with top producers, audience awareness never informed the choices. He splits artists into the system hacker, who reads the current game (followers, streams) and tries to game it for positioning, and the craftsperson, obsessed with getting better through slow hard work — and the craftsperson is always bigger, with more followers, more tickets and more devout fans. On freshness: Diplo has done many styles and all feel like him; artists who stumble onto a beloved sound get stuck because they let the audience drive them in the studio, and it goes stale for the audience because it went stale for them. Refresh by going back to the beginning, re-challenging yourself, travelling, collaborating, experiencing a scene, leaving the studio. (6) Your point of view and taste is everything. You can guess your favourite artist's taste because their POV is clear in the work — which doesn't mean one genre; the greats jump genres and tempos but keep a consistent way they cook. Mid-tier acts look to peers for inspiration: "a great way to get to the middle… absolutely the wrong method to get to the top." Top artists don't; when they see a lot of people doing the same thing, that tells them where not to go. Mid-tier artists are "great mimics" who get "caught chasing the dragon." "Your taste and your unique life experiences are your superpowers." (12) Make it remarkable — meaning "to remark about," not "incredible." When artists say their brand feels broken, he first assesses whether people are impacted and whether it's remarkable; for broken brands the answer is usually no. The majority of the time it's not the music that's the issue — the music is often pretty good; the story and the marketing of that story is what's lacking. Filter everything: will people remark about this?

Business. (3) How many people can you bring to the party? Tickets sold, merch bought, people listening. What does not count: tenure, niceness, ease to work with, how hard you work. In rooms full of "suits" the conversation is metrics and potential revenue — and that's 100% fair; it's their job. Nothing to do with the music, the genre or your personality. To upgrade status, slot times and money: use your creativity to sell more tickets. (4) Perform like you're already a headliner — the Lady Gaga and Dada Life stories above, plus the PSA about being a good opener. (5) The greats are as good at advertising and branding as at making music. Planning benchmarks: the biggest artists run a 24-month strategy plan with tentpoles mapped; mid-tier teams plan 4–6 months, organizing around the release schedule rather than story ("not a terrible strategy, but it'll definitely keep you in the middle"); newer artists often have no marketing calendar at all, forget to post, then rush lackluster content. On adapting: Control was originally promoted with newspaper ads and a street team flyering windshields across LA, then email blasts and text messages, then fully digital ad buys with no street team. Don't be a snob about how the next generation discovers things. (8) Don't quit your day job until it's time. The most-asked question from mid-tier artists in the $2K–$5K per show range. Quit only when music is the primary income and the thing driving your quality of life; once survival enters, stress enters, and that stress doesn't make good music. Arnold Schwarzenegger is the model — a millionaire before he ever acted. He wanted to be Hercules on screen but watched friends take bad roles that damaged their brands just to eat, so he worked as a bricklayer, invested in multifamily real estate, and once secure could choose roles strategically. Most artists don't learn this until $20K+ per show, when the cars, houses and sold-out festivals arrive and don't bring the happiness they worked for. "Find ways to keep the act of making your art pure and not bring the audience or previous successes into the studio with you."

Ownership and money. (7) Save your money or invest in real estate, or both. It won't last forever; every artist has dips, and how you manage them defines how long you stay and where you fall. Top artists spend on things that make themselves or their art better, or on appreciating investments; many bought multifamily real estate. (9) Own your masters — "it's your original art. If you made it, you should own it."

Self. (2) Have a mission. The greats have something to prove to themselves. "A hobby finds its way to the bottom of the totem pole"; a mission sits at the top. He's seen artists with a 103-degree fever throwing up in a bucket behind the DJ booth then performing at a level where nobody knew. (10) Health is paramount. Asked which big artists he knows cold plunge, his answer was all of them — he listed a dozen household-name dance artists. They're biohackers, and roughly 95% don't drink heavily or do drugs. "Tough to do all this hung over." Not a judgment of partiers, just an observation. (The Level 5 version: cold plunging, NAD, stem cells, meditation, clean food, little or no alcohol — body and mind treated like an F1 car. He recommends starting at any level.) (11) Obsession beats talent every time — the one unifying trait of every top artist he knows. Once they master one area they move to another voraciously; they compete with themselves. "If you want to run faster, run with people who are faster than you." Part of the obsession is team building — top artists fill their gaps well, and it's "very rarely about cost and more about the caliber and pedigree of the people they keep around." "You're the sum of the five people you spend the most time with — so if you want to up your game, up your crew."

7. Money mistakes and warnings

Mistake The warning
Not owning your masters The biggest regret of more artists than he can count
Trusting a business manager unvetted "Staggering" how many stories he's heard of business managers stealing from artists — "it happens far more than you'd think"
Quitting the day job early Keep it as long as possible at part-time level; it buys creative freedom. All-in with no safety net produces desperate decisions that compromise the art — and compromised art fails, so you can move backwards
Jumping blind You do eventually have to jump, but "don't jump blindly with zero safety net"
Confusing busy with progress Separate look gigs from income gigs
Not knowing cash flow or burn Not just how much comes in but when it comes and goes, and how long you survive if things slow
One income source A professional with only one big source should diversify or can drop a level fast
Hiring the wrong people to execute Named the #1 mistake in 20 years — no budget for the right people, or moving too fast without vetting. "Perfect script + wrong CGI team = the whole thing crumbles"
Paying for scale you don't need "You don't need a million-dollar budget. You need people who believe in the mission"
Spending on placement instead of story Investing in creative and story beats playlisting or track breakdowns — "this is the stuff that really moves the needle"
Too many small shoots On a major artist they consolidated into "super shoots" capturing many items in one production. At come-up level: don't shoot one thing — shoot as many things as possible that day
Buying the advance, not the deal Expanded An advance is a loan against your own royalties, recouped from your share only. Read term, options, reversion and 360 scope before the number
Going viral for the wrong reason It "can be super damaging" — it attracts the wrong audience, and "one or two viral moments won't sell hard tickets"
Building only on streams "It is easier to build recurring revenue from products than from streams"
Motivation drift If it's only for money or fame, "these games eventually will probably get boring… you'll run out of stairs to climb"

8. Exercises — Phase 6

What "done" looks like: you know who owns every recording and composition you've released, and you're collecting from a PRO. You can state your monthly burn and break-even show size from memory. One non-music aspect of the game is being trained on a schedule this quarter. Every gig is classified look or income. You've priced one scarce thing on story rather than cost, and it sold. One habit has survived six months without willpower. You have a 24-month plan on paper and you'd happily send your brand deck to a talent buyer tomorrow.

Reminder: the contract, tax and financial specifics above combine channel claims with standard industry practice and are general information only, not legal or financial advice. Before signing a label, management, agency or publishing agreement, pay a music lawyer. It's the cheapest money you'll ever spend.

q.label: Write the results you want in the next 12 months, ranked, with the top three circled.
q.help: Results, not goals — a goal feels distant, a result either happened or it didn't. Write them aggressive but realistic, rank them, circle the top three, and make sure everything in your monthly and weekly plan ladders up into those three. This is the sentence you should be able to say without hedging when someone asks what you're chasing this year. Keep them countable: tickets, cities, finished tracks, list size, revenue.
q.eg: Top 3: (1) sell 300 hard tickets in two cities, (2) 6 finished on-brief tracks, (3) 1,000-person email list.

q.label: Lay out the 12-month plan: every tentpole moment by month — releases, show announces, tours, art drops, campaigns — with the guiding idea for each chapter.
q.help: The nested horizon is a 12-month high-level calendar of tentpoles, a 6-month detailed calendar, and a 30-day day-by-day map. Cadence signals level: a major artist runs one and often two 'bomb' moments a month; a touring artist runs 5-6 major strategic moments a year; mid-tier planning at 1-2 months out will keep you in the middle. Each release is a campaign and each campaign is a chapter of roughly 1-2 months with its own guiding idea, so name the idea, not just the date. Leave room to work in-the-moment events into the calendar.
q.eg: Q1: single + numbered shirt drop (chapter: 'night shift'). Q2: self-promoted room #2. Q3: EP. Q4: three-city run.

q.label: State your leverage: what exactly are you bringing to a label that they cannot buy — audience, system, story, catalogue, rights?
q.help: None of the five levels require a label; what they require is leverage and an audience. Cult has had songs signed to majors for brand-new clients purely on a pitch deck with a strong brand story and mood boards — the deck was the leverage. So be concrete: the traction numbers above, the content system that runs without a label's marketing team, the banked catalogue and content runway, the foe hierarchy and belief system, the fully owned masters. One highly connected fan community can easily outperform a much larger disconnected audience — if that is your case, say so with numbers.
q.eg: Owned masters on all 6 tracks, 12 weeks of content banked, a property averaging 40k views, 210 paid hard tickets.

q.label: Write the ask: exactly what you want from a label, what you want the money spent on, and what you will not give up.
q.help: Be specific enough to negotiate from. Name the deal shape you want and the terms you care about: term and options ('one album with four options' is a deal they can extend and you can't exit), reversion of masters, recoupment (recovered from your royalty share only, and recoupment is not repayment — they usually still own the masters), and 360 scope, since a 360 takes a percentage of touring and merch, the two things this playbook says actually pay. Then say what the money is for — video and hero shoots, ads, tour support, a predator on retainer — because spending on creative and story is described as moving the needle more than playlisting or track breakdowns. Get a music lawyer before signing anything.
q.eg: Two-single deal, no options, masters revert in 5 years, no 360. Money goes to two tentpole videos and a paid ads test.

phases.goal: A clear picture of who does what now, which function is pulling you out of your superpower, and who you hire first and when.
phases.intro: You do not need people yet — you need to know which person comes next and why, so you don't spend money you don't have on help you can't use. The #1 mistake in twenty years is hiring the wrong people to execute the vision, either with no budget for the right person or by moving too fast without vetting. Answer these as a hiring plan with triggers and numbers, not as a wish list.

items.h: You don't need people yet. You need to know which person comes next and why, so you don't spend money you don't have on help you can't use.

1. Why you build a team later, not earlier

You cannot hire your way out of not knowing what you want. Step one of the team framework: "Before you hire anyone or make anything, you need to know what result you're actually chasing." And: "The best artist teams are not just hiring random creative people. They're following a specific sequence." The failure isn't lack of talent — it's talent pointed in different directions. "If everyone is talented but moving in different directions, the whole plan breaks."

Chris's verdict after twenty years: the #1 mistake is hiring the wrong people to execute the vision — no budget for the right people, or moving too fast without vetting. A perfect script handed to the wrong CGI team and the whole thing crumbles.

Three more reasons to wait:

  • You can't recruit until you know your superpower. Level 2's shift is to analyse what's working, ask why is money actually coming in, then find collaborators for the rest. Find what you do best, focus on that, and find specialists for everything else.
  • Wearing every hat is the training. At Level 1 you are the team, correctly — someday you'll own the restaurant, so it's good to have washed dishes and worked the bar. A brief also beats a body: contractors execute, they don't originate.
  • Money isn't the gate. "You may not have budget, but you have time and the same amount of hours in a day as your favorite artists." And: "You don't need a massive team. You just need clarity, intention, and consistency."

Who enters when. Level 1 — nobody. Level 2 — your first manager, typically a friend who believes, plus paid collaborators or equity-against-profits for anything pulling you out of your magic skill. Level 3 — booking agent and business manager, plus contracted specialists who audit parts of the business. Level 4 — major scaling, possibly dozens, including people dedicated to owning the audience rather than borrowing it. Level 5 — hundreds of people and multiple companies, with an inner circle (CEO, CCO, CFO, head of strategy, head of operations, head of day-to-day, head of legal and IP) whose decisions are mostly about what not to do.

The eight-step sequence — identical at every level

Stadium act or bedroom come-up; only headcount changes.

  1. Define results — where are you going and why?
  2. Vision — the story, the era, what's happening with the character now.
  3. Production planning — what gets made, who's needed, locations, formats, budget, timelines, assets.
  4. Capture and execute.
  5. Post — editing, colour, graphics, sound, captions, cutdowns, photo selects. "A lot of content is either won or lost in post, because it's where the story actually gets shaped."
  6. Distribution plan — the calendar; where each item goes and why.
  7. Operations — deadlines, approvals, file organisation, budgets, communication, ownership. "This is where a lot of artists and their teams will drop the ball." Creatives make good art and organise badly; this is the predictable failure point.
  8. Analysis and postmortem.

Underneath runs the Ocean's 11 framing: you are Daniel Ocean — the mission is yours, the job is too big alone. The brand manager is Rusty Ryan, making sure every specialist knows their job. The big-moment team is Basher, the explosives guy, whose only purpose is bombs for the brand — "the bigger the bomb, the better."

2. Every role explained

Two models sit underneath. The modern band (five functions): the one-man band is dead — the modern band is Producer (sound architect, usually you), Creative Director (builds the universe), Marketeer (launch strategy, social, calendars, collabs, email, PR), Executive Manager (relationships, doors, budgets, contracts, getting you paid) and Performer (face, voice, soul). It beats a traditional band on four counts: less drama, more speed, higher quality ("probably most important"), and the business is built in from day one. The predator: one person who is Producer + Director + Shooter + Photographer + Editor — the single highest-leverage hire for a smaller artist.

Money note: the agent percentage is the channel's; the rest of the ranges are marked Expanded. All of it is general information about how deals are commonly structured — not legal or financial advice.

Role What they actually do When Cost Good vs. bad
Manager Opens doors, creates opportunities, closes things; runs budgets, contracts, scheduling, makes sure you get paid and the merch order doesn't fall apart Level 2 — usually a friend who believes Expanded commonly 15–20% of artist income; at your level a handshake or profit share Good: a doer, not the type who promises intros that never happen. Bad: artists forget the role, or wait for someone to "reveal themselves once the music pops off," and disrespect it because it doesn't look creative — "that's a huge miss." "A good manager is often the difference between a mid-level artist and a top-tier one."
Creative director Brand story, narrative and visual language for the era; "writes the script on this era's movie"; builds the universe, not just the tour flyer Come-up: only "if you have the budget" — not your first hire Expanded project retainer (Cult sometimes spends half a year on one brand) Their job is not "make cool stuff" — it's understand the story, understand why, build a plan, and make every downstream decision support it. Ask if they'll teach you as you go — "the good ones and the confident ones may be more than happy to teach"
Art director / brand manager Brings artist + CD vision to life and oversees all content-producing teams — creative leads, video (directors, producers, DPs, shooters), photo, designers, motion, editors Once 2–3 people are making things at once Expanded salary/retainer at scale; at your level, you Ideal background: was an artist first (speaks the languages), or a producer type who learned to talk to artists
Designer Expanded Logo/mark, single art, flyers, banners, DSP default images, merch, layout, typography, motion graphics As soon as you have an identity to apply — single art before music videos Expanded per-asset, then a small retainer Typography plus what it's paired with is 80% of your visual identity; "one bad font choice can make all your visuals feel cheap." A-Trak's logo tests: works as a sticker? on a chain? small on the back of a record? on a light pole at 3 a.m.?
Photographer The image bank: press, candid/documentary, campaign Immediately — "as soon as possible" Expanded half/full day rates, or trade Ten photographers given the same mood board return ten different results — pick for the result, not niceness. At scale, brands deliberately rotate photographers
Videographer / DP Shoots content, live capture, videos; the DP owns how a branded piece is shot Same as photographer — same person at your level Expanded day rate or per project Avoid tripods ("sticks") — static cameras distance the viewer. "The camera should feel like a person in the room, not a machine observing it." On the Fred Again viral clip the operator sensed the drop, grabbed the camera and danced — "likely the difference between a good video for social and a viral moment"
Editor Cuts, colour, captions, formats, cutdowns When shooting outpaces editing. Tour teams run 2 remote editors; brand teams 2 freelance editors — more editors = more content = more awareness Expanded per deliverable; the cheapest way to buy back time Judge on story sense, not effects — and on speed, since tour content has a shelf life: don't play a big festival and post about it four months later
Social / community account manager The actual posting; knows this week's platform mechanics. Major level: one each for Instagram, TikTok, YouTube. Touring level: one across all channels plus a junior assistant on cutdowns When posting, not making, is the bottleneck Expanded part-time/contract The harder related hire is the marketeer — harder than a creative director, because producers and CDs run in the same circles while marketeers are data-minded. Look for someone who sees marketing as "a strategic game of chess meets deep social experimentation." "Find people that love marketing the way that you love making art"
Booking agent Sells your show, negotiates fees, expands market access Level 3, once demand exists in cities you don't live in 10–20% of gross performance fee. Example: a promoter offers $2,500, a good agent raises it — you make more, they make more You can book yourself; an agent adds markets and reputation. Across the table sits the talent buyer, who checks your socials — how often you post, what kind, what you're doing now — before making an offer
Publicist / PR Expanded Press placement, interviews, premieres, releases, talking points. Major level: 5 press agents — 2 US, 1 Europe, 1 Asia, 1 Australia, often different agencies per region When you have a real story to place Expanded monthly retainer, minimum term Expanded Good ones ask about your story and foes before your release date. Either way: write talking points before every interview — interviews are "a great tool for storytelling and plot setup"
A&R Expanded The label person who signs artists and shapes the record. Chris has held the role Expanded Not a hire — a relationship, relevant in label talks Expanded none to you Expanded Good ones sharpen what you already are; bad ones want the last thing that worked — "if they want Coke, make more Coke," except what made the Coke exciting was that it was fresh
Label Funds, releases, markets, distributes, usually for rights and a split None of the five levels require a label. They require leverage and an audience; the typical ladder is "fading into the distance" Expanded rights and royalty splits Own your masters — "if you made it, you should own it" — the biggest regret of more artists than he can count. A label helps now mainly as a platform to stand on, alongside official remixes, bootlegs, samples and covers
Business manager The money: accounts, payments, taxes, budgeting, cash flow Level 3, when real money moves Expanded percentage of income or flat monthly The loudest warning on the channel. It is "staggering" how many stories he's heard of business managers stealing from artists — "it happens far more than you'd think." Vet hard. Pair with Level 2 literacy: cash flow (not just how much, but when), monthly burn, and profit gigs vs. "for the look" gigs
Lawyer Expanded Negotiates contracts — label, publishing, management, agency, sync, brand — and protects ownership. At icon level: head of legal and IP Expanded Before signing anything longer than one project Expanded hourly, flat per deal, or a percentage Expanded Good ones specialise in music and explain what you're giving up in plain English

Roles the channel says get missed. Project manager — the master calendar: what happens when, who owns it, which assets must finish before the next move; often part-time, and at come-up level you own it. Data analyst — tracks ticket demand, streaming, engagement, city-by-city fan behaviour and content performance; called out as new and, with brand strategist, one of the two most commonly missing roles at touring level; you own it as a time block. Brand strategist — recon, references, strategic thinking, pitching concepts that stay on brand. Ads manager — given a budget, builds and optimises paid campaigns for shows, products, merch. Copywriter — captions, scripts, press releases. Tour manager — scheduling and A-to-B logistics. VJ / LD — live visuals / lighting director.

3. How to find the right people

Two governing principles: find people who love the vision, and play to strengths, not titles. You evaluate on observed behaviour and demonstrated passion, not résumé.

Where to look. Your existing circle, read for strength — the channel's examples: a roommate who's insane at social media becomes the marketing lead, a cousin who's crazy good with Ableton becomes the producer. Recruit hungry over credentialed — Chris asked a close friend with zero management experience purely on personality fit; they worked side by side for years with a lot of success and the friend went on to manage other successful artists. For photo and video, find 8–10 candidates in your city on social and DM them for rates; same for illustrators and designers. For the marketeer, post on Indeed: "Music group seeks marketing director." For senior collaborators, approach people whose work looks seasoned and fits your vision — Nolan, Spielberg and Wes Anderson reuse the same crew not out of loyalty but because they can execute the vision.

How to vet. Portfolio against your mood board, not in the abstract. Are they a doer or a promiser? Do they love the category, not just you? Will they teach you? For relationship roles, personality read beats experience.

Test projects Expanded. The channel's version is structural — tentpoles get hired video-by-video or contracted across an album, and photographers get rotated. Copy the shape: one paid, small, dated, briefed job before any retainer, graded on three things — hit the brief, hit the date, easy to work with when given notes.

Red flags. No budget for the right person, or moving too fast without vetting. An unresearched business manager. Anyone who wants to change your point of view because of what's trending. Lane collision — a creative director entering can make the manager feel like they're managing two people with two visions, so clarify lanes early, in writing. Rushing and shipping a mediocre brand.

How to brief them — the highest-leverage thing here. Give them a sandbox: "Remember they're artists themselves, but you've now given them a sandbox they can exist in." Over-specify: "The more specific you can be, the better"; "none of them will be bummed on more information." Annotate every reference to call out the exact element, with a written brief. Keep boards tight — too many elements is the most common mood board failure and confuses you as much as them. Write three feeling-objectives per shoot (confident, relatable, powerful), then build the board to deliver them through lighting, styling, set pieces, poses and wardrobe; keep a pose pool, since their guides run 40–50 poses. Send the brand bible — to contractors, to promoters so they know the rules of the brand, and to labels and partners. When Chris was a talent buyer, receiving one "immediately made them more expensive in my mind." Free blank template: comment "cult playbook."

How to keep them. Pay on time. Recruit to the cause, not the invoice — these are experienced professionals, not friends: you don't motivate them by grinding them harder, you communicate vision and trust them to do their job. "Your skill isn't just what you can do, it's how well you rally the troops." Hire for caliber and pedigree over cost. In any contractor relationship the exchange is money on one side and time on the other. And: "You're the sum of the five people you spend the most time with — so if you want to up your game, up your crew."

q.label: Map the five functions of the modern band — Producer, Creative Director, Marketeer, Executive Manager, Performer. Who does each one right now, how many hours a week does it take, and is it your magic skill?
q.help: The one-man band is dead; the modern band is these five functions, and at come-up level all of them are you plus maybe a manager. Two functions must exist no matter what: making the content, and managing the flow of the content. You personally own project manager (the master calendar — what happens when, who owns it, which assets must finish before the next move) and data analyst (a time-blocked study of performance). Where a function has no human, it becomes a named calendar block, because unnamed work doesn't happen. Include anyone real: a friend managing, a photographer you use, an editor.
q.eg: Producer: me, 10 hrs (magic skill). Creative Director: me, 3 hrs (not). Marketeer: nobody — Tue 7-9pm block.

q.label: Which function most pulls you out of your superpower? That's hire #1 — name the role, what they'd own, and what changes the week they start.
q.help: Find what you do best, focus on that, and find specialists for everything else. For most smaller artists the answer is the predator — one person who is Producer, Director, Shooter, Photographer and Editor in one body, named the single highest-leverage hire and the come-up artist's first investment priority. If you can only pay for one thing this year, pay for repeated days with this person and make each one a super shoot. Write what they own end to end, not a task list, and write the lane agreement alongside it: what you decide, what they decide, what you decide together.
q.eg: Predator. Owns capture and post for one super shoot a month, 20+ assets. I stop editing and get 6 hours a week back.

q.label: Write the trigger for that hire: what has to be true — money, volume, or a date — before you make it?
q.help: Roles arrive in a sequence. Level 1 is nobody. Level 2 is your first manager, usually a friend who believes, plus paid collaborators or equity against profits for anything pulling you out of your magic skill. Level 3 brings the booking agent (10-20% of gross performance fee, once demand exists in cities you don't live in) and the business manager (vet hard — it is 'staggering' how often business managers steal from artists). An editor gets hired when shooting outpaces editing; a social manager when posting, not making, is the bottleneck. Make the trigger a number and a date you'd actually act on.
q.eg: Predator retainer starts when live income clears $1,500/mo for two months, or Jun 1 — whichever comes first.

q.label: List 8-10 photographers/videographers in your city, DM every one for rates, and log rate, turnaround and portfolio fit against your mood board.
q.help: The stated method is exactly this: find 8-10 candidates in your city on social and DM them for rates, and do the same for illustrators and designers. Judge portfolio against your mood board, not in the abstract — ten photographers given the same board return ten different results. Vet on whether they're a doer or a promiser, whether they love the category and not just you, and whether they'll teach you as you go. Then run one paid, small, dated, briefed test project before any retainer, graded on three things: hit the brief, hit the date, easy to work with when given notes.
q.eg: Name / IG / $400 half day / 5-day turnaround / board fit 8-10: strong on-camera flash, weak in low light.

items.h:
4. The next-phase marketing team

Three buckets hold at every level; only headcount changes. (1) Tour content — short shelf life, turn and burn. (2) Day-to-day brand content — the ongoing show. (3) Big tentpole / brand-story moments — music videos, cinematic tour trailers, stunts, pop-ups, key performance moments, hero shoots, short-film-style branded videos.

Major level. Tour: tour manager, 2 videographers who also shoot photo and edit, 2 remote editors taking footage off the road. Brand: a project manager assigned only to content; a creative lead/content strategist pitching ideas; one go-to DP; rotating freelance photographers; 2 freelance editors; freelance copywriters; community managers, one each for Instagram, TikTok, YouTube; an ads manager; a data analyst; a PR agency. Tentpoles: 1–2 "bomb" moments a month, and 99 out of 100 times the big ones go to an outside agency — hired video-by-video or across an album — always with internal CD and brand manager keeping it on-brand.

Touring level. Tour crew is four people: artist, tour manager, visual person (VJ or LD), and one dedicated content person — the predator. Brand side: creative direction and story; freelance photo, video, design and motion as needed; an ad or PR agency as needed; one community account manager across all channels plus a junior assistant on cutdowns. Tentpoles drop to 5–6 major moments a year.

Two cost levers used on a major artist — copy both at zero scale. (1) Better sequencing: define what happens at which stage, better approvals, better data, better cross-team communication. (2) The annual budget view: they found they were doing far too many tiny shoots and consolidated into "super shoots" capturing many items in one production.

Come-up level — you. It's you, or you plus a manager. Two functions must exist: making the content, and managing the flow of the content. Priority one is finding your predator — and when you shoot, don't shoot one thing, shoot as many things as possible in that day. Dial in pre-production so you "get a ton of meat off the bone." Personally own project manager and data analyst. And choose ONE place to make and distribute content, focus there until it's working, then expand.

5. What to do when you can't afford anyone

Cover the five functions with one body. Producer and Performer are you. Creative director, marketeer and executive manager are calendar blocks with names, because unnamed work doesn't happen. "If it's on the calendar, it usually gets done."

Buy the one role that multiplies everything. The predator. If you can only pay for one thing this year, pay for repeated days with this person and make each one a super shoot.

Trade instead of paying. The template is Chris's own party. Attempt one: he copied the local model, became his own street team, went out every night for weeks handing out thousands of flyers — and got 10 people outside his friend group, about 40 in a 150-cap room. Attempt two: an art show with music in his downtown LA loft, stacked with people who each carried relationships — a dozen local artists, 24 DJs across multiple rooms including two known headliners, bartenders and barbacks with their own friend groups, a clothing company doing live screen printing with limited shirts, and a paid flyer feature in LA Weekly. Break-even was 150 people at $8. Result: almost 800 people. The principle: "cool people know cool people" and "not more expensive, more creative." Practically: shoot with a photographer building their book for usage and credit; swap edits with another artist; give a designer a merch cut; co-host a night so four small audiences become one room.

Outsource the diagnosis even when you can't outsource execution. The thing you can't do alone is see yourself. In the superpower process a third party reviews all your notes and looks for patterns where you're strong by your own account and others' — their job is to "define what's already there." Chris had the whole playbook and still made every mistake on his own project: with clients he was a coach with a bird's-eye view, with himself he brought baggage and perfectionism. Cheap substitute: the ten-friend survey, pushing past the history answer with "minus obligation and history, why are we still friends?"

Build the army with no payroll. Three factions: mentors and guides (DM the one you've been meaning to contact), creative collaborators, and mental fighters (workout partner, therapist, meditation, a book you'll actually read). Then allies: people who celebrate risk, push you when you're playing small, and stand with you when a crowd turns. Wrong-tribe markers: people obsessed with your streaming numbers, people who secretly resent your success, people pushing you toward something because it's popular.

Never outsource: your point of view and taste ("your taste and your unique life experiences are your superpowers"); the on-brand/off-brand call — the magic in the channel's favourite anecdote is the artist saying within seconds, "No, sorry. It's not my brand"; quality control — you know deep down what your best is, and the common failure is shipping something you know isn't it; leadership — "leadership isn't doing everything yourself, it's owning the results"; making the art for yourself first — "if you aren't excited, they aren't excited"; and your relationship with your community.
6. Exercises — Phase 7

What "done" looks like — Phase 7

  • You can name the one result you're chasing this year without hedging.
  • You know which function you own and which one you'd buy first if $1,000 appeared.
  • You have a brand bible a stranger could execute from, and you've sent it to someone.
  • You've run one paid test project and made a keep/don't-keep call.
  • You have a predator, or three named candidates with rates.
  • Nobody on your list is there because they were available.

phases.goal: A colour-coded week you actually run, one focus for the year, and one dated public commitment with a real stake behind it.
phases.intro: Every framework in this playbook fails in the same place: execution. The diagnosis is blunt — you don't have a creativity or drive problem, you have an organisation problem, and it's leaving 80%+ of your output on the table. These answers are mostly for you and stay out of the brand book, but they are the reason the rest of it will or won't happen.

items.h: Every framework in this playbook fails in the same place: execution. This phase is the person doing it.

1. The mindset shifts at each level

The real boss at every stage is your own previous operating model.

Level The shift
1 Sacrifice — friend time, streaming, the summer blockbuster. Most people who never graduate fail here, on conviction. Plus being okay with hearing no: send it out, expect silence, assess → analyse → learn → try again.
2 Be open to help and scaling (pay collaborators or give equity against profits). Hone in on your superpower — you can't know who to recruit until you know what you do best. Self-belief and the jump — you have to jump eventually, but not blindly with zero safety net.
3 Singular focus; kill shiny object syndrome. In his mid-20s Chris was waiting tables, running a promotion business, co-owning a clothing store, freelancing as a designer and DJing to fund it. Valentino Khan told him, endearingly, "I only have Valentino Khan." If it doesn't serve the level-up, it falls down the totem pole. Plus attention to state — social shows crowds and planes and hides airport food, three-star hotels and no sleep regimen.
4 Abandon old views on getting things done — doing everything yourself was your strength, now it's a hindrance. Time becomes more valuable than money. Get a coach. Defeat your old self: "Who do I need to become to operate at this level?" Jimmy Iovine didn't love business but forced himself to learn it so he could defend his creative ideas.
5 A different suit — people wait to be told where the battle is. Never slip into other people's jobs. Bigger swings — fear never leaves; you set it aside and decide. Health as performance engineering. From a results-driven mind to a mind of devotion around growth.
Bonus The internal climb. Icons frequently describe emptiness at the summit; the next mountain is internal — and you can climb it at any level.

Three that span all of it: "consistency beats hunger every time," "hard work beats talent when talent stops working," and "You're no longer just an artist. Now you're leading a company."

2. Time management and procrastination

The diagnosis

You don't have a creativity or drive problem, you have an organisation problem — and it's leaving 80%+ of your output on the table. The differentiator between artists who go from zero to millions is systems, not talent.

Two reasons you haven't built them. You're borrowing the wrong systems — entrepreneur and athlete routines are built for predictable lives; yours isn't. "Your habits can be consistent even if your schedule is inconsistent." And organising feels weird if you're creative — it felt weird to Chris too, a chronic procrastinator who made procrastination a game, lagging then trying to hit "the game-winning buzzer shot." Do it anyway.

The deeper diagnosis: open-ended projects with no hard deadline die. He started an EP he hoped Mad Decent would release. No formal deal, no deadline. Because he revered the label he'd get near a cohesive EP, decide "this isn't good enough," burn it down and restart — repeatedly. The EP never came out and the relationship cooled. Meanwhile brutal turnarounds on major-label club remixes — sometimes a week, sometimes 48 hours — changed his career, because "you don't have time to overthink things."

The three tools

  1. Set a date for an action-inducing event — something that will happen and forces you to create for it. His hack with a modest following: post "new remix coming this Friday" with no remix started and no idea what he'd remix. Those bootlegs became the most awareness-generating work he ever did: tens of millions of plays, support from artists he respected, international bookings. Doja Cat gave herself 30 days to write a whole album to avoid overthinking, and won the Grammy for Best Rap Album. The deadline can be invented; something or someone must actually hold you accountable.
  2. Define the stakes — money; time (Four Thousand Weeks — a lifespan is roughly 4,000 weeks); or embarrassment. Tony Robbins' mechanic: give a friend an unflattering photo with instructions to post it if you miss the date. "One creates real urgency to commit and one doesn't."
  3. Create the work-back — a schedule built in reverse from the end date, with strict dated deadlines on every prerequisite. He planned this channel as a 4-month work-back; it took 5 months, and without it he estimates 8 or 9. The chain: launch in August with 12 weeks of videos shot and edited → handles and distribution set up → videos edited → videos shot and artists interviewed → artists coordinated to the studio → pitch deck → brand finalised → mood boards and ideation → big-picture vision meetings. "An instruction manual of the game you're about to play."

The exception: he believes in the "just start" method. Don't over-plan early — create, make, experiment. The work-back applies once you get serious and want to bring it to a professional level.

The time-audit method

Results, not goals — a goal feels distant; a result either happened or it didn't. Write the results you want in the next 12 months, rank them, circle the top 3. Repeat for this month (every item must ladder up to a top yearly result), this week, and daily including weekends — before doing anything, name the day's top 3. Two standing commitments: one 2-hour self-review every 3 months and 1 hour a week to block the coming week.

Before scheduling anything, run the leverage question: does this need doing at all, and does it need to be me doing it? High-output people keep what they enjoy plus what makes them effective and give the rest away. Related, from a Jay Shetty podcast: efficient is clearing your list and enjoying the checkboxes; effective is moving the ball downfield toward the bigger goals.

Deep work blocks

Know thyself first — pressure or steady chipping? Habitual or free-form? Morning, midday or evening? Home, outdoors, or somewhere populated like a coffee shop? Rhythm comes from the answers; blocking comes after.

Group similar tasks so "your brain is playing in the same sandbox" — don't bounce call → creative → call → errand. Block everything, not just work: sleep, meals, breaks, walks, meditation, school runs, bedtime stories. Colour-code it — his friends-and-family colour is green, and he checks for "a healthy amount of green every week." Granularity: 30-minute blocks mornings and evenings, 15-minute increments during the day — 15 forces compression, because something you'd block 30 for may take 15. His company converted internal 30-minute meetings to 15-minute meetings; use 10-minute meetings where you can. Plan the week Sunday evening or Monday morning, before any work.

The creative exception — what separates this from business time-blocking. If inspiration strikes, push one of the day's top 3 to tomorrow and chase it, as long as the week's total gets done. Red flag: if that happens constantly and weekly results slip week after week, reassess — "if all you're doing is digging for potential gold and not hitting other results, you may need to reassess." For off-plan ideas, the capture rule: spend 15–20 minutes getting the bare bones down, save it, return to plan. Talk to your creative brain like a child — "yes, but not right now, is better than saying no."

The 80% rule: "If I accomplish 80% of what I laid out for the week, that week is a win." He admits he's far from perfect and often misses blocks. Run it daily for four weeks to build the habit. Learn to say no by pre-blocking friends, family and fun, then telling people you're already committed — even if the commitment is watching Netflix with your wife.

Real rhythms

Three client rhythms: (A) two weeks making music a few hours a day, bring 1–2 ideas to finished, pick one, then two weeks making its content. (B) the banking method: 3 months writing to create 6 months' worth of music, then 3 months making content for that stretch. (C) Mondays/Wednesdays/Fridays music, Tuesdays/Thursdays/Saturdays content.

The music system runs three buckets — Creating / Working On / Finishing — at one of three cadences: daily (6 hours: 2 new, 2 finishing, 2 moving tracks downfield), weekly (Mon create, Tue finish, Wed–Thu move downfield), or monthly (week 1 create, weeks 2–3 flesh out demos, week 4 finish). Warning: don't put finishing at the bottom of the totem pole — artists who prioritise finishing over creating have far greater output. Target 6 completed original tracks or remixes in a 6-month guiding-idea window.

Chris's own week: Monday most fresh, deep creative work, zero calls; Tuesday–Wednesday calls and agency work; Thursday pre-production; Friday productions; weekends family and recharge.

A realistic week with a day job Expanded

Assembled from the channel's own components. About 12–14 hours.

Day Block Purpose
Mon 60–90 min Create — new ideas only, inside the guiding idea
Tue 60–90 min Finish — one track moves toward done
Wed 45–60 min Capture — shoot to your content property format
Thu 60–90 min Move downfield — working tracks get one step better
Fri 30 min Post + engage, then off
Sat 3–4 hrs Super block — the month's shoot day, or a long finishing session
Sun 60 min + green Plan the week (top 3), 15 min data review, then family and recharge

Non-negotiables: name tomorrow's top 3 before bed; one full green block weekly; the quarterly 2-hour review; and stack shoots into one super shoot a month rather than five small ones.

3. Core tools

Planning. Colour-coded Google Calendar as the master surface, paired with Asana (tasks live there and move onto the calendar by priority); the work-back; the action-inducing event; nested horizons (10-year, 5-year, 1-year, monthly focus, weekly focus); nested content calendars (12-month with tentpoles → 6-month detailed → 30-day day-by-day); the free content calendar template (comment "cult calendar").

Brand and creative.
